styles.visual_cues: Use a column grid, baseline alignment, repeated spacing, asymmetric composition, and generous negative space. Set left-aligned sans-serif type with clear size hierarchy; use black and white with restrained accent colors and grid-aligned photography. Animate along layout axes and settle elements on shared alignment points without disrupting reading order.

tech.implementation: Build typography with CSS Grid and loaded fonts. Align SVG geometry to the baseline grid; animate position, scale, and cropping.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A precise grid gives type, images and negative space a shared rhythm. Motion reveals how each element aligns and where one intentional break matters.

## Visual identity
Make the grid visible through aligned type, pictures and reference rules. Establish one clear order, then let a change of scale or placement show which comparison or statement matters.

## Surfaces and construction
Use a visible baseline and column grid with consistent margins and gutters. Build headlines, rules and picture masks on these coordinates so a crop can reveal a complete aligned group.

## Colour roles
Separate informative ink from the signal accent so its intended exception is apparent. Keep a disciplined neutral field and one accent tied to a change in hierarchy.

Example palette. white field #FFFFFF, black type #000000, red signal #D32F2F.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved copy flush left on the same baseline grid as the figures. Use weight and scale for hierarchy and keep labels close to the values they name.

## Timing and movement
Bring in the grid or reference column first. Introduce the headline on a column edge, then reveal supporting data from that same alignment. Give a dense comparison a settled reading pose before changing the grid. Use a clipped reveal on the leading edge of a new block. Use an abrupt removal when a comparison calls for a clean before-and-after, and let the surviving grid explain what left.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use the grid to compare cause and effect in a fixed spread. Pan exactly one column, quarter-turn into another reading angle, pull back to a wall of outputs or close in on one module. Extend the grid beyond the sheet, split into equal cases or scroll down a column. Give a deliberate exception room to stand out. Use sharp cuts, measured wipes, camera shifts and layout changes.

## Sound options
If enabled, use memory-friendly rhythmic spacing and spot the single hierarchy change rather than each element. With sound enabled, use a few short cues at actual structural changes.

## Characteristic actions
- Establish two baselines, bring several parts into alignment and shift one label for deliberate emphasis.
- Reveal a row, reflow a spread or open a bank of equal cells to compare outcomes.

## Review checks
Check the headline and smallest label at delivery size. On a direct seek, rules, labels and the columns they describe should already share a baseline.

## Implementation tools
Use shared layout coordinates and animate between defined grid states. Use a shared grid for text and geometry with explicit transforms between stable aligned layouts. Define a single column unit, gutter and baseline increment. Anchor each animated rectangle to named starts and spans so a wipe can reveal a whole column or end at the intended divider.

## Project choices
Choose a comparison, an archive wall or information that reads cleanly as a typographic sequence. Build a title sequence, diagram or editorial layout. Preserve the same grid even through asymmetric compositions.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Simple plane geometry explains relationships through scale and position. A spare palette and clear grid make each shape’s role legible as it moves.

## Visual identity
Let flat geometric shapes explain a structural relationship. Assign each circle, bar and plane one role, such as marking a pivot, measuring length or showing the weight that moves it.

## Surfaces and construction
Use matte shapes, sharp joins, fine ruled marks and visible construction lines. Give each primary primitive a visual job, such as a circle for a pivot or a rectangle for a change in length. Set guide marks on the same geometry as the mechanism so the resulting explanation can be read from the drawing.

## Colour roles
Reserve dark ink for fine marks and let the ground separate similar hues. Assign a small set of strong colours to geometric roles. Keep one clear neutral ground.

Example palette. white ground #FFFFFF, black outlines #000000, red shape #D62828, yellow shape #F2C230, blue shape #164B9B.

## Lettering and captions
If the idea calls for text, let a label align with its shape's edge or travel on its axis. Hold the shape and label together long enough to establish their relationship.

## Timing and movement
Let a circle roll in contact with its guide, a bar extend from a fixed endpoint and a block settle at a visible stop. Show the completed geometric relationship before introducing the next operation.

## Framing and viewpoint
Start with a stable composition and push gently as the arrangement resolves. Move or pivot the group when its role changes. Use a solid colour field to match into a new image, track construction lines in a lateral whip, or leave the old grid behind as its parts become the next layout. Vary the entry by scene.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, give a completed alignment or meaningful shape contact a short, dry click. When music is enabled, fit the joined shapes to phrase accents and let smaller guide marks appear between them.

## Characteristic actions
- Repeat a primitive, align the copies into a row and bring the row into a larger functional arrangement.
- Roll a point into a line, turn an incline into a ruler or keep a ghost of the previous measurement.

## Review checks
Check the origin and contact point through each move. Check that changes in size reflect the intended relation and that a line hits its tangent without a visible gap.

## Implementation tools
Place primitives on shared alignment lines with consistent centres. Derive shape area from the value when quantities are encoded.

## Project choices
Try a lever, a chain of additions or a comparison that can be drawn from simple primitives. Keep the same scale or grid through adjacent views when the viewer needs to compare lengths or areas.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Documentary fragments, emphatic type and diagonals make each edit part of the argument. The print layout controls how the eye moves from claim to evidence.

## Visual identity
Set an assertive diagonal against blocks of print and photographic evidence. Give the main claim and its consequence distinct positions and connect them with a shared direction or a meaningful cut.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep graphic bands, picture windows, cut-outs and ruled document fragments on one coherent printed composition.

## Colour roles
Use strong value changes to separate claims from evidence and give each accent a consistent role. Use two dominant print values and a restrained editorial accent connecting cuts.

Example palette. warm print paper #F4ECD8, near-black ink #171717, red editorial accent #C72C2C.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved headlines on the main diagonal or perpendicular to it. Keep supporting copy on a stable axis when the larger shapes move across frame.

## Timing and movement
Send the diagonal scaffold in first, then bring blocks and type in along its direction. Let the largest form land with a firm stop before smaller counter-movements complete the composition.

## Framing and viewpoint
Cut a printed grid between opposing entry directions, values or shapes. Accelerate only while footage stays legible and hold a frozen comparison or document long enough to read. Use a coloured strip sweep, an annotation circle that becomes an opening, a slamming piece, a brief photographic flash, hard value cut or a closer crop of the same still. Build layouts from banners, captions, vertical titles, dated strips, grids, splits, annotated freezes, enlarged documents, stepwise process windows, layered exposures, diagrams drawn from documents and stacked footage. Give the outcome a quiet, readable frame. Fit cutting and holds to the project’s duration and any approved music.

## Sound options
If sound or music is enabled, use a few cuts on phrase accents while factual copy stays readable. When enabled, use different sounds for paper cuts and footage, with room for the selected score or speech.

## Characteristic actions
- Reframe a photo cutout within a diagonal mask and carry one axis into a new arrangement.
- Mark a real line of a document, lift its values into a chart or bring two disparate shots together on a matching shape.

## Review checks
Inspect the crossing where diagonals, type and image crops come together. Make sure the intended reading order survives the strongest tilt.

## Implementation tools
Use local masks for evidence windows and a shared edit schedule for transitions and annotations. Use stable clipping paths and independent photo planes, with cuts at matched visual geometry.

## Project choices
Choose a sourced account, document-led comparison or consequence revealed through montage. Organise a sequence around one editorial relationship. Use materials appropriate to the project. Choose a claim whose consequence can be seen in a changed crop, measurement or repeated object. Use supplied photos only where the image itself provides evidence for that change.

sources.style_evidence: Forceful diagonal crimson band, radial wedges, and a restricted red/black/off-white palette with bold type set on the slash, as in seconds 6–8.
sources.palette_lesson: The author's example palette is a grainy near-black ground, warm off-white type and one saturated crimson accent. Red builds up in stages: first a separator dot, then low-value radial rays, then a full-width flat band, and finally a stamp badge. What defines the style is not the black or the specific red. It is three things: a single dominant dark or neutral ground, one high-chroma signal color kept for punctuation and the hero band, and type with the strongest value contrast. The background never competes, because the sunburst rays sit close to the ground's value. Type that sits on the accent band stays the paper/off-white tone, so the band reads as a backing plate rather than as the canvas. For new subjects, change the ground and the accent while keeping these roles: for example, a deep indigo/ink-navy ground with a signal-orange band, a cold slate/graphite ground with an acid-yellow band, a deep forest or bottle-green ground with a vermilion band, or an inverted light warm-gray paper ground with black type and a cobalt band. Keep one accent hue, keep the rays within roughly 10–15% of the ground's value, and check the contrast of off-white type on the band.

> A few tilted planes use scale, balance and empty space to make an abstract composition feel active.

## Visual identity
Let asymmetry and scale create a clear point of tension. Balance a few tilted shapes on an open field. Use a dominant angled mass, a smaller counterweight and a largely open ground. Let the space between their edges show whether the arrangement is balanced or under tension.

## Surfaces and construction
Use sharp edges and visibly separate tilted planes. Give each plane a crisp edge and constant thickness.

## Colour roles
Use value to separate planes that almost meet. Break the black and white field with one primary accent at the point of tension.

Example palette. white field #FFFFFF, black planes #000000, red point of tension #C92B2B, yellow option #E8BE30, blue option #2453A0.

## Lettering and captions
Use the empty field or a stable edge for approved lettering. Keep the text level unless its rotation is part of the same geometric event.

## Timing and movement
Hold the initial balance between planes before changing it. Pivot one tilted block around a visible corner, let the counterweight slide, and settle with enough clear space to read the new balance.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the frame fixed so angles and distances supply the movement. Use a square-on view so rotation remains a property of the planes.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, place a dry accent when the frame reaches its new balance. Leave the empty field quiet as the tilted plane travels so the arrival reads as the change.

## Characteristic actions
Pivot a tilted bar around its crossing while a smaller square counterbalances it. Use a clean held pose afterwards so the shift in space and weight can be read.

## Review checks
Inspect the start, crossing and final balance. Keep clear separation where a plane grazes another edge unless contact is the point of the shot.

## Implementation tools
Use closed vector shapes in local plane coordinates. Define each pivot at a visible corner or crossing and key the angle and translation separately to control clearances.

## Project choices
Vary weight, orientation and number of planes with the subject. Vary size, orientation or proximity while keeping the number of forms small.

> Strong horizontal and vertical divisions hold flat rectangles in balance. Colour punctuates the structure as panels expand, contract and meet.

## Visual identity
Let the orthogonal grid determine how each field changes. Compose colour rectangles inside a grid of horizontal and vertical rules.

## Surfaces and construction
Use flat rectangles and continuous horizontal or vertical rules. Compute the adjoining edges from the same coordinates so opaque blocks share clean corners as their proportions change.

## Colour roles
Use neutral fields to separate the stronger colours. Reserve red, yellow and blue for chosen cells. Leave enough white to reveal the grid.

Choose an expansion, division or change of emphasis inside the grid. Move the grid density or cell proportions to fit the frame.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Stepped geometry, metallic inlays and formal symmetry give openings and reveals the precision of a machine.

## Visual identity
Build an architectural sequence around a centreline. Use stepped frames, narrow metallic edges and one strong emblem to give each new opening a recognisable destination.

## Surfaces and construction
Build hard-edged relief from stepped masks and use banded reflections on raised metal. Use a narrow highlight band and a separate shadow band for engraved gold. Put that finish on bevels, metalwork and bulbs, and keep the flat dark ground quiet.

## Colour roles
Keep the dark field quiet so bright inlay and the hero accent have distinct roles. Reserve metal for raised edges and steps. Use darker body tones between gold accents.

Example palette. charcoal body #151515, ivory lettering #F6EEDC, antique gold inlay #B99A57.

## Lettering and captions
Fit approved titles into a symmetrical frame and keep small copy out of bright gold banding. Extend or fold markers symmetrically around the line of text. Use distinct lettering for a large architectural title and much smaller inlaid labels.

## Timing and movement
Sequence a reveal outwards from the centreline. Step character poses on their own cadence and move mechanical parts smoothly. Light paired bulbs in a count and give each a short ignition before it settles.

## Framing and viewpoint
Hold a strong centreline. Open and close a view with paired gates, or let an off-axis start settle into symmetry. Use an extreme low view for scale, a cutaway for progress through a building and a revolving overhead for patterned crowds. Close in on dials or badges when the reading matters, skim a sign obliquely as its letters light, then pull from the detail to the skyline. Match related silhouettes across cuts. Bring a featured character close enough for their reaction to read.

## Sound options
If music is enabled, carry its phrase into the reveal and leave the final emblem room. If enabled, separate a gate's mechanical clack from the lighter ignition of its bulbs.

## Characteristic actions
- Open nested stepped frames from a central axis and use a mirrored sweep to uncover the focal mark.
- Try a paired gate, a travelling marquee light or a circular badge that becomes the next location.

## Review checks
Inspect symmetry at the strongest pose, then check metal banding and dark detail in motion. Make a lamp overshoot visible without washing out the engraved lines next to it. Both sides meet on one axis and the ornament leaves the subject legible. Watch the centreline through a transition and protect faces from the brightest ornament.

## Implementation tools
Key the paired panels from mirrored pivots and drive the reflection separately from their silhouette. Build nested vector masks with mirrored offsets and keep metal glints in separate clips.

## Project choices
Choose rays, concentric steps or inlay based on the subject's structure. Vary the motif with fanned rays, graduated steps or fine inlay. Preserve the centred reveal.

> An economical arrangement of type and forms directs the reader through one clear sequence of ideas.

## Visual identity
Show a clear reading sequence through the hierarchy of information. Use simple forms and alignment to organise one clear reading sequence. Use a modular grid to clarify sequence or comparison. Keep one continuous margin across adjacent blocks so a changed image or heading is read as part of the same structure.

## Surfaces and construction
Use clean typography, measured spaces and reproducible shapes. Build flat panels from repeated spacing units and crisp rules.

## Colour roles
Give one accent a navigational purpose. Apply the accent to the active idea. Let size and placement establish the other levels.

Example palette. background #FAF8F2, foreground #202020, accent 1 #235DA8.

## Lettering and captions
Keep the approved hierarchy visible through size, weight and alignment. Tie page numbers or labels to the same margins before and after a swap.

## Timing and movement
Establish a fixed layout before swapping its contents. Move one block across the grid or swap it on a shared edge, then wait for the new reading order to register.

## Framing and viewpoint
Treat the design grid as a fixed camera and reframe on complete layouts. Use wide reading views and crop closely only for actual detail.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, mark the change of hierarchy when the new lead block settles. Let its related rules and labels move into alignment without separate cues.

## Characteristic actions
Carry a key label along a shared baseline into the next information block. At the stop, swap its supporting image or value while keeping the old and new layouts easy to compare.

## Review checks
Check that each panel swap preserves the reading order and margins. In the final frame test whether the main heading reads before its supporting material.

## Implementation tools
Set group alignment from grid units instead of individual offsets. Set type and rule positions on a shared grid and key each change to that grid.

## Project choices
Choose a spread, row or comparison that benefits from ordered alignment. Use posters, instructions or diagrams with the same functional spacing logic.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A miniature arrangement of playful patterned solids feels tactile through firm shadows, deliberate colour and small changes in position.

## Visual identity
Use playful geometric furniture, signs or objects with believable contact on a small set. Give each busy pattern a boundary so a simple silhouette can carry the main action.

## Surfaces and construction
Use a small set of flat tones per surface, contact shadows, a fine shaded dot screen and clean outer edges.

## Colour roles
Group saturated hues by location and use light changes to distinguish times of day. Use high-contrast pattern planes in small areas and give the main object a solid colour. Assign one dominant hue to each large plane and a second to its smaller marks. Use the cast shadow or a neutral edge to separate adjacent planes where two saturated colours meet.

Example palette. background #FFF6E8, foreground #202039, accent 1 #ED718E, accent 2 #3DBAB1, accent 3 #F4C64F.

## Lettering and captions
Put approved lettering on a stable colour field or a solid shape. Use patterned motifs as borders and keep them out of the letter interiors.

## Timing and movement
Let individual curves, wedges and squiggles arrive on different paths, then settle into a common layout. Hold the busiest moment long enough for the main object to read between accents. Give a patterned moving object a quick compression on arrival and a short rebound. Keep the pattern registered to the surface through the squash.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use slow high drift, a turning overhead or a held three-quarter composition. Travel along a cutaway, move closer to an action or track a vehicle along its route. Ease towards stillness when a view must read. Find clear paths around geometry by raising the view before travelling. Let the frame resize, a material or light wave pass, or a section open to connect scenes.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a dry tap for contact and let the selected rhythm guide panel entrances. If sound is enabled, give small prop motions restrained contacts and keep background loops unobtrusive.

## Characteristic actions
- Pass an accent through two patterned planes before docking it into a three-dimensional composition.
- Move a small vehicle through layers, open a pattern-cut section or send a shifting light across the set.

## Review checks
Check the noisiest overlap at thumbnail size. Keep the main block distinct when decorative shapes touch or pass behind it.

## Implementation tools
Store repeat patterns in object space and keep camera geometry, motion and cast shadows synchronised. Project pattern UVs onto separate faces. Animate the assembly without sliding textures.

## Project choices
Choose a block, park or compact machine with enough distinct activity to reward a held wide. Combine geometric blocks, arches or plinths. Vary the pattern scale between objects while keeping each face stable.

sources.palette_lesson: The background changes on purpose with each life stage, and that is the main lesson. The opening is near-black navy for an abstract, pre-life pulse. Childhood uses naturalistic sky-teal, pale green and green with a warm yellow sun. Adolescence uses a saturated indigo-to-magenta gradient with a striped warm sun and neon cyan, yellow and orange confetti. Adulthood uses desaturated stepped greys with only small red and brown accents. These specific hues are this author's choices for this story, not rules of the style. What defines the style: each scene has a coherent flat palette of about 3–6 families; a thin white line/HUD layer stays readable on every background; a small warm accent (red heart, red tie, red ball) carries over between scenes; and saturation and value shifts are used as storytelling, not decoration. For new subjects, choose the field from the emotion of each chapter. Options include deep teal night ocean, dusty terracotta desert at dusk, cold blue-white winter morning, lime-and-mint spring, warm amber interior lamplight, slate-blue rain, and black-and-violet club space. Then check that the white line and HUD keep enough contrast; on very light fields, switch the line to dark ink.

sources.palette_lesson: These colors are the creator's choices for this short, not a fixed recipe. Each scene uses one saturated, nearly flat background family (golden-yellow stripes, deep indigo, slate blue with a screenshot collage, mint, periwinkle, a yellow/pink/cyan wipe) and changes family at every hard cut to mark a new idea. The parts that stay constant are what define the style: a pastel mascot with a black contour, caption type in white or yellow fill with a near-black stroke, a white outer keyline and a hard offset shadow, plus small multicolor confetti. The heavy dark stroke plus white halo is what keeps captions legible on any field, light or dark. For new subjects, choose the background from the topic and mood. Options include: deep teal or ink navy for tech or night topics, coral or tomato red for urgency, a soft lilac or sky-blue dot grid for calm explainers, charcoal with a neon-lime ring pulse for gaming, warm terracotta or olive for food or lifestyle, or a desaturated photo or screenshot wall as evidence. Keep one dominant field per scene with a quieter same-hue pattern (dots, stripes or rings at low contrast), and reserve the most saturated accent (yellow or hot pink here) for the key word. Recheck contrast between the mascot's pastel fill and the field: pale lilac on mint or butter yellow relies entirely on the black contour.

> Repeated print panels and registration offsets change the meaning of a familiar image through colour, placement and scale.

## Visual identity
Let repeated prints change meaning through scale or placement. Build the sequence around a repeated printed image that can be read in several panels. Change its ink, crop or scale in a way that shows a new state while preserving the source outline.

## Surfaces and construction
Use opaque screen fills, a stable dot pattern and discrete ink passes on a physical sheet. Give the main drawing its own contour layer so slightly offset colours read as registration.

## Colour roles
Use a few distinct ink plates and let overlapping ink produce mixtures. Build strong spot separations and leave a dark key shape for instant recognition.

Example palette. background #FFF6D6, foreground #171717, accent 1 #E8393E, accent 2 #F1C932, accent 3 #2671C6.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved words inside a print panel with a dedicated flat fill. Keep halftone away from small counters and punctuation.

## Timing and movement
Show a clean print impression first. Repeat it in a new location or scale, then shift the next ink layer a little to reveal registration without softening the main contour.

## Framing and viewpoint
Pull out from individual dots to a print, then widen until repeated sheets cover the wall. Push into a circle and match its shape, pass through a hole in a printed character, track across a wide strip or fill the frame with a tile that flips. Move toward a repeated pattern as a change spreads across it. Keep titles and enabled captions in free space.

## Sound options
If enabled, give the selected panel one crisp accent and leave repeat panels unaccented. If effects are on, use dry squeegee and stamp textures to mark the print actions.

## Characteristic actions
- Repeat one subject in three plates and change one colour separation to direct attention.
- Stamp a motif in several positions, vary the next impression or flip one tile.

## Review checks
Compare each panel at viewing size. Confirm that repeated prints retain the same outline and that the colour change carries a clear difference.

## Implementation tools
Render spots and masks separately so opaque areas can cut out the layer below. Render colour plates in separate masks and control registration by layer, including halftone and keyline.

## Project choices
Choose a recurring image that changes meaning in the series. Use repeat grids or poster-like framing. Preserve the central silhouette across colour changes.

> Dense patterns make the eye perceive motion or depth as adjacent lines shift their spacing and phase.

## Surfaces and construction

> Flat browser fragments, unpolished type and hard-edged blocks build a deliberately raw, readable page.

## Visual identity
Use raw interface fragments as a legible visual argument. Use raw web fragments and hard blocks to organise an abrasive but readable composition.

## Surfaces and construction
Use hard blocks, visible dividers and economical crops. Keep screenshots and interface fragments sharp. Show hard crop edges and plain panels.

## Colour roles
Separate high-contrast working elements from large neutral fields. Give the main information the strongest contrast and mark one interface action with an accent.

Example palette. background #FFFFFF, foreground #000000, accent 1 #CEFF24.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved copy as visible interface labels and keep the reading order aligned to the block structure. Keep text inside its own high-contrast field during state changes.

## Timing and movement
Show the full interface slab before a field snaps open or a selection changes. Keep the layout common between states so the viewer can track the change through a sharp cut.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a flat viewport grid with deliberate hard cuts between crops. Show the full structure before cutting to a control or detail.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a short input sound at the actual click and a dry snap as the replacement block lands. Keep scrolling or layout movement quiet unless the brief gives it a source.

## Characteristic actions
Show a selected item in its original block, then replace that block with the result on the same grid lines. A second view can expose the margins or controls that changed.

## Review checks
Check that a moving crop cannot hide the label needed to understand the changed control. Verify focus and selected states are distinct if the brief depicts them.

## Implementation tools
Use actual layout flow and deterministic cut or reveal timing. Use CSS or vector layout with stable region dimensions and explicit state changes.

## Project choices
Choose a rough dashboard, archive or composition built from browser fragments. Use browser fragments, type blocks or screenshots according to the idea's assets.

> Torn headlines, tape and photocopied marks give an editorial statement the urgency of a handmade poster.

## Visual identity
Make the poster feel handled, revised and assembled in a hurry. Build a rough editorial statement from torn headlines, tape and copied fragments.

## Surfaces and construction
Use photocopied fragments, torn edges, tape and overlapping print. Keep paper tears and photocopy grain fixed to their own pieces. Build distinct layers for paper stock, printed ink, torn edges and tape. A strip of tape should overlap both pieces and cast a small shadow where it lifts.

## Colour roles
Use colour to keep the main statement apart from incidental marks. Use a small ink palette with one abrupt colour interruption behind the lead idea.

Example palette. background #EFE9D9, foreground #171717, accent 1 #C63A3A.

## Lettering and captions
Anchor approved headlines to a single piece of stock. Keep the most frayed edges and heavy marks away from the line the audience needs to read.

## Timing and movement
Tear, tape or stamp as a short physical action, with room for the new fragment to settle. Hold the resulting statement before disturbing the layout again.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use close overhead framing with room to see the tape and a few rough margins. Frame wide to establish the statement and crop to the material when it changes.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, spot a paper slap or tape pull at visible contact. If enabled, attach tear and tape cues to the actual material.

## Characteristic actions
Replace part of a cutout headline mid-beat and pin it with a tape strip.

Rip, tape or stamp one piece into a new reading position.

## Review checks
Inspect the fragment through contact and release. Loose fibres, tape and printed marks should follow the same sheet as it moves.

## Implementation tools
Cache torn shapes in their material coordinates and independently key each layer. Animate separated clipped paper plates with registered grain and small contact shadows.

## Project choices
Choose a short statement, a protest-like layout or a sequence of corrected fragments. Use an original flyer, zine spread or typographic statement based on the brief.

sources.style_evidence: The title is ransom-note lettering: each letter is on its own paper chip in a mismatched typeface and color, set in an irregular, deliberately imperfect layout, with chips pasted on one by one (s1–s4).
sources.palette_lesson: The warm tan cork, brown wood frame and dark slate-navy room are this author's scene choices for a 'nerdy desk at night' story. They are not rules of the medium. What makes the style is how roles are split. The ground is one muted, textured surface. Saturated color comes from the letter chips, which mix roughly six families (cream, black, red, yellow, green, pink/sky blue) so that each letter contrasts with the ground. A single emissive accent (green CRT phosphor) carries the night scene, and the warm skin and red-tie figure stand out against the cool wall. For a new subject, choose the ground for the setting and keep the chips high-contrast against it. If the ground is dark, use more pale and saturated chips. If it is pale, use more black and saturated chips. Recheck legibility when chips overlap the pinned notes.

sources.style_evidence: Ransom-note cutout headline letters on mixed black, white and pink tiles, torn paper edges, a deliberately irregular pasted layout, and a limited palette of pink, black and white with one blue accent (s1-s4).
sources.palette_lesson: The grid stays in every frame and the accent roles stay fixed: one hot accent (magenta) is used as backing paper, halftone and stamp ink; black and white carry type and characters; cobalt blue and mustard yellow appear only rarely as third accents (one tile, one scrap, the blob's offset rim, the smiley). Scenes alternate between loud and quiet. Headline beats flood the frame with pink, and dialogue beats drop back to the plain grid so the bubbles can be read. The specific colours (sage graph paper, hot pink) belong to this author's example. They are not style constants. What defines the style is a light ruled/grid substrate, black-and-white cutout and pixel figures, one saturated print-ink accent, and white sticker borders that separate figures from any background.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Scratches, worn ink and imperfect edges show how a design has been handled and aged.

## Visual identity
Make wear read as the product of handling rather than uniform noise. Make wear look like marks accumulated on a physical substrate.

## Surfaces and construction
Put scratches and abrasion where surfaces rub, fold or touch. Layer dry scratches, scuffs and stains at distinct sizes on one material surface.

## Colour roles
Keep a stable base palette and use wear to reveal underlying tones. Keep damaged values close to the substrate and protect contrast at the focal point. Choose the underlying stock and topcoat as separate value groups. Let a scrape show the lower group and use a softer mark only where wear changes the shine without removing pigment.

Example palette. background #E4DCCD, foreground #302E29, accent 1 #8C5140.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved copy in a clearer area of the worn surface or give it independent ink weight. Allow damage at edges where letter shapes still read.

## Timing and movement
Reveal abrasion by changing its angle to the light or by pushing a worn surface into view. Keep the speed low enough to see individual marks enter the light separately.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a fixed or shallow raking view so texture scale stays plausible. Use grazing light or an oblique close view to reveal the texture.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a brief scrape when material visibly brushes or moves. If effects are on, use friction cues tied to the worn surface.

## Characteristic actions
Drag a local abrasive mark across ink so the underlying stock emerges.

Move light or a layered object to expose different marks.

## Review checks
Check that scratches follow the surface through movement. Inspect light and dark positions so texture stays visible without filling the clearest letter shapes.

## Implementation tools
Seed surface-local marks and vary their size by wear mechanism. Bind seeded wear masks to surface coordinates and separate the reveal from texture itself.

## Project choices
Choose stock, painted metal or a handled object with specific marks. Use one worn material family such as print, painted metal or wall plaster.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A few carefully placed forms carry the idea through scale, spacing and small changes in attention.

## Visual identity
Use empty space and scale to make one relation easy to read. Give a few precisely positioned elements enough space to carry the idea.

## Surfaces and construction
Choose simple consistent geometry with deliberate margins. Use simple contours and consistent edges without decorative layers. Reuse one stroke weight and corner treatment across related objects. Make an exception at an object that must be compared or manipulated so it can be identified before the movement begins.

## Colour roles
Reserve contrast for the element carrying the change. Keep one clear contrast pair and reserve any accent for a genuine change.

Example palette. background #FAF9F5, foreground #202421, accent 1 #406B5A.

## Lettering and captions
If approved text is present, align it to a single stable edge and reserve enough clear area for the longest line.

## Timing and movement
Begin with the complete relationship in stillness. Use one clear move, scale change or removal, then hold the new spacing long enough to compare it with the opening.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the viewport quiet and crop only to show a relevant difference. Use a stable, generous frame and move only to clarify the change.

## Sound options
Use silence between events when permitted. If an effect is enabled, spot the single visible change. With effects enabled, use a single restrained cue when attention changes.

## Characteristic actions
Remove or reposition a single block to expose a new comparison. Keep one anchor, such as a baseline or another block, in place through the change and hold the result.

## Review checks
Review the first and final stills at a small size. Each element should point to the change, support a comparison or carry approved text.

## Implementation tools
Represent the few active objects as vectors or light layout layers with explicit start and rest positions. Use a common timeline and render stationary parts from the same state through the hold.

## Project choices
Choose subtraction, a small comparison or one shifting relationship. Change proportions, spacing or emphasis while keeping the composition sparse.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A designed spread places headline, illustration and evidence in reading order. Movement introduces information as the reader needs it.

## Visual identity
Make a spread reveal information in reading order. Build a spread with visible reading order from headline through evidence and annotation.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep images, columns and annotation zones on a shared layout. Place cropped images and text on a shared column and margin system.

## Colour roles
Give headings, figures and source notes clear value roles. Use paper, ink and one accent to separate the lead from supporting detail.

Example palette. background #FAF5EA, foreground #252A30, accent 1 #A84235.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved headings, decks, captions and figure labels on a common column grid. Tie a small caption to its image by distance and alignment.

## Timing and movement
Set the title and leading image before flowing in blocks of secondary material. Time a page turn after the viewer can associate the main image with its heading.

## Framing and viewpoint
Start on a complete spread and move along column boundaries towards a supporting image or figure. Keep a margin or header in view as a reference and return on the same edge.

## Sound options
If narration is enabled, let it complement the text. Keep reading holds free of extra effects. If audible, attach soft page or marker cues to visible editorial action.

## Characteristic actions
Open an image crop across a column and connect the relevant detail with a caption.

Advance from headline to evidence and pause for the annotation. Keep one image or column edge in frame during a detail push. Land on a figure with its caption and enough surrounding context to show where it came from.

## Review checks
Test the reading order of each settled spread. Check facing pages and portrait crops for orphaned captions and broken alignment.

## Implementation tools
Lay out content from shared grid units and animate grouped sections. Use a fixed grid, independent image masks and text measurements for multi-line blocks.

## Project choices
Choose a report, an illustrated story or a visual comparison. Use a cover, a comparison spread or an annotated feature with the same page system.

sources.style_evidence: A book/museum-plate layout: a large serif headline, a short body paragraph, small-caps section labels, a grid of charts, orthographic plates and a stats table inside a ruled border.
sources.palette_lesson: The aged-parchment field, sepia wash and brown ink are this author's choice for a period military subject. They are not a rule of the style. What actually defines it: one quiet, low-chroma page tone acting as the canvas; a single dark ink colour for all type, hairline rules, charts and orthographic plates; a realistically lit hero object whose own materials (here iron and timber) carry the only rich colour; a translucent wash stain (here sepia) that grounds the object instead of a hard drop shadow; and UI states shown by inverting ink fill (filled versus outlined pills, a muted inactive pill), not by bright accent hues. Contrast between the dark ink and the light page must stay high for small serif text. For new subjects, pick the page tone from the subject's context. Examples: a cool blue-grey drafting paper with navy ink for a naval or aviation object; a pale celadon or jade-grey ground with deep green-black ink for a botanical or ceramic object; a warm graphite-grey board with off-white ink, as a dark inverted plate, for an engine or watch movement; a soft terracotta or clay-pink stock with deep oxblood ink for an archaeological artifact; a chalky stone white with slate ink for an architectural element. The grounding wash should take a darker, desaturated tone of the page hue, and object materials should stay true to the subject.

The near-black field and that particular blue are this author's choices for a sober news/tech brand mood. They are not a constraint of the style. What defines the style is: one dominant field, one high-contrast text color for statements, one reserved accent for the punchline and for structure, and card panels only slightly separated from the field by hairline borders. Depth is handled with blur and dimming rather than extra colors. For other subjects the field can change while those roles stay the same. Examples: deep ink-navy with warm-white type and an amber accent for finance; off-white newsprint gray with charcoal serif and a vermilion accent for a print-journalism feel; dark forest green with bone-white type and a citrus accent for climate stories; slate-plum with pale lilac cards and a coral accent for culture coverage; a light cool-gray field with near-black type and a cobalt accent for a daytime product look. > Generous space, measured type and exact cropping give a single subject the attention of a carefully produced editorial spread.

## Visual identity
Give a single object the attention and spacing of a premium editorial image. Give one item visual priority through controlled type, space and deliberate crops.

## Surfaces and construction
Use crisp crops, coherent materials and carefully controlled backgrounds. Use one polished or tactile material family and avoid competing finishes.

## Colour roles
Let the product own the strongest contrast or reflection. Start with subdued tones and save the brightest response for the item's finish.

Example palette. background #F4EFE7, foreground #29251F, accent 1 #817159.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved type in the clearest part of the image or on a dedicated margin. Use spacing and size to distinguish the headline from the secondary line.

## Timing and movement
Use a slow controlled reveal for the main image or wordmark. Stagger small details behind it and let the longest approved line finish reading before the next crop.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a clean detail angle or measured push that protects the silhouette. Use a strong opening wide, followed by precise crops at the scale of the detail.

## Sound options
If sound is enabled, keep a small contact cue or texture under the idea's chosen track. If effects are enabled, keep contacts sparse and tied to the product. If effects are enabled, use a close material cue for the single handled object. Keep any transition sound short enough to leave the product's reveal and reading hold separate.

## Characteristic actions
Let a restrained highlight travel across one surface before revealing the full object.

Reveal one feature at a time and hold long enough to inspect it.

## Review checks
Review the title over the brightest and darkest image areas. A crop or move should preserve both the product detail and the intended negative space.

## Implementation tools
Control material reflections separately from camera and type timing. Separate material passes from title layers and use explicit light and camera curves.

## Project choices
Choose a texture, a detail feature or an object shown in one deliberate sequence. Vary the crop, paper treatment or finish to fit a product, portrait or editorial feature.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A drawing develops on one page as loose construction lines become confident contours and selective colour establishes form.

## Visual identity
Make the drawing process carry the explanation. Show the loose gesture, the contour that corrects it and the colour shape that identifies what the scene is about.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep fine paper texture and irregular pencil edges anchored to the page beneath separate colour blocks. Build rough marks, final outlines and fill patches as separate strokes. Keep the fine paper grain fixed beneath the drawing while the view follows the tool.

## Colour roles
Let the line stay readable over local colour and keep annotation accents distinct. Use pale construction strokes, stronger final lines and a small fill in the active drawing area.

Example palette. background #F7EFDF, foreground #343E42, accent 1 #BC705A, accent 2 #758D72.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved text off rough exploratory lines. Where a label is part of the drawing, use a leader from a clear margin to a specific detail.

## Timing and movement
Draw the large gesture first and fit shorter contour marks to it. Let the final pen lift separate drawing from a held finished pose.

## Framing and viewpoint
Let the paper move under a virtual drawing view. Push tightly onto linework, zoom out as a sketch becomes legible, turn or slide the page and track the stylus when the viewer needs a guide. Match a detail to its larger copy, use a quick push that settles on a discovery and give the entire page a reading view. Leave space for enabled text and use page gestures or colour changes between views.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use stylus contact for prominent strokes with silence between groups. If enabled, match pencil drag to the movement and let colour fills have a softer contact.

## Characteristic actions
- Lay down a guide, correct it with a darker contour and fill only the part under discussion.
- Draw the contour first, fill it with a slightly offset block, or let a colour pass open the next shape.

## Review checks
Inspect intersections and line ends at normal size. The gesture should stay recognisable as new detail appears.

## Implementation tools
Trim strokes by arc length and give the page, drawing and colour layers separate transforms. Animate pressure-aware stroke paths and clip fills to the settled outline.

## Project choices
Use a build-up from rough to clear, a reworked note or successive ideas on one page. Use product, portrait or scene sketches. Keep the drawing centred around one page and visible progression.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Graphite lines, texture and pressure make the viewer see the strokes that build volume and explain the subject.

## Visual identity
Let line pressure and accumulation show the work of drawing. Describe form with graphite contours, corrections and directional marks. Show the evidence of pressure in long light construction marks, shorter dark accents and lifted highlights. Let the viewer see where a rounded form turns through the direction of shading.

## Surfaces and construction
Use separate graphite contours, directional shading and an anchored paper tooth. Keep paper tooth visible through soft graphite. Build midtones with grouped strokes.

## Colour roles
Use reserved paper for highlights and give constructed tones a clear order. Use the value range from bare paper to dark graphite and leave highlights open.

Example palette. background #F5F2EA, foreground #383838.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved pencil labels above a faint guide or in clear margins. Keep cross-hatching outside small letter shapes and use a clean leader where the note refers to one patch of shading.

## Timing and movement
Lay down light construction lines, press into selected edges, then collect graphite shading in passes. Let a stroke change direction at the visible turn of a form.

## Framing and viewpoint
Hold the paper plane steady and move closer only to show a useful group of marks. Track the tip close and pull back to show the form as a whole.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a light scratch for a long graphite stroke and a softer rub for shading. Let the sound stop at the pen lift and vary its strength with the visible pressure.

## Characteristic actions
Change hatch direction around the curve and reinforce one corrected contour.

Lay construction marks first and build dark values with overlapping strokes.

## Review checks
Check whether the heaviest lines are on the intended edge and whether shading follows the planes of the form. Texture should stay attached to the paper.

## Implementation tools
Drive each stroke reveal by length and vary width and grain by pressure. Reveal stroked paths in drawing order with stable granular marks per stroke.

## Project choices
Choose a contour study, a layered shading pass or a visible correction. Choose studies of people, objects or places with visible drawing decisions.

The medium constraints are visible paper between strokes, line-built tone, no gradients, and one accent hue. The red sun suits a heat topic; for other subjects, swap the accent to suit the subject (e.g. cobalt for water, moss green for forest) and keep it to one pigment. styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Fine overlapping marks and pressure changes turn small pen strokes into contours, shadows and solid shapes.

## Visual identity
Build form through small, purposeful variations in the density of ink. Use pressure and repeated fine lines to make a subject read like pen work.

## Surfaces and construction
Use fine pen lines with visible joins, overlaps and pressure differences. Apply narrow ballpoint marks with local buildup on lightly warm or white paper.

## Colour roles
Keep the main pen colour consistent so values come from stroke density. Reserve bare paper for highlights and use the darkest overlapping hatch where the plane turns away from the light.

Example palette. background #FCFAF4, foreground #172C49.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved notes with the same stroke weight as the drawing. Leave paper between lettering and dense ink accumulations.

## Timing and movement
Accumulate small strokes in the same direction as the hand. Build darker values by crossing groups of strokes and leave a pause where the pen lifts to a new region.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the camera level with the sheet and track only when a long line exceeds the crop. Move between tool scale and page scale to show how the lines add up.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, give a pen pass a short dry sound and leave the hold quiet. With effects enabled, use brief pen contact when the mark appears.

## Characteristic actions
Reinforce a turning edge with several narrow strokes until the form deepens.

Build a dense patch through short groups of strokes and hold the finished area.

## Review checks
Check that clusters grow from the visible pen tip and stop there. Where lines overlap, use density to darken the form without obscuring the main outline.

## Implementation tools
Seed stroke variation locally and reveal each stroke from its path length. Use length-based vector reveals with stroke width and opacity fixed to the pen pressure plan. Store each pen stroke with its start, direction and length. Build darkness from overlapping strokes so a rewind can remove individual passes without fading their neighbours.

## Project choices
Choose a material, shadow or region that becomes clear under cross-hatching. Choose a portrait, diagram or observed prop and vary the density to show its form.

## Visual identity
Let one quickly drawn change give a simple idea an expression. Use quick drawn contours and expressive small marks to show a clear reaction.

## Surfaces and construction
Use elastic linework, paper texture and a small set of repeatable shapes. Give the figures slightly uneven lines, stable proportions and a quiet drawing surface.

## Colour roles
Spend an accent on the reaction or subject that matters. Use a light palette with one cue colour near the changed expression or prop.

Example palette. background #FFFBF2, foreground #34343D, accent 1 #E6AF9C, accent 2 #94C1B3.

## Lettering and captions
Fit approved words beside the associated doodle and give captions a quieter area of the sheet. Keep expressive scribbles clear of punctuation.

## Timing and movement
Draw each doodle in short connected runs with distinct pen lifts. Let a completed doodle react briefly before sketching the next one into view.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a straightforward page crop that keeps expressions and gestures in view. Use a close enough view for the tiny gesture without losing its context.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, spot one small gesture while leaving drawing pauses quiet. If on, use short pen or action cues instead of a constant chatter of sounds.

## Characteristic actions
Redraw brows or a hand shape to change the meaning while the body stays put.

Show the main pose, add a revealing detail and hold the recognition beat. Let a scribble become a prop, then add a small reaction or movement to the drawings around it. Pause on the new relationship before starting another stroke.

## Review checks

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Visible marker strokes build a diagram on one board. Previously drawn marks stay in place as a new relationship becomes clear.

## Visual identity
Make an explanation take shape through deliberate marks and corrections on the same board. Let viewers see which relationship is established before an arrow, label or revision changes it.

## Surfaces and construction
Add board sheen, marker deposit, erasure residue and small physical elements only where they show contact.

## Colour roles
Keep essential strokes dark and use a small accent for the changed term. Use black marker for main structure and one highlight for the linked point or update.

Example palette. background #FFFFFF, foreground #23282C, accent 1 #245B9B.

## Lettering and captions
Put approved words in open board regions and write each line in its natural order. Keep connectors attached to the object being explained.

## Timing and movement
Draw the main relationship first. Add a branch only after its parent mark reads, and erase a region before drawing its replacement in the same space. Let the pen travel visibly to the start of the next stroke when that change matters. If a cut hides a long gap, resume on the correct next mark.

## Framing and viewpoint
Move around one drawing surface. Pull back from the small marks, travel with the stroke, hold for reading or whip to a new area and return to an earlier drawing. Include two regions in the same view for comparison. Move close to one symbol, track a long diagram or pull beyond the edge to see the wall and board. Add motion blur to a fast board move if it helps the viewer track it.

## Sound options
If enabled, use light dry-marker contact at primary strokes and silence between drawing groups. With sound enabled, attach selective squeak and removal sounds to the visible tool. If effects are enabled, separate the scratch of a moving marker from the tap of a pen lift or the wipe of a correction. Time each to the visible contact instead of running a continuous bed under still marks.

## Characteristic actions
- Draw the main elements in reading order, connect the crucial relationship and hold the completed board.
- Track a pen through a connection, clear one region, place a magnet or return to an earlier diagram.

## Review checks
On a direct seek, the final state of erased and redrawn marks should appear without remnants. Test the board at its widest view for reading order.

## Implementation tools
Share stroke reveal timing between the pen point and its drawing mask. Reveal real vector strokes in order. Keep erasure masks local and preserve the board coordinate system.

## Project choices
Choose a dependency, process or correction that fits on a coherent board. Explain a system, sketch or workflow. Maintain a clear completed diagram at the end.

sources.palette_lesson: These frames use a monochrome palette: black strokes and type on a flat near-white field, gray for secondary labels and code comments, and no hue accents. Hierarchy comes from stroke weight, bold vs regular monospace and gray value. The near-white canvas is this author's example, not a rule. What defines the style is a single flat, untextured field with one high-contrast line color and at most one value step for secondary text. For new subjects the field can follow the scene, provided the line color is inverted or adjusted to keep strong contrast. Options: a deep charcoal or ink-navy field with off-white lines for a night or technical topic; pale cool gray-blue for infrastructure or data; soft sage or mint-gray for health or nature; slate with pale lines for security; a muted terracotta or dusty rose field with dark lines for a warmer consumer story. > Flat shapes and consistent figure proportions make subjects clear at a glance. Shared parts give the moves and transitions a consistent look.

## Visual identity
Explain an action with a small set of linked flat shapes. Use flat colour fields and simplified figures with shared shapes.

## Surfaces and construction
Use clean vector silhouettes with consistent part proportions. Build clean vectors with matching corner radii and a consistent icon scale.

## Colour roles
Give repeated objects stable colours and let the active part carry emphasis. Assign distinct colours to figures, props and key states within a small palette.

Example palette. background #F7F3E9, foreground #243746, accent 1 #267D82, accent 2 #DD7353, accent 3 #EAC664.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved lettering on broad flat fields. Align a label to the part it names and keep glyphs outside moving cutout edges.

## Timing and movement
Move the main flat shape first and attach smaller decorative shapes to its motion. Let each cluster finish in a clear silhouette before introducing a neighbouring one.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a flat or shallow view that retains clear spatial relationships. Use an uncluttered whole view before cutting into a meaningful component.

## Sound options

Move one flat part into a figure and let its matching shape signal the result.

Check every join at full size and in the final crop. Preserve flat fills and clear colour separation where different parts overlap.

Use reusable symbol paths and independent scene transforms. Use editable layers with stable shape geometry and keyed transform groups. Build overlapping shapes as closed paths with stable origins. Parent accessories to the main part so a deliberately simple silhouette survives whole-group motion.

Choose a character action, a short process or a progression that reads through shape. Use people, diagrams or environments with a common vector vocabulary.

Warm amber appears only as a story signal, when the house-character's windows light up. Contrast with the subject comes from value (the off-white head against a dark field) and from warm against cool. The cream radial glow at 7s is a light-transition effect, not a canvas colour. The interior at 8s switches to a near-black void around a dark plum-brown isometric room, and saturated hue-coded roofs (orange, lavender, teal, yellow) separate the characters. What should transfer: a dominant environmental colour family with tonal-step depth, a light-valued hero with one or two signature hues reused across its parts (here teal), restrained warm emissive accents tied to events, and categorical hue-coding for ensemble characters. The navy/teal night recipe and the specific roof colours are this video's example, not constraints of the style.

tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Small gestures and specific details in the setting tell the story through illustrated scenes that have room to settle.

## Visual identity
Let a small character action and a specific detail of its setting carry the story. Use the same figure shape through page changes and give the action the space of a complete illustration.

## Surfaces and construction
Use varied contours, local mark texture and separate depth layers. Use warm page textures, drawn edges and reusable character poses.

## Colour roles
Keep the character clear within a scene palette tied to place and mood. Assign stable local colours to characters and use temperature to distinguish settings.

Example palette. background #F6E9CE, foreground #493E32, accent 1 #BA7254, accent 2 #6F8871, accent 3 #D5AB55.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved text inside a clear paper area and away from the character's face. Leave deliberate space for a caption when designing the illustration.

## Timing and movement
Hold an establishing drawing long enough to read the place before moving the character or turning a page. Give the reaction pose a clear pause after the action.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame from a viewpoint that shows the character, prop and consequence together. Frame the environment first, then move only enough to see the relevant gesture.

## Sound options
If sound is enabled, let footsteps, fabric or page movement support visible story actions. If enabled, tie contact and ambience to the actual illustrated place.

## Characteristic actions
Have a character recognise and touch a small object, then hold the changed expression.

Reveal a prop, hold on a gesture or let a small change in light carry attention.

## Review checks
Check continuity of the main character's proportions and palette between pages. Check that a small movement preserves the recognisable shape.

## Implementation tools
Keep illustration, depth planes and character poses separately keyed. Layer original illustration assets with independent face, hand and prop pose timing.

## Project choices
Choose an intimate discovery, a small task or a visible change in the setting. Use an encounter, discovery or quiet routine from the idea's story. Use a setting with one clear landmark and a figure with an identifiable gesture. Let small props support the turn in the story while keeping the cast and milestones from the brief.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Printed panels, a recurring figure and moving paper pieces turn a historical change into a readable visual sequence.

## Visual identity
Use the page layout to show whose action or reaction matters. Let a full panel describe the situation and a narrower panel isolate a meaningful detail from the same moment.

## Surfaces and construction
Build panel borders, paper figures and texture as separate layers. Give a cutout enough thickness and cast shadow to distinguish it from the printed panel under it.

## Colour roles
Keep the newly placed patch related to the existing print while distinguishing the changed region. Use ink mass to lead the eye. Reserve one subdued period tint for timelines or archival context. Hold deep ink for silhouettes and frame borders. Use midtones for background layers and let a small feature carry the brightest cue at an important change in panel.

Example palette. background #FFF2D9, foreground #1C2230, accent 1 #C9403C, accent 2 #E1B744, accent 3 #3768A1.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved dialogue in a balloon with an unambiguous tail. Place captions outside the path of motion or the face in that panel.

## Timing and movement
Land each panel as a complete readable drawing. Let panel order and the change in poses carry the action, then expose a close-up where an impact or reaction needs emphasis. Use a new drawing between important puppet poses only where a turn loses its silhouette. Let framed panel changes do the work of a larger cut.

## Framing and viewpoint
Move within the printed page. Close in on a map or action, shake briefly for impact, then pull out to show its place on the page. Slide across a gutter for parallel action, whip across one for a time jump or drop diagonally into the next row. Tilt towards the tabletop to reveal the paper layers. Let a narrow panel sit beside its neighbour. Use motions of the page and panels for scene changes.

## Sound options
If sound is enabled, use scene sound at the panel change or an understated paper cue for a page turn. If effects are on, distinguish cutting, tearing and the heavier landing of stacked stock.

## Characteristic actions
- Introduce a panel boundary at a change of time and match a recurring pose across the cut.
- Cut along a marked border, peel back a patch or press two layers that resist lying flat.

## Review checks
Check panel order and balloon order together. Test the frame where a gutter enters and verify it never divides a word or covers the action.

## Implementation tools
Attach map regions to masks and keep the pivot and cast shadow on the same piece. Lay out panel masks first and key poses against the same elapsed-time cues across overlapping panels.

## Project choices
Choose a boundary change, a regional comparison or a chain of events linked across panels. Tell an event at several scales. Use accurate supplied dates and locations when presenting history.

sources.palette_lesson: Only 5–8s carry style evidence; 1–4s are dark app/browser screen recording. The yellow side fill is pillarbox surround, not the comic canvas. The author's own choices are the lemon-yellow surround, the orange sunburst with orange-red dots and a teal inner image, which complements the warm frame. What the medium actually requires is a limited set of saturated print-ink families, black keylines and drop shadows, a halftone dot texture with a fixed grid, light caption/tag boxes, and SFX colors chosen to contrast with whatever image sits under them. The sunburst and border should take their hue from the subject and mood, and the inner image should be complementary or contrasting so the panel reads clearly.

sources.style_evidence: At s8, radial concentration or speed lines and an impact stamp land as a comic-style emphasis beat over a screentone ground.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's example is fully achromatic: a mid-charcoal halftone ground, black-ink objects with white keylines, off-white paper cards and white LED dots. A darker near-black overlay is used for the spotlight beat. The measured composite dominant shifts from mid grey (s1–6) to very dark grey (s7–8). That reflects the dimming overlay, not a second palette. What defines the style is not grey itself. It is the print constraint: tone made by dot density in one ink against a substrate, plus solid ink badges and stamps, with emphasis carried by luminance and inversion rather than hue. For new subjects the ground can be any single ink-on-substrate pairing that suits the scene. Keep paper cards (or the subject's equivalent) as the brightest plane. Reserve the darkest overlay for focus moments, and check that the small text on cards stays legible over the dot screen. If one accent is added, it should be a spot-ink color with a fixed semantic role (e.g., 'hit' state), not decoration.
