styles.visual_cues: Authored manga illustration with subject-specific storytelling: people, animals, creatures, monsters, objects, machines, environments or abstract subjects as required by the brief. Use controlled ink line weights, selective screentones, cinematic panel composition and purposeful negative space. Choose establishing views and expressive or structural close-ups that reveal the actual subject; human faces, eyes and hands are optional, never a required template. Keep subject design, form and spatial continuity consistent. Animate motivated actions, transformations, panel reveals and camera moves with readable holds. Drawing quality must carry a still frame; generic icons, dashboard cards or a blanket dot filter are not substitutes for refined manga drawing.
styles.note: The source directly names or describes this visual direction. The source reference mentions manga; some source prompts are partial.

tech.implementation: Subject selection: Manga is a visual storytelling language, not a requirement for human characters. Let the brief choose people, animals, creatures, monsters, objects, machines, environments or abstract subjects; do not default to a person, human face, eye close-up or hand insert. Do not anthropomorphize objects unless the story calls for it. For animals use species-specific proportions, stance, joints, gait and surface forms; for monsters establish coherent invented anatomy and repeatable features; for objects and machines use perspective, structural joins, material response, function and mechanical articulation; for environments use spatial depth, scale, architecture or natural forms; for abstract subjects establish consistent visual rules and meaningful transformations. Apply convincing volume, clear silhouette, intentional line-weight hierarchy, purposeful ink masses, contact and perspective to every subject. Select panels and details for this story, never a mandatory portrait/eye/hand montage. Human anatomy, eyes, hands, hair and clothing examples below are conditional techniques only when the selected subject actually has those features; they never require adding a human or human features. Separate subject line art, form/material layers, environmental perspective, shadow masks, screentones, panel borders and lettering. Include hair/clothing shapes only when present. Study the reference at full resolution before building: identify contour weights, proportions, hand anatomy, hair clumps, cloth folds, spatial perspective, tone placement and panel-to-panel continuity. Use original characters and settings; do not copy reference characters, dialogue, watermarks or branding. At 1280px width use roughly 3–5px silhouette emphasis, 1–2px structural contours and 0.5–1px fine detail, scaled with delivery size; use tapered filled strokes for eyelashes and select contour accents, with clean joins instead of uniform icon outlines. Construct convincing subject volume, functional structure and contact. For subjects with those features, construct face volumes and eye placement, hands with readable gesture and joints, hair with grouped strands and directional highlights, and fabric folds rooted in tension or contact. Reserve solid ink for occlusion, deep shadows and focal accents. Clip a small number of stable screentone densities and directional hatching to form and shadow planes; retain quiet white highlights and gutters instead of dotting every surface. Keep screen-tone spacing stable during masking, scaling, and pose changes, and inspect moire at actual delivery resolution. Establish foreground/midground/background and consistent perspective; do not let construction lines show through opaque objects. Choose asymmetric panels according to narrative function, selecting wider settings, relevant structural/material details or expressive close-ups without forcing a portrait/eye/hand sequence or any repeated template. Let panels appear in deliberate reading order and hold long enough to understand; use subject-appropriate action only when supported by the beat: weight transfer, animal movement, mechanical articulation, material deformation, motivated camera motion, or blink/breath/hand action when those features exist. Avoid perpetual wobble, indiscriminate speed lines, bouncing panels or changing character identity between shots. Derive all pose and panel states from seekable composition time. Finish a representative still before adding motion: inspect silhouette at thumbnail size, anatomy and line joins at full resolution, tone clipping, gutter consistency, lettering fit and subject continuity. Do not substitute a simple eye symbol, abstract nodes or triangles for an illustrated story. Code-only drawing contract: Author every story illustration directly in editable SVG paths or deterministic Canvas drawing code, including faces, hair, hands, clothing, environments, screentones and panel masks. Do not substitute AI-generated images, raster artwork, image sprites, traced generated artwork or a finished illustration with reveal overlays. Improve the code-drawn shapes themselves: use authored Bezier contours, tapered filled strokes, grouped strand shapes, intentional shadow planes and selective procedural hatching. Simplify anatomy deliberately to a coherent graphic manga vocabulary when necessary; do not promise generated-image detail that the code cannot reproduce. Animation must control the authored drawing layers and derive all states from time. Use actual subject/story artwork; do not turn this style into a backstage director-and-crew viewer. Respect approved palette and assets; a reference accent color is not permission to expand the selected palette. SVG refinement workflow: Block subject volume, silhouette, pose or structural arrangement, contact and perspective first; face landmarks and hand gesture apply only when relevant; then refine organic contours with cubic C/S Bezier paths and aligned tangent directions at smooth joins, reserving cusp corners for intentional points and creases. Improve control handles before adding more nodes. Express pressure-like ink accents as closed tapered filled shapes, not uniformly thick strokes. When the subject has eyes, build the eye from appropriate lid, lash, iris, pupil and highlight layers and reuse consistent proportions in close-ups. For a subject with hair or hands, group hair clumps around the skull with curved strand flow and reserved highlight shapes; construct fingers as overlapping curved volumes with joints, not an angular mitten. Give opaque subject shapes real base fills before adding clipped screentones and directional hatching. Keep secondary contours and texture subordinate to silhouette and focal ink masses. Inspect and revise the unanimated SVG at thumbnail and full output sizes before layering motion. Detailed paths must serve anatomy and form; increasing path count or blanket texture is not quality. Keep character, eye, hand, clothing, tone, panel and lettering layers individually editable and deterministically seekable. Artist-construction pass: Establish subject axes, mass balance, articulation, support and contact in a temporary construction view before final contours; head axis, shoulder gesture and palm/pen contact apply only to a figure doing that action. Choose one light direction; make shadow-side crevices and foreground overlaps heavier, and allow thinner or broken contours on lit edges instead of uniformly outlining every form. When hair is present, build hair as skull volume, root flow, large overlapping clumps, smaller strands and light-consistent highlights; avoid a rigid helmet with evenly spaced white slots. If a hand uses a pen, construct a pen grip from wrist angle, palm volume, thumb mass and finger gestures, checking actual contact and occlusion. Review the still with tone hidden, in an ink-only view, at full size, at thumbnail size and temporarily mirrored; correct eye alignment, jaw shape, silhouette and accidental tangencies before adding texture. Tone must follow surface and light, not decorate every region. Assess anatomy, expression and focal hierarchy by inspecting the rendered still; valid XML, extra paths, a longer SVG budget and passing technical tests do not prove drawing quality. Only then add deterministic movement. These construction and inking rules apply to any subject in this style; do not impose the sample character or composition. Character-quality construction (only for a subject with relevant head/face/body features, never a requirement to add them): Choose head yaw, pitch, tilt, gaze and emotion before final paths. Block skull volume, jaw planes, face centreline and a curved feature line; a 2D rotation is not a three-quarter head turn. Place eyes, brows, nose, mouth and ears on those forms using proportions appropriate to the intended character. A far eye must be angle-aware, narrower and nearer the nose where perspective requires; do not mirror identical front-facing eye symbols to represent a turned head. Keep eyelids wrapped around eye volume, with gaze shared by both eyes. Coordinate lid opening, brows and mouth to communicate the intended emotion rather than adding highlights for decoration. Establish a line of action and shoulder/torso relationship, and connect the neck to jaw and shoulders plausibly; avoid a static frontal mannequin when the story needs character acting. Build hair volume over the skull with overlapping clumps and root direction, not a black helmet hiding weak construction. Review an ink-only character with tone and highlights hidden: pose, head angle, gaze, expression, silhouette, near/far feature placement and hand-to-prop contact must read before detail. Compare full-size, thumbnail and mirrored views; correct structure before adding texture. Reuse design proportions across shots while authoring angle-specific contours. Maintain code-only editable drawing and derive movement from deterministic time. Eye-integrity pass (only when the chosen subject has visible eyes): Construct the pair on one head-volume and feature-line model with one shared gaze target; project each eye and iris for that view rather than independently nudging pupils by arbitrary pixels. Perspective can narrow the far eye without accidentally changing its lid opening or expression into a squint. Author the eye opening, sclera, lid contour and its clip path from matching landmarks in the same local coordinate space; changing an opening requires changing its mask and lid together. Keep iris and pupil clipped inside the eye opening, nest highlights inside the iris, and draw upper lids/occluding features above them. Check the visible iris against both lids at neutral and extreme gaze positions; avoid detached pupils, inconsistent occlusion and collapsed dark blobs. At preview-card scale simplify iris texture and catchlights before enlarging or distorting anatomy; fine screentone and multiple tiny highlights are optional. During gaze motion move the iris/pupil/highlight assembly together inside the lid mask; during a blink change the opening/occlusion coherently rather than scaling a complete eye symbol. Before animation, inspect an eye-pair crop and the whole head in a neutral pose at full size and actual card size. Then inspect gaze extremes, blink keyframes and the settled expression, including direct/backward seeks. Fix perspective, shared gaze, expression, clipping and small-scale readability before publishing; valid SVG or general render checks alone do not pass this eye review. Do not add eyes to subjects that do not need them.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Choose libraries by role and scene requirements; the available options are not a required bundle. Prefer existing suitable dependencies. Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Ink, screen tones and panel order carry the story. Composition moves between actions and details to control what the reader notices.

## Visual identity
Let the panel decide what is seen and when, with the reading direction supporting the story. Strong ink masses and deliberately framed sequential drawings.

## Surfaces and construction
Use bold mass, fine contours and page-anchored screen tones behind separately drawn pose changes. Strong ink masses and deliberately framed sequential drawings. Build the artwork in editable code. Do not substitute AI-generated images. Draw forms with smooth contours, tapered accents and consistent anatomy or perspective per subject.

## Colour roles
Reserve the strongest blacks for silhouettes or a change of mood and preserve clean gutters. Use ink, paper and a small set of tones. Preserve black mass around the focal action.

Example palette. background #FFFFFF, foreground #171717.

## Lettering and captions
Fit approved words in a speech balloon with a clear tail or a caption block in a quiet area of the panel. Keep patterned screen tone out of the lettering. Show narration captions and character speech with distinct treatments if both are enabled.

## Timing and movement
Establish a readable panel and its black shapes before adding speed lines or cutting to a reaction. Hold the strongest pose after the effect clears. Use a small shake at the moment an impact changes the panel. Keep long reading holds on strong drawings and use a short burst of new poses for the point of action.

## Framing and viewpoint
Pan with the reading direction, push into a meaningful detail and match to a related shape. Glide across gutters at a readable measure, pull from a panel to the full page or hold while the grid reconfigures. Move close on an emotional panel and let a slanted split lead into another panel. A flip-book sequence is the place for visible page turns.

## Sound options
If sounds are enabled, select the contact or drawn impact to spot. Leave reaction panels room. If sound is enabled, separate page movement from physical action and preserve quiet held panels.

## Characteristic actions
- Freeze one action, branch it into a detail panel and reconnect it to the wider action. Draw a new angle-specific silhouette for a head turn. Vary gaze, tilt, emotion and shoulder alignment with the turn.
- Ink a border in, split a panel at an impact, merge panels for scale or let a figure break through the frame.

## Review checks
Check line weight, screen-tone grain and panel reading order at delivery size. Make the silhouette and direction of action readable without effects. The page has an obvious reading order and silhouettes remain stable between panels. Where the subject has eyes, check one shared gaze and keep iris highlights inside the iris. Inspect hands, ink weight, folds, gutters and stable tone spacing at delivery size. Check that screentones and line weight stay stable at scale and that gutters establish the reading order.

## Implementation tools
Tie page layout and panel transitions to shared coordinates and mask each panel before animating the frame. Render halftone texture in stable panel coordinates and crop or redraw detail at its own scale. Build the drawing, tones, balloons and panel masks in independently timed layers. Keep tone coordinates attached to the ink drawing so dots and texture stay registered during a crop.

## Project choices
Choose a reveal, a chase across panels or an alternating wide and close exchange. Use dialogue, reactions or physical action. Keep original actors distinguishable across panels.

candidates.usage_guidance: Consider bounded pupil following with optional delayed brows, slight head tilt, and scheduled blinks. Require suitable facial layers or a rig, preserve expression and drawing cadence, and do not interpret this as viewer eye tracking.

Consider a progress-controlled handoff between outgoing and incoming chapters with synchronized copy and readable endpoints. Choose one compatible transition treatment and make both forward and backward state evaluation coherent.

Consider meaningful narrative steps with synchronized copy and visual states, plus optional within-step progress or sticky graphics. Use only scene-level motions that serve the story, and schedule the same states by time for video.

Use a cinematic opening with separately animated illustrated objects, speed-line accents and expressive motion text. Stage the action across panels and end in the approved composition. Prefer this over pupil-only movement or tiny ambient wiggles.

Limited-color lettering can replace phrases with reading holds and controlled glyph poses. Optional only when actual scene assets support the defining action; preserve the style palette and medium and choose no reference when unsuitable.

A monochrome punctuation crop can connect authored panels without screen-tone distortion. Optional only when actual scene assets support the defining action; preserve the style palette and medium and choose no reference when unsuitable.

Targeted drawn speed rays can reveal a centered mark; preserve screen-tone scale and avoid luminous particles. Optional only when actual scene assets support the defining action; preserve the style palette and medium and choose no reference when unsuitable.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Held cels and decisive poses sit over painted backgrounds. Separate layers let the camera move while preserving the drawing.

## Visual identity
Stage crisp character cels against painted depth. Make a held pose, change of gaze or moving light carry the scene, with the painted set giving each action a clear scale and direction.

## Surfaces and construction
Paint background planes separately and use hard shadow edges and fine rim light on the cels. Give painted backgrounds soft value changes and keep character edges crisp. Separate highlight and shadow cels so a light sweep can change their values without redrawing the face.

## Colour roles
Assign a restricted subject accent while keeping painted backgrounds in quieter tones. Keep cel fills opaque with discrete shadow shapes and soften the painted distance.

Example palette. background #F4EFE5, foreground #293447, accent 1 #668DA0, accent 2 #C47C67.

## Lettering and captions
Compose for enabled subtitles before framing faces or gestures. Give approved lettering a flat or softly shaded field where action detail stays visible.

## Timing and movement
Keep the strongest acting drawings on held poses. Add short runs of new drawings for turns and impacts, while lighting and the background move on their own smoother tracks. Use smooth moving light over held drawings, and let a sharp impact drawing lead into a held peak. Keep each change in a painted shadow tied to its cel.

## Framing and viewpoint
Crane over multiple painted planes, track sideways with distinct rates of parallax, or frame a rear view down a receding passage for speed. Hold a bust while light sweeps across it, isolate a prop with soft background highlights, cut tight to eyes or pan over a painted still. Use a radial burst and held impact pose, move through a portal, or stage a steady two-shot for conversation. Revisit an earlier composition to show what changed. Use deliberate cuts and motivated flashes. Keep the cels and any enabled captions readable.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, land action sound on the drawn contact. Leave breathing room around held poses. When enabled, distinguish cloth, steps and prop sounds from the environment, leaving room for speech.

## Characteristic actions
- Hold a reading pose, change to a strong anticipation drawing and pan along one background layer.
- Rest on a backlit pose, use a drawn impact frame or sweep light across a held face to change the mood.

## Review checks
Inspect the change between held drawings. Make sure cel outlines, main shadows and the background perspective remain aligned during the turn.

## Implementation tools
Keep pose drawings, multiply shadows, painted planes and light sweeps separately seekable. Sample cel exposure in held steps, register painted planes and keep line work crisp at target scale.

## Project choices
Use the approach for a quiet encounter, a journey through scale or a sudden action beat. Use a reaction, machinery or a landscape reveal. The project supplies its own cast and design.

> Rounded forms bend and stretch in long arcs, putting the force and direction of each action into the silhouette.

## Visual identity
Show the direction and weight of actions with flexible forms. Use flexible tube limbs and bold rounded poses to communicate a physical action. Use rounded forms and curved limbs with clear hand and foot anchors. A pose should read from its bend and silhouette before facial details are added.

## Surfaces and construction
Use rounded segments, clear hands and continuous contour through the joints. Build round body shapes with clean joints and stable ink weight.

## Colour roles
Use strong outer values to keep funny or fast poses readable. Keep bright and dark masses separated so limb arcs read at a glance.

Example palette. background #F4ECD9, foreground #1C1B18.

## Lettering and captions
Place enabled type along an open arc or in a still area of the frame. Leave room for extended hands and feet at their widest reach.

## Timing and movement
Lead each action with a clear bend and let the curve travel through the limbs. Stretch into the action, compress at contact and hold a clean recovery pose.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame the full contact and allow room for a limb to extend. Use a stable whole-body view for the action and close in only for a readable reaction.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, spot the decisive landing or reach instead of every bend. If effects are enabled, give real contacts stronger emphasis than in-between motion.

## Characteristic actions
Stretch one arm to reach a visible target and let the body recoil in response.

Anticipate, stretch through contact and let the silhouette settle in one readable pose.

## Review checks
Check each curved limb through the stretch and collapse. The hand and foot should stay attached on fast arcs and squash frames.

## Implementation tools
Drive curves and grips from a shared pose state with deliberate holds. Use articulated curves with pinned end points and replacement drawings for extreme poses.

## Project choices
Choose a physical task, a supporting prop or a short action with an obvious recovery. Vary the gesture or distance while keeping the pose rhythm and grounded weight.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Visible brush marks follow the surfaces of a spatial scene and change with its light, distance and viewpoint.

## Visual identity
Make lighting and form read through placed brushwork on 3D surfaces. Let visible brush marks explain three-dimensional form and light.

## Surfaces and construction
Use broad strokes for mass and finer strokes at the focal edges. Use directional painterly texture on models and keep marks aligned with their surfaces.

## Colour roles
Keep value groups coherent when viewpoint changes. Use controlled colour masses and let the key light separate planes without a hard glossy coat.

Example palette. background #EFE4D1, foreground #38454A, accent 1 #7D9A95, accent 2 #BB7C65.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved lettering on a broad light or dark value region. Avoid placing small glyphs over noisy brushwork or a rapidly changing specular edge.

## Timing and movement
Move from a stable painted pose and let camera or light expose a change in planes. Put the greatest movement on the form and keep brush texture attached during shifts.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a measured oblique view that reveals depth and preserves the brushwork. Move slowly across the surface so stroke direction remains readable.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, choose a sparse cue at a real contact or reveal. When audible, use environment or material sound relevant to the depicted action.

## Characteristic actions
Turn a painted object until the same brush marks visibly follow changing facets.

Move the light or view while keeping strokes attached to the object.

## Review checks
Inspect a moving close-up for texture swimming. Shadows should describe the figure while shaped brush marks keep their direction on the surface.

## Implementation tools
Anchor stroke direction and density to surface coordinates. Use surface-aligned brush textures and simplified material response in the project's 3D pipeline. Store broad painted colour in surface coordinates and keep directional marks on a separate map. Drive the changing light through the 3D scene so those marks retain their placement.

## Project choices
Choose a product, landscape or object whose shape is revealed by lighting. Choose a painted object or terrain scene with one consistent brush scale.

Consider a full camera circuit around a stationary subject with angle-specific annotations and a closing front view. Require complete geometry or sufficient captured turntable views. Consider a progress-controlled handoff between outgoing and incoming chapters with synchronized copy and readable endpoints. Choose one compatible transition treatment and make both forward and backward state evaluation coherent.

Use real depth geometry or a clearly identified 2.5D approximation. Do not translate a camera through a flat illustration and call it a dolly.
Requires real 3D depth or an explicitly labeled parallax alternative. Orbit the camera, not the subject; avoid uncontrolled full rotations.

Use Lighting State Progression when time of day, weather or world state advances the story. Preserve this style’s material grammar and fixed environmental anchors; coordinate lighting, shadows, reflections and state-owned accents. Keep approved base material colors and medium limits. An authored front is optional; do not infer its precise method from source stills.

Orbit a fully modeled painterly hero (for example a sculpted character or still-life object) on a painted ground. Brush textures must be mapped to the surface or stable in object space, so marks don't crawl as θ changes, and the back must be painted as carefully as the front. Keep the stylized key light fixed in world space so the painted light-dark masses visibly travel across the form. Use moderate orbit speed and full holds.

sources.style_evidence: 3D environment with soft, controlled colour masses, painterly cloud shapes, stylized grass and rounded tree canopies. There are no glossy photoreal highlights, and the surfaces read as handled colour rather than PBR realism.
sources.palette_lesson: Colour here is a lighting and biome choice, not a fixed recipe. This example uses a midday temperate meadow: a soft, desaturated blue sky, white volumetric-looking clouds, a dominant saturated yellow-green field, and two small accent families (lavender-violet and ochre/rust) scattered as clusters. A neutral man-made focal object uses charcoal, off-white and warm timber. The transferable rules: one dominant ground colour field, one atmospheric sky gradient, and two or three sparse complementary accents placed in clusters near the camera. The focal object stays neutral, plus one warm accent so it reads. Keep values soft and contrast moderate. Haze should lighten and desaturate distance. The blue sky and green grass are this author's scene choices, not part of the style. The same craft works at dusk, in a dry summer or in snow by swapping the ground and sky families while keeping the accent-cluster logic.

sources.style_evidence: Stylized 3D environment with soft, painterly color masses in grass and sky, warm stylized lighting, haze and god-rays, and no glossy photoreal highlights. Grass blades act like directional painted strokes on the forms.
sources.palette_lesson: The colors seen here belong to this author's chosen scene. Golden-hour peach-amber haze, yellow-green and ochre grass, olive hills, chestnut and honey animals, and a teal plus red-brown costume accent describe one windswept-plain setting at one time of day. They are not rules of the style. What defines the style is the treatment: a 3D scene shaded as soft color masses, with atmospheric perspective that fades distant layers toward the sky color, one warm or cool key light, and saturation held at a moderate level. The UI belongs to a separate flat layer of light cream cards with dark text and one accent hue. For a new subject, build the palette from that subject's own environment and time of day. Then keep three roles: a hazy sky and depth gradient, a dominant ground-cover mass, and a small complementary accent on the hero subject. Recheck caption contrast against whatever the sky or ground becomes.

> Rhythmic paint marks and deliberate colour groupings describe a scene with the energy of a worked canvas.

## Visual identity
Let directional marks and colour changes suggest the energy of a place. Use directional marks and rhythmic colour to describe a simplified painted scene.

## Surfaces and construction
Lay related brush groups over visible underpainting. Organise brush strokes into persistent groups that follow surfaces or visible currents. Keep stroke length and direction tied to the plane being painted. Use small clusters of bright daubs to describe a change in light without breaking the larger value mass.

## Colour roles
Use local hue contrast to structure the scene before adding detail. Lay related and opposing pigments beside one another with a chosen painted reference.

Example palette. background #EEE2C2, foreground #344F60, accent 1 #B58B42, accent 2 #638873, accent 3 #B26B57.

## Lettering and captions
Put enabled text in a quieter colour patch or a held margin. Leave several brush widths between the lettering and the main edge cluster.

## Timing and movement
Lay groups of brush marks according to the surface direction. Start with broader bands of colour, add shorter strokes when the form turns and rest before introducing new colour movement.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame a complete painted field before moving closer to the strongest directional area. Show the overall value pattern before moving in on the particular marks.

## Sound options
If audio is enabled, let longer phrases follow larger colour or stroke changes. If enabled, use scene ambience and brief contacts in the represented space.

## Characteristic actions
Lead the eye into a turn by shifting the direction of a cluster of marks.

Change the light or brush grouping while holding the main silhouette.

## Review checks
Check that brush marks keep their size and direction as a layer moves. At a small size, the stroke groups should resolve into a clear form.

## Implementation tools
Place strokes along form directions and seed variation per region. Keep brush assets registered to the painted plane and animate reveals or whole layers.

## Project choices
Choose a landscape, interior or still life with a strong visible rhythm. Use an original figure, still life or outdoor scene with a deliberate stroke grammar.

sources.style_evidence: Directional swirling brushwork in the sky, a flame-shaped cypress, rhythmic paint dabs, and a strong contrast between deep blue and yellow. The video explicitly uses one specific painting as its reference rather than generic swirls.
sources.palette_lesson: The deep ultramarine and cobalt, cyan-white and gold-yellow scheme belongs to this author's chosen reference painting (a night scene), not to the style itself. What defines the style is the medium logic: a dominant cool or warm field built from many directional brush dabs rather than flat colour; a small set of high-value complementary accents (here yellow halos and warm windows against blue) that act as light sources; and dark, saturated forms (the cypress) that anchor the composition. The near-black gallery wall and gilt frame are a presentation device around the canvas, not the canvas colour. The interface borrows the painting's blue and gold so it stays subordinate. Inside the 3D world the palette shifts with distance, from deep blue-green to lighter grey-green up close. The single most saturated warm accent, the orange cat, is reserved for the object the viewer should find. For a new subject, pick the field from that subject's light — daytime, dusk or interior — and keep one complementary accent family for focal points.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Transparent washes and distinct brush marks develop on one sheet, with unpainted paper supplying the light.

## Visual identity
Let washes and brush marks make the subject take shape on one visible sheet. Leave paper exposed at highlights and transitions so soft pigment boundaries remain part of the image.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate transparent washes, dry bristle lines, ink details and unpainted areas. Let pigment collect at a wet boundary and show paper tooth through the edge of a drier stroke.

## Colour roles
Create light through reserved paper and use overlapping washes to show local tone. Build transparent glazes and reserve unpainted paper for the strongest lights.

Example palette. background #FBF6EB, foreground #3C4E58, accent 1 #8EA8B6, accent 2 #BF8E7A, accent 3 #9BAE8E.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved lettering in reserved paper or a sufficiently even wash. Keep strong blooms away from letters with small counters.

## Timing and movement
Let the initial wash spread from the painted boundary before introducing a second pigment. Slow the inner spread at drier edges and reserve crisp detail until the strokes have settled. Let an edge of new paint reveal the underlying scene where a transition needs to stay on the paper. Move thin mist independently from dry marks.

## Framing and viewpoint
Travel laterally across the painted space, tilt along a tall subject or hold as marks appear on the sheet. Ease close for detail, withdraw to reveal a map-like arrangement or hold the viewpoint while time changes. Use a wash clearing to paper, a brush edge or a sliding sheet to bring in a new scene. Leave visible margins and a clear place for any approved words.

## Sound options
If enabled, use restrained brush or water cues, leaving room for the selected music or voice. If sound is enabled, let water and paper cues follow the brush rather than drive every frame.

## Characteristic actions
- Lay a soft wash into a shallow shape and follow it with a local dry edge as the main form arrives.
- Paint in the first layer, let an edge bleed or let a wash carry the next view across the sheet.

## Review checks
Look at the dry edge and at the darkest overlap. Keep the paper grain and unpainted gaps visible through the bleed.

## Implementation tools
Animate wash density and stroke order in paper space and keep sheets stable between views. Combine fixed paper texture with transparent wash masks and distinct wet and dry edge rules. Separate dry deposits, wash spread and paper texture. Use a seeded edge to control pigment concentration and let multiple translucent passes darken their overlap.

## Project choices
Choose a changing place, a specimen with a note or a comparison that uses colour meaningfully. Paint natural forms, diagrams or settings. Maintain transparent overlaps and visible paper.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Loaded ink gathers into dark strokes and spreads into soft washes. Open paper keeps the marks distinct.

## Visual identity
Give open paper equal weight with the dark strokes and make a single gesture feel consequential.

## Surfaces and construction
Use a narrow brush mark for a dry tip and a wider, softer field where loaded ink spreads into wet paper. Keep a separate paper layer visible through thin ink and within dry gaps.

## Colour roles
Use ink dilution to express depth and reserve the approved accent for an important mark. Use the paper as the lightest value. Keep dense ink close to the focal stroke and reserve a small accent if approved. Reserve bare paper for air, water or distance. Grade near detail from dark wet ink into pale brush deposits and keep the paper visible at dry edges.

Example palette. ivory paper #F4EFDF, dilutable black ink #242724.

## Lettering and captions
Put approved words in open paper areas. Match nearby mark weight only where this preserves a clear distinction between a caption and the painted subject.

## Timing and movement
Move the thick part of the brushstroke first, then pull the tip into a thinner end. Let moisture spread briefly from dark marks and keep untouched paper available between painted forms. Hold the main painted pose before the gesture, then expose a few purposeful pose changes. Keep wet bleeds and brush travel independent so the spread can continue after the hand stops.

## Framing and viewpoint
Hold on open paper or travel along it horizontally like a handscroll and vertically like a hanging scroll. Track a figure with lead room and slower distant layers. Use spare high wides and low views under a dark wash, then isolate a decisive mark with a sharp close cut. Move into a bloom or mist to change scale, withdraw until the small mark joins the composition and revisit an earlier view to show change. Keep the open paper visible.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use distinct dry brush and soft wet-paper sounds. Let open space have silence. If effects are enabled, separate the brief brush contact from any environmental bed.

## Characteristic actions
- Lead with one dry stroke, follow with a misty wash and preserve a clean unpainted focal opening.
- Carry a brush gesture into a character action, enter a growing wash or reveal a dry white gap in one loaded pass.

## Review checks
Inspect whether the wash stays local to the deposited ink. Check that dry brush gaps and the thinnest stroke ends survive at delivery size.

## Implementation tools
Animate ink load and diffusion from paper-space masks instead of colouring objects with a screen overlay. Grow wash masks from fixed seed points and texture their borders differently from dry brush.

## Project choices
Choose a scroll journey, a brief gesture in open space or a landscape made legible by one dark mass. Use landscape, animal or calligraphic marks. Keep a visible reserve of untouched paper.

sources.style_evidence: Monochrome black ink on paper: a single brush stroke draws the ridge, stippled ink fills the peaks, and diluted pale ranges plus fog show distance, with large empty space. Composition follows Chinese shan-shui layered recession.
sources.palette_lesson: The colors that define the style come from the medium: carbon-black ink thinned into a ladder of greys, with a faint cool blue-grey cast in the most distant, most diluted layers. The paper is a pale substrate that shows through as fog and empty space. The warm off-white paper tone in this clip is the author's example for an autumn moon-night mood, not a requirement. Keep the ink value ladder (dense black foreground, mid-grey mid-ground, pale tinted distance, unpainted paper as mist) and choose the substrate per scene: cool grey-white xuan paper for winter or dawn, pale silk-celadon for spring water scenes, aged tea-brown silk for historical subjects, or a deep indigo-dyed or dusk-blue field with lighter pigment for night (inverting the value logic carefully). One restrained accent such as a vermilion seal or a pale moon wash is optional. Check that text keeps contrast against both the paper and the fog layers.

sources.style_evidence: Each character is preceded and surrounded by a diluted grey ink bloom that diffuses over time, together with pressure-like stroke ends and a large amount of deliberate empty paper. The ink treatment is closest to sumi-e, though there is no landscape imagery.
sources.palette_lesson: This is a monochrome ink-on-paper scene. Black ink is the only solid pigment, diluted grey washes add tone, and the ground is a pale warm-grey paper with fibres and a soft vignette. Mid-grey type is used for captions, and a thin grey line is the secondary graphic. The pale warm-grey paper colour is this author's example, not the definition of the style. What defines the style is the medium: one dense ink plus its own dilutions, a visibly fibrous paper ground, and the halo being the same ink diluted rather than a shadow or a new hue. No seal colour or other chroma appears in seconds 1–8. For new subjects, the paper can be cool grey, blue-grey, pale celadon, unbleached kraft or a dark charcoal sheet. On a dark sheet, invert to pale ink or gofun white and keep tonal dilution as the second value. An optional single restrained accent, such as a vermilion seal, should only be added if the subject justifies it. Recheck caption contrast after any change, because the low-contrast grey captions are already near the readability limit.

> Opaque layers and the direction of visible strokes describe surfaces, light and the buildup of pigment.

## Visual identity
Build the image from strokes that describe the light and orientation of the subject. Let choices of brush direction, thickness and overlap reveal form as the paint accumulates.

## Surfaces and construction
Put thin underpainting beneath broad loaded strokes and reserve fine strokes for important edges. Use opaque daubs for impasto or matte gouache fields as the subject requires. Give directional highlights to raised ridges and keep opaque strokes distinct at an overlap.

## Colour roles
Set a value structure first and use a local colour event for the decisive change. Use opaque colour deposits with visible ridges and reserve wet highlights for the highest strokes.

Example palette. background #F1E6CF, foreground #3E4C48, accent 1 #9B604C, accent 2 #A89656, accent 3 #63818A.

## Lettering and captions
Reserve a broad, even value for enabled lettering. Keep brush ridges out of fine lettering unless painted lettering is part of the approved design.

## Timing and movement
Lay a flat value mass before brushing opaque colour over it. Bring highlights in as separate short strokes, and hold the arrangement long enough for the overpainting to read.

## Framing and viewpoint
Move along the painted surface as if it had relief. Combine a slow truck and push in a wide, tilt up from ground or reflection, close in during a quiet moment and draw back from a detail. Turn as the view rises to overhead, return to a familiar wide, or hold while light travels across it. Use a macro slide to show the brushwork and a rapid pan into another painted plate. Keep crops inside the prepared artwork.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, distinguish a short palette-knife scrape at a raised deposit from a softer brush pass. Let each cue end when the tool lifts.

## Characteristic actions
- Build colour ridges in several overlapping strokes and move light across a restrained area.
- Rework a patch with a knife, move light across relief or let movement uncover the next cluster of marks.

## Review checks
Check the order of layers at the most covered pose. Keep edge thickness and paint grain tied to each patch of colour.

## Implementation tools
Seed the stroke field per surface and drive the reveal in stable local coordinates. Compute shallow directional ridge normals or textured strokes. Keep each paint deposit fixed in canvas space.

## Project choices

sources.style_evidence: Every frame's terrain is built from opaque, palette-knife oil/gouache-like slabs and thick white impasto foam with relief shading. The on-screen label 'OIL ON CANVAS' is author framing, not evidence; the visible brushwork alone supports this match.
sources.palette_lesson: Here the colours come from the subject: a beach at low tide gives turquoise/cyan sea, white foam and warm sand-ochre ground, with small saturated sprite accents (red/white umbrellas, purple pearls, green props) and cream plus golden-yellow caption type. Those hues are this author's choice for a beach, not rules of the style. The style constraints are different: (1) opaque paint covers the whole frame with no blank canvas showing; (2) each terrain zone gets a limited family of 2–3 close values built from overlapping knife slabs; (3) the brightest impasto (here the white foam) carries the relief highlights; (4) game sprites use small, saturated, high-chroma accents so they read against broad painted masses; (5) UI type is cream or white with dark outlines so it stays legible over any paint. For a new subject, take the terrain families from that environment and re-check caption contrast against the busiest area.

sources.style_evidence: Thick, visible oil-like strokes and impasto-style dabs on the canvas at 1–5 s. A gilt frame presents the image as a framed oil painting.
sources.palette_lesson: The deep ultramarine and cobalt, cyan-white and gold-yellow scheme belongs to this author's chosen reference painting (a night scene), not to the style itself. What defines the style is the medium logic: a dominant cool or warm field built from many directional brush dabs rather than flat colour; a small set of high-value complementary accents (here yellow halos and warm windows against blue) that act as light sources; and dark, saturated forms (the cypress) that anchor the composition. The near-black gallery wall and gilt frame are a presentation device around the canvas, not the canvas colour. The interface borrows the painting's blue and gold so it stays subordinate. Inside the 3D world the palette shifts with distance, from deep blue-green to lighter grey-green up close. The single most saturated warm accent, the orange cat, is reserved for the object the viewer should find. For a new subject, pick the field from that subject's light — daytime, dusk or interior — and keep one complementary accent family for focal points.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Powdered marks accumulate into velvety shadows or coloured layers. Preserved paper and softened edges show volume.

## Visual identity
Use soft tonal accumulation to describe weight and volume. Choose charcoal for dense tonal masses or pastel for layered pigment. Show the hand's pressure through dense dark strokes, broad powder deposits and areas lifted to paper. Use an identifiable contour as the structure the smudges describe.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate powdered broad marks, sharper contours and erased highlights. Allow powder, smudged edges and uncovered tooth to remain visible on a fixed sheet.

## Colour roles
Carry strong light through exposed paper or selected light pigment. Use charcoal values or a consistent pastel family, with paper left clear in highlights.

Example palette. background #EDE7DC, foreground #353330.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved lettering on a clear ground away from smudges. Keep soft grain outside the smallest letter shapes.

## Timing and movement
Block the largest dark with the side of the charcoal or pastel, then bring in thinner edges. Show one smudge or lift as a visible change in tone and pause on it.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a still paper view and show the grain in a limited close-up. Frame marks closely for technique and widen once the subject reads.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a soft dry rub for broad shading and a shorter stroke sound when a hard edge appears. Leave lifted highlights nearly quiet unless an eraser is shown.

## Characteristic actions
Lift pigment from the focal edge while keeping soft residue beside it.

Build a dark mass, lift a highlight or sharpen the edge that carries the form.

## Review checks
Check that highlights can read as exposed paper or lifted pigment. Keep grain scale consistent between a close view and the wider drawing.

## Implementation tools
Composite pigment and erasure in page coordinates with separate pressure maps. Composite seeded pigment and eraser masks in paper coordinates.

## Project choices
Choose a contour study, a texture comparison or a changing light direction. Use a tonal study, drawing or colour field with one dominant powdered medium.

> The weight, order and spacing of authentic brush strokes carry the written characters and the rhythm of their making.

## Visual identity
Let the authentic order and weight of the written strokes carry the action. Let authentic brush strokes and spacing express the meaning of the supplied characters.

## Surfaces and construction
Build loaded brush edges, ink variation and open gaps where the bristles spread. Show wet ink, dry edges and pressure variation on a quiet paper field.

## Colour roles
Use paper and ink as the main values with a small approved accent where useful. Use ink and paper as the main pair, with a vermilion seal only when appropriate.

Example palette. background #F5EFDE, foreground #20211E, accent 1 #B4382A.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved characters and script direction. Keep any additional caption in a distinct quiet area so readers can see which marks belong to the calligraphy.

Draw in the natural stroke order and show the brush press, change direction and release. Hold complete characters before moving to the next part of the sheet.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame the character column or line with room for intentional blank paper. Keep the writing surface clear and show the full character after a close pass. Use a plan view for stroke order and open spacing. Move to a shallow angle only to show brush pressure or wet ink, with enough of the current character left in frame.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, distinguish the brush's first contact, the loaded sweep and its release from the paper. Let the darkest stroke carry the most audible pressure.

## Characteristic actions
Draw a pressure-weighted stroke from entry through taper and hold its relation to adjacent characters.

Check stroke joins, pressure changes and white space when the character is complete. Use the actual authored strokes for an inspection at any point in the drawing.

Choose a phrase or character that benefits from seeing how its form is made. Choose a verified calligraphic script and composition suited to the supplied text.

> The composition takes shape against a wall, from broad paint passes to the lettering, outlines and marks that make it readable.

## Visual identity
Show the wall's material and the sequence of a painted design. Treat street lettering as paint applied to a real or clearly illustrated wall.

## Surfaces and construction
Use paint fills, rough masonry and separate shadow or overspray near real edges. Keep wall pores, sprayed edges and distinct overlapping paint passes surface-bound.

## Colour roles
Give the message clear value contrast against the wall. Choose a coherent lettering palette and reserve contrast around the main word.

Example palette. background #E7E1D4, foreground #272631, accent 1 #BC4861, accent 2 #388A8B, accent 3 #CEA248.

## Lettering and captions
Place enabled copy in deliberate mural areas with flat enough fill to read. Let the wall texture show through larger letters where the brief allows it.

## Timing and movement
Sweep each spray pass along a continuous path. Let successive passes increase paint at the edge, then add a stencil lift or final contour after the main shapes settle.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a front or shallow corner view that allows the letters to be read on the wall. Frame the wall as an object before moving close to the working marks.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use short spray bursts corresponding to visible paint passes. If sound is enabled, a visible paint pass or handling cue can mark progress.

## Characteristic actions
Lay a broad colour fill, cut in its outline and leave a credible overspray edge.

Build a broad fill, pass over it with an outline or reveal the completed wall.

## Review checks
Inspect overspray at adjoining masks and examine the wall in a moving view. Marks should follow the wall surface and keep believable edge softness.

## Implementation tools
Anchor paint and texture in wall coordinates and key material changes separately. Build stable wall and paint masks with local seeded spray density and committed passes. Separate the sprayed mask, overspray and wall texture. Anchor each stencil edge to the wall coordinates and time the paint build-up independently from the stencil lift.

## Project choices
Choose a wall composition, layered correction or spread of paint from one point. Use a mural, original letter study or wall diagram with one coherent hand.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Backlight separates a strong silhouette from the environment. Readable profiles, spacing and held poses carry the action.

## Visual identity
Let strong outlines carry the action, with gestures and gaps between overlapping figures showing intent. Keep facial details subordinate to the silhouette and place emphasis on the moment a profile changes.

## Surfaces and construction
Compose distinct light, ground and subject layers, adding reflected or glancing light only where it helps.

## Colour roles
Keep the main shapes at opposite values and reserve middle tones for depth. Keep profiles on distinct clear values. Use accent colour only to carry a deliberate response. Separate figure and ground by value first. Use an accent on the object that changes hands or enters the scene, and check that its silhouette reads against both.

Example palette. background #F5E9CF, foreground #253442, accent 1 #647F81.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved lettering outside the silhouette's full travel, especially where an arm or prop crosses a foreground figure. Give captions a stable high-contrast patch if the background changes.

## Timing and movement
Introduce the strongest full-body silhouette first. Change pose by exposing clear space between limbs and give overlaps a pause before separate shapes cross again. Use a quick decisive silhouette change and give it a short settling motion when the subject has weight. Hold the clean outline when several figures need to be read together.

## Framing and viewpoint
Bring a strong profile against a large light source, track low at water level for group movement or pan sideways to show sequence. Whip to shift attention, withdraw high and wide to show scale, hold a medium view at a key beat or circle a frozen gesture. Keep the silhouette against light. Use an occluding near figure or a matching graphic shape for a transition.

## Sound options
If a track is enabled, use its measured timing for the strongest hits. Preserve the visible phrase on mute. If audible, use physical sounds as accents and allow the chosen music space to read.

## Characteristic actions
- Make two shapes land in synchrony, then give a single shape a delayed response with clear intent.
- Hold on the single expressive gesture or move the light behind a group as their poses change.

## Review checks
Scrub through the closest overlap and inspect at a small size. Check that the face, hands and objects important to the action remain distinguishable by outline.

## Implementation tools
Use separate scene layers and keep the light and pose timing tied to the same clock. Key each silhouette from shared cue times and align silhouettes at the intended landing positions.

## Project choices
Choose a waterline, backlit stage or horizon where silhouettes remain clear. Use dancers, shapes or objects. Keep expression in profiles and spacing.

sources.palette_lesson: The colours are scene-driven, not a fixed recipe. The night title uses a near-black warm field lit by one amber sun. The daytime chapter switches to an amber/apricot gradient sky over dark brown soil. The amber in these frames is this author's example for a dawn/sunset and shochu-warmth subject, not a style constant. What should transfer is the structure: one dominant ambient field per chapter (dark night or a luminous gradient), one semantic subject colour reused for emphasis text and transition wipes (here plum = sweet potato), off-white or dark-brown type chosen for contrast against that field, and a single cool/neutral accent reserved for a process element (white water streaks). For new subjects, derive the field from the setting and process stage and recheck text contrast whenever the field flips from dark to light.

sources.style_evidence: Every shot relies on solid dark silhouettes: marching figures, rows of audience heads, pursuers. They read through outline and pose against backlit fields, with clear depth layers and almost no internal detail.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-black, cool slate and blue-gray world is this author's choice for an oppressive, broadcast-dystopia mood. It is not a fixed rule of the style. What defines the craft: (1) a narrow, low-saturation environment value range; (2) one dominant light source per shot (tunnel core, projection screen, ceiling strips) that sets the silhouettes; (3) exactly one saturated hue reserved for the protagonist or turning point, with matching local light spill. The orange-red accent is meaningful because nothing else in the frame is warm. For new subjects, change the environment's color family and keep the single complementary accent: deep teal-green sea cave with a coral accent; dusty violet desert dusk with a lime or acid-yellow accent; warm sepia factory haze with a cobalt accent; cold snow-white overcast field with dark figures and a crimson accent; murky olive jungle with a magenta accent. Recheck that the silhouettes still separate from the glow field, and that captions on bright surfaces keep their contrast.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Cut photographs, torn paper and printed type move on separate levels of the same tabletop composition.

## Visual identity
Arrange physical prints on a visible work surface. A torn edge, covered corner or exposed film border can show how two images relate when a piece shifts into place.

## Surfaces and construction
Use cut photo edges, torn colour paper and different stock thicknesses to form the layers. Build torn edges with fibres and soft wear, and keep those details attached to the stock. Give each photo an independent thickness and shadow so stacked corners retain their order.

## Colour roles
Keep older print tones coordinated and use an accent on the new or moving piece. Keep paper aging varied but make focal fragments and copied facts readable against their own ground.

Example palette. background #EDE3CD, foreground #393329, accent 1 #85765D.

## Lettering and captions
Put enabled words on a small paper scrap or on uncovered table space. Keep the main image edge or important face clear of caption layers.

## Timing and movement
Place one printed fragment on the table and let its shadow settle before another overlaps it. Use a deliberate slip, turn or lift to reveal a hidden edge or connection. Step the pose of a small cutout independently from the smooth camera or main table movement. Keep its shadow tied to its current printed pose.

## Framing and viewpoint
Move over a tabletop as a flat page. Establish the composition, track a travelling piece, approach a detail or draw back for scale. Enter a cut hole to find another scene, whip sideways across a seam, match one piece across scales or carry its action through a cut. Track a chart as it builds, then show the complete comparison without losing the paper field.

## Sound options
If enabled, time paper scuffs at contact. Keep recordings appropriate to the content and available rights. With effects enabled, use fibre slides, small handling sounds and a soft paper landing.

## Characteristic actions
- Carry one original printed element across an overlap and reveal a second layer through a cut edge.
- Lift a cutout, align a separate plate or pass through a hole to discover another scene.

## Review checks
Inspect moving print grain, corners and shadows through an overlap. Separate each item's surface wear from its moving contact shadow.

## Implementation tools
Give each cutout a stable mask, depth and contact shadow. Mask identifiable individual paper edges and layer them with consistent shadow depth.

## Project choices
Choose an archive sequence, a material comparison or a series linked by found paper shapes. Use varied licensed or original printed fragments. Track one focal element through several overlaps.

sources.palette_lesson: The base is a quiet, low-chroma desk/stage layer: here, a near-white map with gray-blue linework. White and off-white paper, black ink type, and small saturated accents (tape, pins, marker strokes, play button) carry the color. The color families (pale gray map, sky-blue/coral/purple/yellow tapes, orange marker) are this author's brand-specific example, not a rule. The style constraints are: (1) a subdued, low-contrast environmental ground that relates to the subject, (2) paper surfaces lighter than or distinct from that ground, with visible torn edges and soft shadows, (3) black or near-black ink for readable copy, (4) a limited set of saturated accents assigned to tape, pins and annotations, with one hot accent (orange) for emphasis strokes. The butter-cream full panel is a transition wipe, not the canvas.

sources.style_evidence: A tactile craft layer: headline tiles rotated slightly like cut labels, tape strips holding cards and notes, a sticky note, contact shadows, all on a grainy paper surface.
sources.palette_lesson: The warm kraft paper ground, espresso-brown type, caramel/amber emphasis and cream tiles are this author's palette for a coffee-shop example: the redesigned site and the stage share that palette on purpose. They are not a requirement of the style. What the style needs is a single textured matte surface as canvas, with a soft vignette. One dark ink handles headlines and step pills, one warm accent handles emphasized words, number dots and active buttons. A separate annotation-ink color goes to script and arrows, and props like sticky notes and tape carry their own prop colors. Embedded screen content keeps its own palette, and here a clashing 'before' palette was used deliberately against the harmonized 'after'. For a new subject, choose the surface color from the product or brand mood, then re-derive ink, accent and annotation colors so headline text and labels keep strong contrast against that surface and against any card they sit on.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> One strong paper colour and cut openings make the subject legible as flat pieces unfold or pivot.

## Visual identity
Use the outer and inner edges of cut paper as the drawing. Let overlapping pieces reveal figure, depth and the useful gaps between them as the scene changes.

## Surfaces and construction
Give each sheet a cut edge, paper fibres and thin cast shadow. When a part bends, keep the crease and stock surface attached so the shadow follows the actual cut piece.

## Colour roles
Separate the hero and ground by value. Use a small reflective foil accent only when it belongs to the artwork. Use one strong paper hue and let the open cutouts carry contrast and pattern.

Example palette. background #F2EAD8, foreground #304849, accent 1 #C17F63, accent 2 #829776.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved words on a flat paper piece with a clear margin. Move that piece as a unit if it forms part of the composition.

## Timing and movement
Slide cut shapes on distinct layers and give the nearest piece a clear leading edge. Settle the stack before moving the next piece across its cast shadow. Use discrete drawings or poses for paper figures and continuous light for a cast shadow or flying paper piece. Give a cut line time to close before lifting the fragment.

## Framing and viewpoint
Track the scissors at close range, hold a frontal paper emblem, drift across parallax layers or use a low wide to make a raised piece feel large. Look down over the worktable, push into a lit cutout and draw back to show its neighbours. Use a peel, fold, lifted sheet or cut opening between pictures. Rotate about a rosette when radial order matters. Keep flat layers square enough to read as paper.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, spot scissors or a light paper rustle on visible movement. When audible, time dry scissors, lifted paper and a small settling sound to contact.

## Characteristic actions
- Unfold a continuous stencil across a fold axis and reveal a second cut through shared negative space.
- Fold and cut, release an attached figure or let a peeled layer reveal another shape.

## Review checks
Inspect bevels and shadow offsets at the narrowest gap. Check that each moving piece retains its own depth and silhouette.

## Implementation tools
Transform cut layers in their own plane and drive shadow distance from their actual separation. Use cutout masks with continuous bridges and pivot their grouped halves at the fold line. Store cutout contours in the local coordinates of each sheet and assign their actual thickness to layers. Let shadows and light trails follow the moving contour rather than a rectangular frame.

## Project choices
Choose a repeated ornament, object or silhouette that can be recognised by positive and cut-away shapes. Use plants, figures or abstract decorative cuts. Preserve the connected sheet.

sources.palette_lesson: The colours that define the style are the medium's own: a lightly textured paper canvas with fiber speckle and a soft vignette, matte opaque paper pieces in a limited set (about four to six families), a near-black rounded heavy display ink for text, and small muted geometric confetti. The author's specific colour choices (warm greige paper for the statement scene, mint/sage sky with yellow-green to forest-green hills, a mustard sun, navy and coral confetti, a lime highlighter) are one example tied to a growth and enablement subject. They are not fixed tokens. Note that the canvas tint already changes with the scene in this source, from warm off-white to cool mint, which shows the background is meant to follow the scene. In new projects, keep the paper grain, the matte cut-paper layers and the dark ink type, and choose the paper tint from the subject. Keep strong contrast between the dark type and the light paper, keep accents sparse, and do not let the highlighter or confetti compete with the headline.

sources.style_evidence: Every object is a flat cut or torn paper shape with a visible white paper-core edge and limited flat paper colors. There are no outlines, shapes are layered as stacked sheets, and the grain is uniform.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's colors belong to the subject and scene: a sky-blue sky band, a row of muted multicolor houses (teal, terracotta, ochre, slate blue, sand) and a kraft-tan street for an outdoor 1920s town, then teal striped wallpaper and reddish-brown wood for the lab. The background changes per scene, so there is no fixed canvas color. What defines the style is the medium: matte, slightly desaturated paper stocks, fine fiber grain, a white torn-paper core on every edge, flat fills without outlines, and a small set of ink colors for type (dark navy plus one crimson highlight, with pale grey for words not yet reached) on cream label strips. Keep the white tear rim readable against whatever field you choose. Light fields need a slightly darker paper behind the rim, or a soft contact shadow.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A connected sheet takes shape fold by fold. Creases, overlapping faces and contact shadows show where the paper moves.

## Visual identity
Keep the source sheet recognisable as successive creases turn it into a more complex form. Pause at a partly folded pose where the viewer can still see how the original outline became the new volume.

## Surfaces and construction
Crease a flat sheet into facets joined at fixed hinge lines. Give opposing paper faces different light responses and model contact shadows where facets touch.

## Colour roles
Use related paper hues across one sheet. Let light angle, face direction and contact shadows separate the folded facets, with a darker reverse side if showing it makes the fold easier to read.

Example palette. background #F4F0E5, foreground #304347, accent 1 #BA6F5C, accent 2 #7C9A86.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved marks or labels where the fold will not conceal their essential parts. Give subtitles a clear area outside the sheet's swing when the idea enables them.

## Timing and movement
Finish and settle a fold before starting another that depends on it. Let a flap travel around its crease, pause where it first touches the opposite face, then hold the finished form for inspection.

## Framing and viewpoint
Choose an angle that shows the crease edge and the moving plane together. Use short views along and across the crease so the viewer can see both rotation and final contact.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, distinguish a dry crease cue from the sound of the sheet settling. Time the first to visible pressure at the hinge and the second to the closing flap's contact.

## Characteristic actions
Fold one flap around its actual hinge from the flat sheet into a stacked face. Open or reverse a fold to show a shape change, then hold the result with the crease still visible.

## Review checks
Check sheet continuity, crease registration and panel overlap along the full move. At the most compressed stack, check that each visible face is on the correct side of its crease.

## Implementation tools
Parent facets to a fold hierarchy and key each crease angle explicitly. Check both direct seeks and reverse playback.

## Project choices
Choose a plausible fold sequence for an object, emblem or abstract form. Pick a subject whose outline changes in readable stages.

> A few distinct ink plates build the image. The colour changes where the plates overlap and registration slips.

## Visual identity
Show the order of make-ready, ink passes and overprint through the picture. Give each pass a visible contribution, such as a new part or a third colour where ink layers meet.

## Surfaces and construction
Build a separate density and knockout mask for each spot ink. Put registration offset and ink grain in the plate's coordinates so they travel with the print and retain the same overlap colour.

## Colour roles
Let the overlap create a third colour without introducing an unrelated ink. Build a small ink set and allow transparent overprint to create new combinations. Specify inks as separate print passes and use their intersection for a predictable third value. Give any dense small detail a single ink so slight offset does not erase the edge.

Example palette. background #F4EBD8, foreground #254687, accent 1 #D95664.

## Lettering and captions
Give approved type a single ink pass at small sizes. Keep off-register duplicates for large lettering where the edges remain legible.

## Timing and movement
Bring colour passes into registration one at a time. Hold the first ink impression while the second crosses it, then reveal the overlap colour as the new print settles. Keep the plate offset stable across held positions. Change registration only when a visible pass starts, the stock shifts or the action calls for a brief kick.

## Framing and viewpoint
Track beside a small moving figure or hold wide while it crosses, then hold horizon, disc and subject as one graphic. Use a low angle for foreground scale, a held two-shot for reaction or an overhead for pattern. Enter the dot screen, then pull far enough to see the printed sheet. Use a roller pass, overprint, shape match or clean cut between views. Keep any text on open sky or paper.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, give each printed pass a separate feed and release. Keep the mechanical cadence steady and align the sheet landing with the visible registration change.

## Characteristic actions
- Expose two clean separations, then register one slightly off centre to reveal the secondary colour.
- Add an ink layer to change the reading or carry a roller pass into the next picture.

## Review checks
Check the overlap colour and the offset at delivery size. Print texture should follow the same paper throughout the pass.

## Implementation tools
Combine ink densities in page coordinates and move the print as a single surface. Composite ink masks with controlled multiply overlap, stable grain and independent fixed plate offsets.

## Project choices
Choose a two-plate composition, an overlapping diagram or a limited-ink story sequence. Try a poster, sequence of symbols or an illustration. Keep the ink count and registration intentional.

> Dot screens, paper and print layers turn shading and numbers into a legible editorial image.

## Visual identity
Treat the picture as an editorial sheet that can call attention to a photo, document or measurement. Use changes in dot density, a stamp or a frame edge to locate the evidence.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep paper grain, spot ink, dot screens and document pieces on layers that move with the sheet.

## Colour roles
Use overprinted shadow or highlight to give related ink shapes depth. Keep documents on warm paper and use a single ink to mark the evidentiary feature.

Example palette. background #F8EFD9, foreground #253E56, accent 1 #C25143.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved small labels on a flat patch. Apply dot shading to large lettering only when its outline remains visible at delivery size.

## Timing and movement
Grow or replace dots according to tone on a stable grid. Let a tonal edge travel through the pattern and hold a full view where the dots combine into a single image. Let an incoming print or stamp overtravel slightly and then settle. Keep small line changes on separate steps so the underlying dot screen stays registered.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep a front-facing printed composition. Use a slight pulse or restrained push to tighten attention, quick decay on an impact and a short photographic flash for a revelation. Pan along the board to connect exhibits, punch into the dot pattern, slide to another folder or back out to the desk. Reserve open areas for headline, captions and small readouts. Make scene changes with a hard cut or dot-pattern reveal.

## Sound options

sources.palette_lesson: The constraint that defines the style is a strict two-or-three-ink system. One saturated spot colour, near-black and near-white swap figure/ground roles, and tone comes only from halftone dot density. The particular acid green, the single magenta title burst and the black terminal opening are this author's example (a brand-like choice), not requirements. What carries over is the polarity flips: dark emissive screen → light printed paper → accent colour promoted to full-bleed ground, with black type always as the key plate. For new subjects, pick one spot ink plus one contrast ink to suit the scene, keep a neutral dark or light partner, and make sure heavy type keeps contrast against the dot field wherever it is densest.

sources.style_evidence: The whole stage, the floor band and the confidence-bar fills are built from a consistent, regular halftone dot screen with clear outlines. Tone comes from dot density, and the dots stay anchored as the cards move.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's example is fully achromatic: a mid-charcoal halftone ground, black-ink objects with white keylines, off-white paper cards and white LED dots. A darker near-black overlay is used for the spotlight beat. The measured composite dominant shifts from mid grey (s1–6) to very dark grey (s7–8). That reflects the dimming overlay, not a second palette. What defines the style is not grey itself. It is the print constraint: tone made by dot density in one ink against a substrate, plus solid ink badges and stamps, with emphasis carried by luminance and inversion rather than hue. For new subjects the ground can be any single ink-on-substrate pairing that suits the scene. Keep paper cards (or the subject's equivalent) as the brightest plane. Reserve the darkest overlay for focus moments, and check that the small text on cards stays legible over the dot screen. If one accent is added, it should be a spot-ink color with a fixed semantic role (e.g., 'hit' state), not decoration.
