> Solid ink bands and distinct printing passes build a poster whose key shapes hold together at a distance.

## Visual identity
Let sequential stencil impressions build a legible poster. Keep one printed contour as a reference while a second ink arrives and changes the shape or strength of the image.

## Surfaces and construction
Use opaque spot shapes, visible registration and flat printed tone bands. Build a separate stencil for each ink. Use solid coverage, clean knockout openings and a controlled overlap that explains where the second pass has landed.

## Colour roles
Step values from far to near and reserve a bright accent for one meaningful part. Assign each flat ink a deliberate role. Use an overlapping ink only where the printed effect calls for it.

Example palette. background #F4E9D4, foreground #233E45, accent 1 #B95A43.

## Lettering and captions
Use solid ink for small approved words and reserve a colour pass for larger lettering where an overlap shows the print method.

## Timing and movement
Lock the first flat ink pass before lowering the next stencil area. Show a visible overlap or slight registration variance, then let the finished print sit still. Move the screen pull at a steady rate while the ink is being laid down. Reveal the result on the frame lift and use clear transitions between ink passes.

## Framing and viewpoint
Track the printing pass with a sheet edge visible, hold overhead while layers arrive and pull back when the mesh lifts. Tilt towards a reading band, travel through a dark foreground, crane through stacked graphic planes or pan across a row of prints. Magnify the mesh to show its weave and withdraw to place the finished poster on its wall. Use print operations and changes between finished sheets to join views.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, distinguish the squeegee drag, frame lift and sheet contact. Align the drag with the line of wet ink and let the dry reveal settle quietly.

## Characteristic actions
- Register a broad colour shape against a clean mask and expose a clear title or symbol.
- Pull ink through the mesh, lift the screen for a reveal or register a new sheet beneath it.

## Review checks
Check knockout holes and ink overlap at sharp corners. Confirm that registration variance stays consistent with each ink layer.

## Implementation tools
Clip separate ink shapes against print passes and keep registration stable in page coordinates. Reveal opaque ink plate masks with a travelling screen edge and cache the paper texture.

## Project choices
Build a travel poster, a stack of design variations or a poster that shows how it was printed. Print a title, emblem or illustrated poster. Keep broad flat ink areas and controlled layer order.

> Debossed type and side light show pressure in thick paper. Small shifts reveal the impression and ink.

## Visual identity
Show the effect of physical pressure on thick stock. Use pressure and side light to show letterpress marks on thick stock.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate the paper surface, ink impression and relief lighting. Give ink a slightly uneven edge and the impression a shallow paper depression.

## Colour roles
Keep impressions legible before adding a fine accent or highlight. Use a few solid inks with paper as an active value and avoid competing fills.

Example palette. background #F6EDD9, foreground #343932, accent 1 #914839.

## Lettering and captions
Treat approved words as set type in the chase where appropriate. Keep any separate captions out of the moving impression area.

## Timing and movement
Show the type or block approach the stock, make contact, hold under pressure, then lift to expose the impression. Give the paper time to relax after the lift.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a raking detail view for the impression and a frontal frame for reading. Use raking light close to the stock and widen to show the full impression. Use a shallow view to show the clearance between press and paper, then cut or ease to a flat view where the indentation and wording can be read together.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, separate the press contact from the lift of the paper. Put a lower impact under the platen and a lighter fibre sound where the sheet releases.

## Characteristic actions
Lower the type form onto the stock and reveal the ink and impression at contact.

Lower the plate, hold on contact and reveal the impression under side light.

## Review checks
Check that indentation, ink and pressure follow the same letter positions. Inspect the contact pose for gaps between the press and stock.

## Implementation tools
Compute the relief or shadow pass from the same type or shape mask. Drive an ink mask and shallow relief from the same registered type outlines.

> Carved light marks emerge from dark relief-print masses. Hatch direction explains form and the work of the blade.

## Visual identity
Let the viewer see how cuts in a block become light gaps in a print. Show one carved contour and the matching impression so the subject can be recognised across the reversal.

## Surfaces and construction
Give each cut a direction and width, and use the plate edge to locate the impression.

## Colour roles
Let black mass and unprinted light describe volume, with extra colour only where approved and relevant. Use opaque relief ink and open paper for value, with clear directional cuts near contours.

Example palette. background #F2E6CA, foreground #262820.

## Lettering and captions
Cut approved lettering as part of the block only where its strokes can survive the transfer. Keep enabled captions separate from fine hatching.

## Timing and movement
Carve a visible gouge, clear its chips, then reveal the printed impression in a separate beat. Keep the direction of each cut consistent with the grain. Use anticipation, a held cut and a small follow-through. Start a new impression on a clean edit where the printed image needs to change as a whole.

## Framing and viewpoint
Track the blade or brightest cut, then withdraw to show how those marks build a world. Hold the full print for reading, skim a close view to show the material and make a quick push that settles on a decisive detail. Use an opening as a frame, cut between impressions, rise to show the whole and shift focus between plates as one is peeled up. Keep dark and light distinct and leave printed words in their own margin.

## Sound options
If enabled, use brief carving accents for structural marks and preserve the quiet paper reveal. When audible, a blade scrape and paper handling can identify the material changes.

## Characteristic actions
- Carve the light edge in staggered segments and build the main form from the resulting contrast.
- Reveal the cutting tip, print a new impression or peel a sheet away to expose a changed area.

## Review checks
Check the positive and negative areas before and after the print flips. Confirm the intended direction of words and that fine ink bridges stay open.

## Implementation tools
Use local engraving masks and keep paper, ink and plate movement independent. Keep solid black masses and cut light paths through them. Align cut direction to form and grain. Model the gouge and grain as separate masks and preserve the same carved outline across the print. Reverse the block image at the impression stage and verify any approved lettering there.

## Project choices
Choose a single image, a progression of impressions or a repeated cut that changes tone. Use a landscape, figure or symbol. Preserve bold silhouette and predictable ink coverage.

sources.palette_lesson: The red-brown sepia monochrome here is this author's grading choice for a 'cursed vintage film / moon level' scene, not a requirement of the style. (1) Use one tinted tonal ramp: a dark ground, mid forms and pale highlights for effects, puffs and interactive items. > Photocopied fragments and rough page joins create a zine whose headline, images and annotations remain easy to follow.

## Visual identity
Assemble one readable zine statement from copied photographs, coarse print and torn stock. Make a physical correction or replacement visible through the overlap, with the main words given a clear place.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep toner, paper joins, tape and torn fragments on separate levels. Keep halftone photographs, rough paper edges and visible tape or bindings at believable scales.

## Colour roles
Give dark toner enough contrast to preserve headline and source marks. Use strong black and white with an optional accent to establish the focus.

Example palette. background #FFFFFF, foreground #000000, accent 1 #BF3232.

## Lettering and captions
Protect the approved headline from noise and edge tears. Place supporting text on a less damaged strip with clear line spacing.

## Timing and movement
Drop each ripped or photocopied piece into the page. Let the coarse contrast appear on a distinct scan or stamp, then pause on the readable layout.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use overhead page framing and make cuts along deliberate page or crop edges. Use straight-on reading views and move close to show meaningful imperfections.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, match the photocopier feed, paper slap or tape pull to its specific visible action. Let the resulting layout settle without another accent.

## Characteristic actions
Slide another photo fragment under a tape hinge and reposition the headline above it.

Copy a fragment, paste it over the previous version or reveal an annotated margin.

## Review checks
Inspect the copy texture at its darkest threshold, then compare the complete layout at delivery size. Keep the headline readable and check that grain and tear details follow the moving paper.

## Implementation tools
Seed photocopy grain per surface and key each piece independently. Prepare clipped halftone textures per fragment and layer each independently on the timeline.

## Project choices
Choose a rough poster, note sequence or collage assembled in a visible order. Use an original zine, flyer or photo sequence with one dominant message. Choose a page whose source snippets, correction or replacement can be seen as physical layers. Use only approved text and imagery as the page's main content.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Trimmed edges and contact shadows make flat artwork feel like a collection of stickers being placed and rearranged.

## Visual identity
Use contact and overlap to make graphic pieces feel like stickers. Let a collection read as physical stickers placed on one surface.

## Surfaces and construction
Make the face, backing and cut border one flexible object with a distinct rim. At a lifted corner, keep a small contact shadow and an open gap that reveals the paper or adhesive beneath it.

## Colour roles
Distinguish the active sticker from its backing or its neighbours. Keep sticker centres readable and reserve a shared accent for related pieces.

Example palette. background #F3EBD9, foreground #273F49, accent 1 #FFFFFF, accent 2 #D78267, accent 3 #77A397.

## Lettering and captions
Fit approved words inside broad sticker faces or on a separate label. Give the label its own clear border and keep words inside the trim.

## Timing and movement
Peel a corner, pivot the sticker around its last contact point, then press it flat. Stagger nearby stickers so the main icon lands first and remains visible.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame from above or at a low angle that reveals the raised corner. Show the backing before the first piece arrives and hold each important placement.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a short peel and a soft seat on contact. If audible, use a brief peel cue and a softer landing.

## Characteristic actions
Lift one corner, rotate around the remaining contact and press the sticker flat.

Peel, slide and seat a piece, then move its neighbour to make room.

## Review checks
Inspect border thickness and shadow at the most curled corner. Check that face and outline follow the same deformation.

## Implementation tools
Keep contour, edge and shadow masks attached to the same sticker path. Separate each sticker image, border and shadow group and key the peel at its contact edge.

## Project choices
Choose a collection, a sequence of placements or an evolving diagram. Arrange icons, objects or words into a new order while keeping the border and substrate consistent.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Small pieces of consistent scale form the image through colour, orientation and the gaps between them.

## Visual identity
Make the image emerge from discrete pieces at a consistent scale. Resolve a recognisable picture from individual coloured tesserae.

## Surfaces and construction
Give individual tiles slightly different surface responses and readable grout lines. Give glass, stone or leaf tiles consistent scale, gaps and local depth.

## Colour roles
Group similar values so the assembled picture remains clear. Use coherent colour groups and selective specular response in the active region. Give each tile a stable base hue and a restrained shaded edge. Group values across the image so its main shape reads from a distance even where gaps and grout are visible.

Example palette. background #E4D8BE, foreground #39494B, accent 1 #47777B, accent 2 #9B694C, accent 3 #B19A61.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved letters with enough tiles per stroke to read in the wide view. Put smaller enabled captions in an independent clear band.

## Timing and movement
Place tiles in meaningful groups from a stable edge or centre. Allow a short settling time as each cluster completes a visible part of the image.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a frontal image view and a shallow oblique reveal to show tessera depth. Use a near view of the tile spacing before revealing the complete image.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use light ceramic or stone contacts when grouped tiles first land and at the final placement. Lower or omit indistinct repeated contacts in a dense mosaic.

## Characteristic actions
Turn over a single colour group and reseat it to reveal the picture.

Lay a row, rotate a piece into place or widen as the image becomes recognisable.

## Review checks
Check gaps and row alignment where new clusters join. Confirm that the full pattern reads at display size and that tiles keep a consistent thickness.

## Implementation tools
Place tiles on a shared lattice with deterministic variations and fill order. Instance tesserae with individual pivots and stable material groups driven by timeline time.

## Project choices
Choose a motif, comparative mosaic or material reveal from component to mural. Build a figure, emblem or repeating field using constant tile spacing.

These are a classic Early Christian or Byzantine-flavoured choice for a pastoral dove-and-fish subject, not a requirement of the style. The constraints that do define the medium are a limited set of discrete tile colours, each with small value jitter from tile to tile, dark grout lines, high-key reflective tiles (gold or glass) used sparingly for glints, and a neutral setting wall around the panel. New subjects should choose their own field colour: deep lapis or midnight blue with gold stars for night or sacred scenes; terracotta and umber stone tesserae for Roman floor mosaics; sea-green and turquoise glass for marine or poolside topics; black-and-white marble for architectural or geometric themes; or emerald and jade for gardens. The surround can be a cool slate, warm limestone, a dark wet-stone grout, or a dim church-interior shadow. Keep enough value contrast between the figure tiles and the field that silhouettes read at tile resolution.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A low-resolution grid defines silhouettes through shaped pixel clusters and clearly held sprite poses.

## Visual identity
Let intentional pixel clusters define both pose and material. Build readable silhouettes from deliberate clusters on a small pixel grid.

## Surfaces and construction
Use small integer grids, clean nearest-neighbour sampling and authored sprite positions. Keep sprites, tiles and edges aligned to whole logical pixels.

## Colour roles
Keep the background and silhouette distinct with an indexed colour range. Reuse a limited palette with stable ramps for light and shadow.

Example palette. background #18253A, foreground #F3EBD3, accent 1 #426A76, accent 2 #8AA386, accent 3 #D3A45E, accent 4 #B56D6F.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved pixel-style lettering only when details survive integer scaling. Set enabled captions over a stable value field when backgrounds scroll.

## Timing and movement
Change poses in discrete drawings and hold each long enough to read. Snap sprite movement to the pixel grid and time pauses around contacts, blinks or direction changes.

## Framing and viewpoint
Pan in whole-pixel steps and preserve sprite scale across viewpoints. Move in whole-pixel increments when the internal scene requires a tracking move.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use short cues on visible sprite contacts or state changes. If sound is enabled, key short action cues to the discrete pose changes.

## Characteristic actions
Cycle a small palette range to move water or light while the geometry stays registered.

Swap a pose or change a nearby cluster rather than sliding the same drawing through every state.

## Review checks
Check coarse pixels at rest and during a pan. On a direct seek, sprite edges should remain sharp and feet should end on the contact pixel.

## Implementation tools
Use pixel-aligned coordinates and keep camera scale and pose exposure independent. Render a low-resolution layer with nearest-neighbour sampling and integer placement. Draw at a common logical pixel scale. Use nearest-neighbour sampling and place sprite roots on integer coordinates so pans and direct seeks preserve square texels.

## Project choices
Choose an action that reads at a low internal resolution and a stable view. Use an icon, original scene or character. Choose the grid based on the smallest required detail.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Regular cubes create depth and readable mass. The grid stays visible as objects assemble or change.

## Visual identity
Let a consistent cube module show the form and its construction. Describe solid forms through cubes of consistent size. Keep the unit cube legible in the outline and in how shapes are built. Give major changes a countable group of blocks so the medium explains the assembly.

## Surfaces and construction
Build solid blocks at fixed dimensions with visible joins and calibrated shadows. Build visible volumes and stepped surfaces from a shared voxel grid.

## Colour roles
Group hue by object or layer rather than by every block. Assign stable material colours and use directional light to make faces distinguishable.

Example palette. background #EEE9DB, foreground #30444C, accent 1 #63928D, accent 2 #C0845D.

## Lettering and captions
Align approved labels with a clear voxel face or place them on a fixed panel beside the block form.

## Timing and movement
Show the voxel form in a stable grid before adding or removing blocks in groups. Pause after each visible layer becomes part of the silhouette.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use an oblique view that shows three faces and keeps the grid size apparent. Use a three-quarter or overhead view to show cube adjacency and depth.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a light click as one cube snaps into place and a heavier contact when a full layer seats. Align each sound with the first frame of the final position.

## Characteristic actions
Fill one layer, then swing the camera slightly to expose its relation to the rest.

Assemble from a visible sequence of cubes or remove one layer to show the inside.

## Review checks
Check adjacent block faces for cracks and the smallest shape for an identifiable silhouette. Inspect shadow movement where blocks are added.

## Implementation tools
Use shared grid locations for placement and calculate shadows from geometry. Instance cubes on integer 3D coordinates and key groups of occupancy changes.

## Project choices
Choose a terrain, sculpture or modular process that benefits from cube-level assembly. Build figures, landscapes or objects at one consistent voxel scale.

sources.palette_lesson: The colours come from the lighting state, not from a fixed swatch. In this example the time of day sets the palette: hazy noon in grey-blue and teal, golden hour in amber with dark olive ground, dusk in violet-grey sky with a red horizon, and night with warm torch pools on cream sand. The medium's constant is the material set (matte pixel-textured blocks, translucent refractive water, line-like glass, emissive torches). The author's own choices are the beach and sea subject, the teal water and the sunset sequence. A new subject should get its own environment and light: a cold blue-white snowfield at dawn, a dim cave lit by blue-green crystals, a misty forest under overcast light, a desert at noon with bleached sky and ochre blocks, or a night town of grey stone with sodium-orange lamps. Keep the overlay UI (dark translucent panels, one warm accent for sliders and buttons) separate from the world palette, and recheck its contrast against each lighting state.

sources.style_evidence: The whole world is built from consistent-size cubes: blocky chickens, cube trees, stepped terrain, block clouds and fence posts. Depth comes from flat-shaded faces and colour blocks.
sources.palette_lesson: The dominant green (the measured composite is a mid grass-green) comes from this example's subject, a daytime grassland biome. It is not a style constant. What defines the style: a limited, saturated per-material palette (one hue family per block type, with a few texture shades in each), flat face shading that gives each block side a distinct value, small saturated accents (red, yellow) used as sparse sprites, and a dark, neutral, near-opaque UI layer with white text and one bright accent colour so the text stays readable over any world. The UI accent green and the hearts are this author's choices. Keep the overlay neutral-dark and pick its accent to contrast with whatever biome is behind it.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Flat facets and broad light describe a miniature landscape or object. Geometry and lighting carry the changes in place and time.

## Visual identity
Build form from the changing values of its visible facets. Give a small figure, prop or terrain feature a recognisable outline so the set's scale survives a move from wide to close.

## Surfaces and construction
Use flat faces and visible plane boundaries to describe terrain, props and buildings. Share edges between adjoining pieces and keep the strongest silhouette distinct from the sky.

## Colour roles
Use broad harmonious ground hues and reserve brighter light for a practical or focal event. Use clear facets and a consistent sun direction. Distinguish terrain groups with a limited set of materials. Choose a restricted local palette per object and let lighting create the difference between neighbouring faces. Keep sky and ground values far enough apart to read the silhouette.

Example palette. background #F1EBDF, foreground #34484C, accent 1 #799C8C, accent 2 #C28A68.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved labels off tiny facets. Anchor words to a broad plane or a separate layer with a stable background.

## Timing and movement
Set a clear pose and move the object or camera on a short path that exposes a plane change. Let facets catch light in sequence while the strongest silhouette stays readable.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use an orthographic camera and change scale with its view bounds. Swing around an object, lower the elevation to emphasise the horizon or raise it for a map-like view. Hold a wide as the place moves, cut close to a landing, track alongside a traveller or truck along a row. Hold the view as the light changes to convey elapsed time. Use clear cuts between wide and close or an upward scale move through the sky.

## Sound options
If enabled, use a light landing cue for the terrain assembly and natural sound only as the idea specifies. If sound is on, give different surfaces distinct contact cues and use a sparse motif only when it fits the selected music.

## Characteristic actions
- Assemble simple terrain facets along shared edges as the camera makes a gentle spatial pass.
- Raise a tile, stack a new segment, let a moving object land or change the sky while the view holds.

## Review checks
Inspect silhouettes at the most oblique turn. Check that normals, shadow boundaries and vertex colours make planes readable without stray highlights.

## Implementation tools
Use deterministic transforms for arrivals and derive lighting from the same scene clock. Share boundaries between meshes, use flat normals and keep light and camera keys deterministic.

## Project choices
Choose a terrain build, tiled route or change that can be recognised from an overhead and a close view. Build islands, neighbourhoods or terrain fragments. Keep silhouettes deliberate and faces clean.

## Visual identity

## Surfaces and construction
Separate outlines, shadow bands and small highlights in the lighting model. Use opaque materials, controlled outlines and stable toon lighting.

## Colour roles

## Characteristic actions

## Review checks
Inspect outline continuity and shadow thresholds across a moving face. Fix any tiny light patches that flicker as the object turns.

## Implementation tools
Quantise shading by light response and evaluate outline width consistently. Use toon material ramps and explicit control of silhouette outlines in the 3D scene. Use explicit cel bands and an outline pass with stable depth and position. Give thin features enough band width to prevent a moving boundary from toggling each frame.

sources.palette_lesson: The author's colours here are a scene choice, not a medium rule. A cool indigo night-sky opening changes into a golden-orange and magenta sunset over a plum sea. Clouds are violet with peach rim light, and the hero object is cream with a small red/green/white livery. The colours that define the style are relational: (1) a few discrete shadow bands per form, with shadows in a saturated hue-shifted colour rather than grey; (2) environmental light carries the warmth while object colours stay flat and matte; (3) one light-valued hero against a darker or more saturated environment, so it always reads; (4) white serif type over mid-to-dark areas. For new subjects, take the background from the setting and time of day. sources.palette_lesson: The colors here belong to this author's chosen subject and setting: an orange tabby, pastel coral, teal and lavender facades, saturated toy-car colors, a blue-grey road and a hazy pale sky. tech.implementation:
Browser preview: neutral #F0EDE5 studio sweep with a procedural PMREM RoomEnvironment. A PBR object (brushed metal and a MeshPhysicalMaterial glass with transmission/IOR) sits on a plane with PCF soft shadows and contact shadows. Renderer output is SRGB with ACES tone mapping configured explicitly, plus a restrained BokehPass depth of field and OutputPass. A GSAP timeline owns a measured dolly/arc camera and an object settle with plausible eased acceleration and no floating. 3s preview: slow 10° arc with a focus pull. Optional caustic recipe: an offscreen render target samples the background for a refraction approximation, and any projected caustic texture is tied to surface and light motion and labeled as an approximation, not path-traced. Full video: the implementation calls for Blender PBR, Cycles and baked simulation. That capability is not available, so this is reported as missing; if installed, render via bpy/Cycles to a transparent_png_sequence, check denoise stability, and composite in HyperFrames.
Optional recipe caustic_optics: Validate reflected/refracted silhouettes and transmitted light together. Water caustics on receiver geometry must move consistently with the surface and lighting, not slide as unrelated decoration. Use offline path-traced assets when the chosen browser renderer cannot provide the optical effect. Identify approximations; do not call projected patterns physically traced caustics.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Credible proportions, materials and lighting make the scene behave like something a camera could record.

## Visual identity
Keep scale, movement and lighting plausible enough to behave like recorded reality. Create a scene whose scale, light and surfaces behave credibly.

## Surfaces and construction
Use measured materials, consistent camera exposure and meaningful surface variation. Use measured material roughness, good contact shadows and consistent scale references. Match texture scale, seams and surface roughness to observable physical cues. Keep reflections and contact shadows consistent with the size and placement of light sources.

## Colour roles
Coordinate colour temperature across reflected and transmitted light. Mix reflected and local colour under the same exposure. Keep important surfaces within usable contrast.

Example palette. background #F0EDE5, foreground #2B302F, accent 1 #827D6D.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved lettering on its actual material plane when it belongs to the world. Place independent captions in a stable field outside fine product detail.

## Timing and movement
Start with a stable pose and introduce movement from a believable physical source. Let momentum, contact and settling fill the move, then allow reflected light to stabilise in the final view.

## Framing and viewpoint
Choose a plausible camera height, lens and focus distance for the subject. Use a viewpoint a physical lens could reach and protect natural focus cues.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, match contact, room tone and distance to visible materials and space. If sound is enabled, keep perspective and acoustic space tied to the view.

## Characteristic actions
Let a moving object approach a surface and settle into clear physical contact.

Reveal the feature through a physical action with a plausible light or focus change.

## Review checks
Check object scale, shadows and reflected highlights as the view moves. Confirm that surface roughness behaves consistently before and after contact.

## Implementation tools
Use physical units and evaluate camera, depth and material response separately. Use scene geometry, reference-based materials and matched lighting, then drive camera and objects from timeline keys.

## Project choices
Choose a recognisable real object, location or comparison with supported references. Choose a measured product view, environment study or plausible action.

tech.implementation:
Background #111C29. About 30–60k Points whose BufferGeometry attributes hold seeded fixed samples: pose A position (e.g. a sphere), pose B (a recognizable silhouette such as a bird or logo shape sampled from a procedural SDF), a per-particle seed, and a color role (#65BEC2 cool body, #CEAF79 warm focal accent, #EFF5EE highlights). The vertex shader computes position = mix(A, B, ease(uMorph, staggered by seed)) plus analytic curl-like offsets from uTime, and size/brightness from density. The fragment shader draws soft discs with additive blending capped by alpha. UnrealBloomPass with a high threshold and low strength keeps edges readable. GSAP's paused timeline sets uTime, uMorph and uTrail uniforms; nothing is integrated per frame, so seeks are exact. 3s preview: drift 0–0.8s → flow into the silhouette 0.8–2.0s → stable hold 2.0–3.0s. Fireworks recipe: birth times and velocities are seeded, and trajectories are analytic (p0 + v·t + ½g·t²) in the shader with fading trails from sampled earlier times.
Optional recipe particle_spectacle: Plan emission, ascent, burst expansion, fading trails, environmental light and a deliberate finale. Use deterministic birth times, seeded velocities and analytic or baked trajectories; retain foreground clarity and stationary background. Do not multiply identical small bursts or use full-screen glow to conceal weak choreography.

> Tiny moving points collect into readable outlines or densities. Their movement reveals how the shape forms and disperses.

## Visual identity
Let clusters and density reveal the shape rather than treating points as decoration. Use particle density and clustering to define a readable subject.

## Surfaces and construction
Use stable particles with coherent depths and a small variation in size or softness. Keep the particle size range controlled and reserve trails for useful direction cues.

## Colour roles
Reserve the brightest points for the mass being revealed. Differentiate particle groups by colour, value or size while maintaining silhouette contrast.

Example palette. background #111C29, foreground #EFF5EE, accent 1 #65BEC2, accent 2 #CEAF79.

## Lettering and captions
Use a clear band for approved copy, or assemble a short approved word from particles and hold its formed state with stable contrast.

## Timing and movement
Emit a readable burst from a defined place or surface, then vary particle speed by when each particle left. Give the resulting cloud time to disperse or settle before the next large burst.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame the entire assembly first, then crop only if the movement remains traceable. Hold wide enough to read the cluster, then inspect one focused region.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, place a short cue at emission and a quieter tail in the direction of dispersion. If music is enabled, use larger phrase changes for clustering and release.

## Characteristic actions
Collect a moving cloud into a stable silhouette and peel away one part as a stream.

Gather fragments, hold the recognisable form and release it by region.

## Review checks
Review the densest frame and the last visible particles. Keep seeds stable so direct seeks show the intended formation and dispersion.

## Implementation tools
Key point identities, life and motion from deterministic time. Use seeded particle paths or baked simulation states driven by timeline time.

## Project choices
Choose a silhouette, transfer or progression with visible states of density. Form an icon, live flow or original figure while keeping a clear target shape.

> A luminous trace on instrument glass reveals how a signal behaves against a stable grid.

## Visual identity
Let a visible trace show how a signal changes on a fixed grid. Preserve a reference sweep or calibrated shape so viewers can compare the next cycle with the earlier one.

## Surfaces and construction
Build a vector-like beam with separate grid, glow and decaying trails on subtly reflective glass.

## Colour roles
Distinguish signal channels by stable accents and keep the origin and reference cues readable. Separate grid, guide and live trace by value, with one bright hue for the measured signal.

Example palette. background #081613, foreground #D8F0DD, accent 1 #76CF9B.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved units and labels on grid markers with enough margin to survive glow. Keep key values clear of the moving trace.

## Timing and movement
Draw successive sweeps from the same time base. Hold one trace long enough to compare it, then move a control and show the changed wave on the next sweep.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use logarithmic magnification with the writing point held in place while the grid refines. Track the beam, push into a rotating mechanism, match corresponding curves, or pull back to reveal the full trace. Magnify a small anomaly and hold with cursors to measure it. Use transformations of lettering, a stopped trace followed by a dive, or the collapse of the display to join views.

## Sound options
If enabled, map a sound to the signal only if the brief calls for it and the mapping is documented. Use sonification only when enabled and map it to the same actual frequency or amplitude data.

## Characteristic actions
- Add one signal component at a time and tie its waveform to a clear phase indicator.
- Grow an epicycle chain, morph a symbolic curve into the measured one or change magnification with an instrument control.

## Review checks
Compare trace positions at repeating phases. Check that phosphor decay and the heads of the sweeps remain visible without smearing the reference grid.

## Implementation tools
Evaluate the waveform by time and derive its afterglow from a bounded set of prior samples. Compute the trace and marker from the same function and composition time. Keep axes fixed. Evaluate paired oscillator coordinates from one time base and draw the waveform in a fixed calibrated frame. Drive beam persistence by each sample's age so direct seeks reconstruct the trace.

## Project choices
Use a waveform comparison, a simple ratio or a mechanism whose path can be plotted. Show phase, interference or a comparison. Use consistent scales across trace changes.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Design grammar from a chosen era gives future tools and spaces a consistent material and visual history.

## Visual identity
Use a consistent period viewpoint on the future. Build a future as imagined from one chosen historical period.

## Surfaces and construction
Choose a material and hardware language for that era. Use period-specific housings, instruments and interfaces with credible material joints.

## Colour roles
Use recurring indicator colours with coherent period tones. Set colours from the era's packaging and electronics. Reserve a brighter hue for active indicators.

Example palette. background #EEE3CB, foreground #314449, accent 1 #6B9693, accent 2 #BC7751.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved control labels near their physical controls. Put captions in a quiet area outside reflected dials and gauge illumination.

## Timing and movement
Establish the mechanical control and its starting reading. Give the handle or switch a short physical throw, then delay the indicator just enough to show cause and response.

## Framing and viewpoint
Choose documentary product framing or a measured set reveal that keeps the era readable. Frame the broader set before an inspection of its controls.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, give the selector, relays and speaker different sounds that fit the depicted hardware. Put each cue after the mechanism visibly engages.

## Characteristic actions
Toggle a physical control and show the matching change in an instrument while both remain visible. A secondary reveal can open a mechanical panel to show the visible drive or signal path.

## Review checks
Inspect control motion and gauge change together. Check that a pointer travels along its marked range and settles at the intended reading.

## Implementation tools
Time mechanical travel and indicator state separately. Build each control and display as a separate stateful layer or scene object.

## Project choices
Choose a vehicle, console or device grounded in one period. Choose a space-age, early computing or analogue-instrument period and keep the references coherent. Choose a system with a distinct idle state and a physical change the dial can reflect. A power-up, frequency adjustment or directional change needs the moving control and result in the same sequence.

sources.palette_lesson: The near-black, cool slate and blue-gray world is this author's choice for an oppressive, broadcast-dystopia mood. It is not a fixed rule of the style. What defines the craft: (1) a narrow, low-saturation environment value range; (2) one dominant light source per shot (tunnel core, projection screen, ceiling strips) that sets the silhouettes; (3) exactly one saturated hue reserved for the protagonist or turning point, with matching local light spill. The orange-red accent is meaningful because nothing else in the frame is warm. For new subjects, change the environment's color family and keep the single complementary accent: deep teal-green sea cave with a coral accent; dusty violet desert dusk with a lime or acid-yellow accent; warm sepia factory haze with a cobalt accent; cold snow-white overcast field with dark figures and a crimson accent; murky olive jungle with a magenta accent. Recheck that the silhouettes still separate from the glow field, and that captions on bright surfaces keep their contrast.

> Scan structure, persistence and controlled signal changes make imagery feel recorded or displayed through an analogue device.

## Visual identity
Make visible imperfections behave like failures of a signal. Make an image read as a signal on an analogue display.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate the glass, scan pattern and image underneath. Use restrained scanlines, screen curvature and physically plausible persistence. Build the source picture, raster effect, phosphor persistence and screen glass separately. Curve the emitted image with its scan lines so the hardware effect follows the display surface.

## Colour roles
Keep signal colour changes related to the intended corruption. Choose a signal palette and keep colour offsets local to brief transitions.

Example palette. background #171C24, foreground #E9E5D8, accent 1 #6A9DAA.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved screen text large enough for the scan-line pitch. Place critical captions in a safe region where display curvature leaves letters clear.

## Timing and movement
Start with a steady phosphor image before bending scan lines or opening a vertical roll. Let persistence trail the change and leave a readable recovered frame.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame the screen or its visible border so the surface treatment has a clear source. Keep a stable crop while faults happen inside the device.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, tie a short signal cue to the interruption and keep steady viewing quiet. If enabled, tie interference sound to the fault window.

## Characteristic actions
Let the display briefly roll or separate colours, then register back into place.

Let a tracking fault interrupt one region before recovery.

## Review checks
Preview at viewing size and scrub to the strongest distortion. Check that display curvature, glow and persistence preserve the main glyphs.

## Implementation tools
Displace raster rows in source display coordinates before bending them across the curved glass. Compute brightness persistence from the sample's age and keep picture damage and phosphor response on separate tracks.

## Project choices
Choose a lost signal, a restoration or a diagnostic display. Adapt curvature, persistence and scan texture to one display type.

tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Deliberate faults in a stable signal reveal where the image breaks and how the system responds.

## Visual identity
Establish a recognisable signal before showing how a specific fault interrupts it. Keep a stable part of the picture in view so the difference between the fault and recovery reads immediately.

## Surfaces and construction
Build a clean image layer and a separate fault mask. Use contiguous scan bands for a tear, block boundaries for dropped data and separate colour channels for misregistration. Preserve a region of the original picture as a reference.

## Colour roles
Keep enough value and colour continuity to recognise the source. Keep the normal palette recoverable after the corruption and use displaced colours sparingly.

Example palette. background #111A24, foreground #F2F0E6, accent 1 #47B3AF, accent 2 #D16A84.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved copy in a clean interval or outside the displaced bands. Check a readable complete state before and after any deliberate break in the letter shapes.

## Timing and movement
Hold a clean signal before the break. Tear a few contiguous scan bands, offset those bands while the rest of the image anchors the view, then restore them in a visible order before the next cut.

## Framing and viewpoint
Hold the crop and subject position through the fault and its recovery. If a cut follows, leave a complete image long enough for the viewer to distinguish the edit from the signal error.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, place a brief clipped sound at the visible onset. An interrupted tone can resume when the picture stabilises if the brief calls for that connection.

## Characteristic actions
Begin with an intact image, displace a group of neighbouring bands at the fault and return them in an order the viewer can follow. Hold a clean frame after the last band realigns.

## Review checks
Scrub to the strongest displacement. The tear should affect the intended bands, and a direct seek to the recovered frame should restore their alignment.

## Implementation tools
Store each tear as a bounded row range with a horizontal offset and explicit start and recovery times. Seed brief signal errors so playback, rewinds and direct seeks use the same pattern. Restore the clean sampler at the recovery cue.

## Project choices
Choose one fault whose cause can be seen, such as a lost block, a slipped scan band or a separated colour channel. Keep its behaviour consistent from the stable image through recovery.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Translucent, softly blurred panes stack over visible scenery while their edges and type stay readable.

## Visual identity
Use translucence to communicate how content sits above its backing. Use frosted panels to organise content above a visible background.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate pane tint, frosted blur, edge and cast shadow. Give panels soft transmission, thin borders and restrained contact shading.

## Colour roles
Adjust foreground contrast against the composited panel. Keep figures and text above local contrast requirements as backgrounds change.

Example palette. background #182837, foreground #F6F7F0, accent 1 #7AAEB4, accent 2 #A698C5.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved lettering over a sufficiently even region of the panel. Use a local tint behind text where the moving background changes its contrast.

## Timing and movement
Move the glass panel and its background on separate tracks so blur and highlights change with visible depth. Settle the panel before introducing a second moving layer behind it.

## Framing and viewpoint
Move just far enough to expose parallax between glass and backing. Settle in a view where the panel stays broad enough to read as the background drifts behind it.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, give a panel's arrival a short cue at its stop. Keep background movement distinct from actual control or contact sounds.

## Characteristic actions
Bring a panel forward while its blur samples the same visible background.

Lift or move a panel to reveal the change in blur and depth.

## Review checks
Inspect the worst case as a bright and dark edge passes behind the panel. Check small text and separation between stacked borders.

## Implementation tools
Filter only the backing and keep foreground type in a crisp layer. Separate backdrop, frost and content layers with explicit clipping and timeline bounds.

## Project choices
Choose a control, layered interface or a comparison of panel depths. Use one group of panels for cards, controls or a lightweight explainer.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Clear, continuous refraction follows a rounded glass surface as it changes shape or moves across the background.

## Visual identity
Let a continuous clear surface reveal its shape through refraction. Show liquid-like clear glass with a readable boundary and continuous refraction.

## Surfaces and construction
Use visible thickness, changing normals and readable edges. Include surface thickness, narrow edge reflections and bounded dispersion. Use a continuous thickness field for the glass and sample the same background behind it. Keep a narrow refractive edge and a separate reflection layer so the shape is readable at rest.

## Colour roles
Separate reflected highlights from the colour of the background. Use a contrasting background feature to show the glass and keep tint subordinate.

Example palette. background #EDEBE3, foreground #293C49, accent 1 #91ACB0.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved copy on a steady face or in a separate flat layer. Keep letters clear of the strongest refractive edge at the panel's widest stretch.

## Timing and movement
Let the glass sheet deform around the action, then return to a stable silhouette. Make refraction and specular edges follow that deformation throughout the move.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a view with a recognisable backdrop and a useful side angle on the edge thickness. Show a strong silhouette first, then approach the detail being refracted.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, cue the visible moment the glass meets another surface. Use a softer, longer sound for a deformation that travels along the edge.

## Characteristic actions
Pull a clear lens into a new shape and let the background bend through the moving boundary.

Stretch or move the surface across an existing detail and hold.

## Review checks
Inspect background distortion at the panel boundary and normal direction as it settles. The scene behind the sheet should remain continuous around the edge.

## Implementation tools
Drive refraction from the surface shape and the supplied background. Drive mesh or field deformation and refractive sampling from the same timeline state.

## Project choices
Choose a lens, moving clear shape or interaction with a layered field. Use a lens, droplet or flexible panel with one coherent material rule.

sources.palette_lesson:
These colours are the author's own example. Cyan-to-violet light gradients, an aqua-to-deep-teal field and then a near-black charcoal stage are scene and brand choices that move from light to dark across the acts. They are not rules of the style. The rules are these:
- Keep one cool ambient field per act behind neutral UI surfaces: white frosted, charcoal opaque or smoked translucent.
- Reserve a single saturated interactive accent (here teal) for selection, send and active states.
- Let embedded media (warm reds, photos/renders) bring the only warm colour.
- Use small semantic status colours (green waveform, orange playhead, violet active outline) sparingly on dark tiles.
For new subjects, choose the field from mood and brand. Examples: a warm coral-to-magenta for lifestyle or creator apps, a deep forest-to-moss for finance or sustainability, a graphite-to-steel-blue for developer tools, a pale mint-to-white daylight field for health, or an inky plum-to-black for a night or entertainment mood. Keep the accent hue distinct from the field and check text contrast on every translucent panel.

sources.style_evidence: The bowl's glass refracts the striped wall and red band into curved, wrapped bands (most visible at seconds 1, 2 and 8), with rim highlights and a visible boundary. The room behind stays recognizable through the glass.
sources.palette_lesson: The palette has three layers. First, the set: a room of navy/off-white stripes, a red band, a dark green wainscot and a black/white checkerboard floor, with a warm brown wooden table. Second, the medium: clear glass and a cool teal-cyan water tint. Third, the saturated accents: orange-red, yellow, blue and orange-white fish against a pale pebble floor. The room colors are this author's example set dressing. Their strong graphic contrast is there to make the refraction easy to see, so they are not a fixed palette. What defines the style is: a neutral-to-graphic backdrop with enough pattern or contrast for glass distortion to read, a tinted transparent medium that stays distinct from the backdrop, and small high-chroma subjects inside it. The dominant colors measured from these frames (warm greys and tans, near-black) come from the wood, the top-down floor views and the dark capture border. They are not a background recipe.

Give rounded digital objects clear, optimistic interface behaviour. Use round early-web and portable-device forms with optimistic bright accents.

Use soft plastic, glossy inserts and a small set of recurring shapes. Pair translucent plastic, rounded chrome edges and compact digital panels. Give glass badges, glossy plastic and metal different edge highlights. Use a matte label or backing where small interface text needs to hold contrast.

> Familiar material and mechanical cues tell the viewer how an interface can be used and which state it is in.

## Visual identity
Make the interface state visible in the control itself. Show whether a switch is up or down, a button is raised or pressed, or a hinge is open or seated. Keep the readout next to the part that changed it.

## Surfaces and construction
Show material contact, depth and stops as part of the control. Model distinct edges, contact areas and surface materials for the chosen control.

## Colour roles
Give active and inactive states adequate value contrast. Match device materials and set active state through value, colour or a moving indicator.

Example palette. background #E7DFD0, foreground #3A352D, accent 1 #8B7151.

## Lettering and captions
Attach approved labels to plausible places on the control surface. Keep their orientation stable as the control tilts and duplicate nothing in a separate label without reason.

## Timing and movement
Show the full physical control and its starting state. Pair finger travel, surface compression or a hinge turn with its indicator change, then pause on the result.

## Framing and viewpoint
Choose a close angle that shows the contact, travel and result together. Use a close view showing both the input and resulting feedback.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, match the detent or spring to the actual switch movement. Use a separate quieter cue for the lid, rubber button or other material being handled.

## Characteristic actions
Press a switch through its travel and update the indicator at the visible threshold.

Press, slide or rotate a control and show the corresponding result. Press a recessed switch, then hold both the depressed surface and its changed indicator. A hinged cover can reveal the equivalent state through a different physical motion.

## Review checks
Inspect the contact pose and the changed indicator. Highlights and shadows should identify the same raised or depressed state.

## Implementation tools
Bind control geometry, motion and readout to one state model. Key control transforms and functional state from one value using the existing renderer choices.

## Project choices
Choose one understandable physical mechanism for each important electronic operation. Use a switch, knob or slider whose physical resemblance explains the task.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Shallow relief and soft directional light show which interface controls are raised, pressed or recessed.

## Visual identity
Let shallow relief explain control state without sacrificing legibility. Show interface depth through subtle raised and inset surfaces.

## Surfaces and construction
Build inset and raised areas with one consistent light direction. Use paired highlights and shadows aligned to one shared light direction. Use neighbouring light and dark shadows from a common light direction. Change their spacing and strength to describe a recessed or raised control, with a solid centre that remains a readable target.

## Colour roles
Separate enabled states with clear contrast in addition to shadows. Keep surfaces close to the background and add sufficient edge, label or indicator contrast.

Example palette. background #E7EBED, foreground #303D49, accent 1 #506F86.

## Lettering and captions
Keep enabled copy at a higher contrast than the surrounding soft edges. Give icons and labels a stable centre during press and release.

## Timing and movement
Show a pressed surface by moving its shallow light and shadow into the recess. Return the highlight and edge together on release and leave a perceptible hold at each endpoint.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the interface front-facing so small depth cues remain comparable. Keep the view close enough for shallow depth to read.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a soft contact at the deepest visible press and a lighter release when the surface rises. Leave changes in shading alone quiet.

## Characteristic actions
Depress a raised control while its label stays still and its shadow reverses. Hold the recessed pose so the viewer can compare it with the resting surface, then return the highlight with the release.

## Review checks
Check that the raised, pressed and disabled states are distinguishable with the colour removed. Inspect the smallest emboss and ensure it survives compression.

## Implementation tools
Derive shadow and highlight offsets from the same surface height. Animate CSS or vector shadow pairs and state values from the same keyed transition.

## Project choices
Choose a control group that benefits from consistent tactile feedback. Use a small control group where subtle depth remains easy to interpret.

> A coherent isometric place stages miniature people and objects so their relative positions explain what is happening.

## Visual identity
Build a legible miniature space on a common projection and give an event to a small figure or object. Arrange the set so a doorway, path or upper layer gives the action a readable route.

## Surfaces and construction
Give floor footprints and lifted lids distinct shadows and keep newly placed objects aligned to the room.

## Colour roles
Use illumination to make movement legible and reserve the rule accent for the step being explained. Use softened local colours with enough difference between near and far scenery and readable cast.

Example palette. background #F3EFE5, foreground #2D444D, accent 1 #6E9990, accent 2 #C98961.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved labels on a planar face when it is broad enough, or keep them horizontal in a separate layer with short leaders to their targets.

## Timing and movement
Build the visible floors or ground first. Add each vertical form along a consistent projected axis, then pause during assembly so depth can be read from overlaps. Keep the projected axes steady during a move. Let small figures advance after the geometry they depend on becomes visible.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the projection fixed. Drift inward gently, track the beginning of a row or travel at the subject’s pace. Widen as a lid opens or hold to allow reading. Step back to include an entire action, travel from outer setting into the people or jump between room, building and site scales. Keep depicted subjects and enabled text readable at the start and end of a move. Use scale, page movement or physical reveals to join views.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use quiet environmental cues and match footstep accents to visible contact. When effects are selected, let card lifts, small footsteps and prop contacts underline a step.

## Characteristic actions
- Use two distinct routes through one set and switch attention by staging different poses.
- Stand a row of pieces in sequence, lift a lid or light stations in their actual order.

## Review checks
Check the direction of all three projected axes. Where separate elements overlap, inspect their z-order at the closest contact.

## Implementation tools
Project all parts from the same fixed axes and sort by depth at the footprints. Assign a local draw order for roofs, overhangs and people where a simple footprint would draw overlap incorrectly.

## Project choices
Explain a place, movement through a space or a small system built around people. Use an original everyday place and cast. Preserve readable routes and positions across the change.

sources.style_evidence: Second 8 is an isometric cutaway room on consistent axes, with desks in a diagonal row, tonal top and side faces, no perspective shrinkage, and data on in-world boards.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's palette is scene-driven. The exterior uses a cool, low-key night (navy sky, layered dark teal-green forests, near-black ground) with a single pale moon. Warm amber appears only as a story signal, when the house-character's windows light up. Contrast with the subject comes from value (the off-white head against a dark field) and from warm against cool. The cream radial glow at 7s is a light-transition effect, not a canvas colour. The interior at 8s switches to a near-black void around a dark plum-brown isometric room, and saturated hue-coded roofs (orange, lavender, teal, yellow) separate the characters. What should transfer: a dominant environmental colour family with tonal-step depth, a light-valued hero with one or two signature hues reused across its parts (here teal), restrained warm emissive accents tied to events, and categorical hue-coding for ensemble characters. The navy/teal night recipe and the specific roof colours are this video's example, not constraints of the style.

sources.style_evidence: Mostly consistent oblique axes, a limited muted palette and light shadows. It is weaker than the others because the render is real 3D with a perspective camera, not flat illustration.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-white page and dark browser frame are screen-recording context (website UI), not a style background. The composition's real palette is inside the map: muted lawn green, soft grey roads, slate-blue water, and buildings in desaturated pastels (cream, blush pink, lilac, blue-grey) with charcoal factory roofs and brick chimneys. One warm orange/amber accent family marks the active state and tags. These colors are this author's choice for a sunny daytime suburban town, and the app even offers Morning/Dusk/Night modes. What defines the style is the medium: flat matte shading with no textures, a restrained desaturated base with one saturated accent hue for interaction or emphasis, soft ambient shadows, and readable 2D labels on top. For new subjects, take the ground plane and lighting from the scene rather than reusing green lawn and white UI.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Softly modelled surfaces and visible weight give digital objects the physical character of shaped clay.

## Visual identity
Give digital forms the weight and handling of sculpted clay. Present digital forms with matte clay surfaces and believable weight.

## Surfaces and construction
Use matte surfaces, soft edges and controlled hand-worked variation. Use rounded edges, sparse surface marks and broad light with clear contact.

## Colour roles
Keep lighting broad enough for the material's colour to read. Use a small matte palette with shadows that explain shape without making clay glossy. Use gentle colour variation where clay is thicker or has been handled. Give the brightest highlight a broad edge and keep the darkest values at actual contacts.

Example palette. background #F2E9DA, foreground #3E4A46, accent 1 #93AD9E, accent 2 #C7917B.

## Lettering and captions
Give approved letters the same thickness as the surrounding clay when they are objects. Place enabled captions on an even background outside their cast shadows.

## Timing and movement
Let a clay shape squash during contact and recover a little after the large move has finished. Hold the rest pose so the rounded form and surface marks become readable.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a low or three-quarter camera that keeps the point of contact visible. Use soft grazing views without losing the subject's overall silhouette.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use a soft clay contact at the compressed pose and a different short sound for handling or lifting. Match the weight to the shape's apparent mass.

## Characteristic actions
Set a rounded object down and let it compress and recover around its contact.

Press, lift or rotate a form to expose its weight and shaped edges.

## Review checks
Check the deepest compression and the returned pose for stable mass. Surface impressions and highlights should remain on the clay as it deforms.

## Implementation tools
Use stable surface texture and explicit deformations at contacts. Use sculpted geometry, rough matte materials and bounded deformation shapes.

## Project choices
Choose an object, surface or character whose clay construction is visible. Choose an original figure, prop or product treatment with consistent clay scale.

> The full miniature set stays legible as the viewer moves around it, with props and boundaries establishing its scale.

## Visual identity
Let scale and boundaries make the place read as a miniature. Present a complete miniature stage with scale and boundaries visible.

## Surfaces and construction
Build fixed floors, props and visible contact between objects. Build foreground, set and props at related scales with plausible shadow contact.

## Colour roles
Use lighting to group the space and separate the important prop. Use related scene colours and reserve the strongest contrast for the live action.

Example palette. background #EEE6D4, foreground #35433C, accent 1 #7B9173, accent 2 #B3885F.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved labels beyond the physical model, or attach them to a believable sign on the set. Keep captions outside the narrowest view of the action.

## Timing and movement
Start with a view of the whole base before pushing towards a figure or opening. Let a foreground element cross slowly and clear to reveal the next level of the set.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use an elevated oblique view. Keep enough depth of field to read key models. Hold one complete wide before moving to a revealing model-scale view. Start with a view that includes the model base and explains its size. Keep one base edge, known prop or figure in the frame as the camera moves into a small room or street.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, place local contacts at their distances inside the miniature. Give the close view a clearer material cue and avoid suggesting that the whole tabletop moves with the camera.

## Characteristic actions
Reveal a small action by moving past a foreground prop without losing the stage outline.

Reveal a hidden side, open a section or follow one subject through the set.

## Review checks
Inspect relative scale, contact shadows and focus at the nearest point. Check that every object still appears attached to the model base during movement.

## Implementation tools
Keep camera collision, depth and shadows tied to the geometry. Build depth-tested miniature geometry and key camera and actor movement independently.

## Project choices
Choose a room, landscape or assembly with an important internal relationship. Create an interior, street corner or bounded terrain study with one readable viewpoint.

For a new subject, choose the ground, sky and fog from the setting and the time of day. Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Choose libraries by role and scene requirements; the available options are not a required bundle. Prefer existing suitable dependencies. Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

motion_guidance.application: Apply shared movement quality to Frame-by-Frame Animation without weakening its visual_cues, materials, typography or existing motion_references.
motion_guidance.cadence_guidance: Preserve the planned drawing or pose exposure rate and held states. Design clear trajectories and coherent action timing without automatically generating interpolated poses. Delivery frame rate may be higher than exposure rate.
motion_guidance.implementation: Prefer existing timeline and renderer dependencies. Evaluate key states at requested composition time, maintain a single property owner, and cache or deterministically replay stateful motion. Do not introduce a library solely to add generic smoothing.

style_renderer.selection_basis: Use visual_cues and tech.implementation for styles, or the selected style and this pattern implementation for motion recipes. Select by visual fidelity and medium, not pipeline availability.

motion_engine.selection_basis: Use the authored action, style cadence, trajectory, material behavior, and simulation requirements. Select one owner for each animated property.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Distinct drawings and deliberate holds put the timing in the poses and make each change readable.

## Visual identity
Make each pose and exposure serve a visible action. Show motion through distinct drawings, with exposure holds that carry intent.

## Surfaces and construction
Use individual drawings with stable proportions and deliberate spacing. Keep drawn proportions consistent and reserve line variation for controlled places. Separate pose drawings from reusable held artwork and register each hand-drawn replacement to the same anchors. Keep moving features on their own layer where the main torso is held.

## Colour roles
Give adjacent poses consistent colour and clear moving edges. Reuse the character and prop palette across frames. Keep shadows registered to each pose.

Example palette. background #F5EEDC, foreground #303C44, accent 1 #72929A, accent 2 #BF7C65.

## Lettering and captions
Leave empty space for enabled captions from the layout stage. Check the figure at its widest pose before setting the caption area.

## Timing and movement
Draw the start, contact and reaction poses first. Add drawings where the path bends or accelerates and hold the reaction long enough for the silhouette to register.

## Framing and viewpoint
Start with a fixed view that includes the action path and final contact. Use an insert only once the body or object is established, then return on a clear pose that continues the movement.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, align an impact to the held drawing where the hand, foot or prop actually hits. Let a quieter follow-on distinguish the recovery from the contact.

## Characteristic actions
Hold the anticipation drawing, switch to a strong contact pose and settle over several drawings.

Anticipate, show the important pose and hold the recovery.

## Review checks
Flip between adjacent drawings at a fast turn. Check volumes and hand or foot contacts before reviewing the timing of the entire run.

## Implementation tools
Assign each drawing a pose index driven by absolute time. Use a cel or image sequence with explicit exposure timings and transparent compositing.

## Project choices
Choose a gesture, material reaction or character action that needs authored poses. Choose drawing rate, pose count and hold lengths to fit the action and the idea.

sources.style_evidence: The sprites show discrete key poses (charge, cast, follow-through) and stepped effect frames instead of smooth tweening.
sources.palette_lesson: The author's example colors are an indigo/violet night sky, near-black pines, a cream moon, cyan for ice and orange-gold for fire. These belong to this night-lake subject. The style itself is defined by medium rules: a small fixed palette, dithered gradients instead of smooth blends, hard pixel clusters with dark outlines, and global palette swaps used as a mood and state device (a cold tint for ice, a crimson tint for fire, a flat lavender-grey flash on release). The UI overlay keeps its own fixed gold/pink/yellow palette and stays readable across all tints. For new subjects, choose a base palette for the environment and keep the swap behavior and the high-contrast HUD, rather than reusing this indigo night.

audio_direction.prompt: Based on the topic, audience, objective, narrative, and the visual and motion characteristics of Frame-by-Frame Animation, suggest an appropriate audio direction. Consider background music, voiceover, sung vocals, sound effects, ambience, or intentional silence. Explain which choices support this particular video; do not assign a fixed genre, tempo, instrument, voice, or mandatory audio layer to the style.
suggestion_dimensions: Whether background music is useful, and its suggested mood, texture, energy, tempo range, and progression.
Whether voiceover helps explain the topic, and its suggested language, tone, pace, and placement.
Whether sung vocals support the topic or distract from narration and essential text.
Whether sound effects, ambience, or silence clarify key actions, transitions, and reading holds.
How audio changes across scenes, supports motion cadence, and leaves space for speech and comprehension.
audio_direction.selection_guidance: Treat these as task-specific suggestions, not requirements to include every audio layer. Honor explicit user audio choices and supplied assets. When inputs are absent, propose a coherent direction and state assumptions; do not silently default to instrumental music or invent available audio assets.

Use render_pipeline to assemble, synchronize, mix, and export audio with picture. Keep speech intelligible, avoid clipping and competing vocals, and inspect the delivered audio and picture together.

suggested_combinations.selection_guidance: Use Frame-by-Frame Animation alone for character performance shots. Choose a hybrid for separate background art or living holds; drawn frames must exist or be produced, because tweening one image is not frame-by-frame.
