styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Drawn cels move independently over a painted set. Pose exposures and layer spacing determine the film’s rhythm.

## Visual identity
Preserve the separate contributions of painted space and drawn cels. Layer inked cels over a persistent painted setting.

## Surfaces and construction
Use ink outlines, cel fills and painted planes with controlled registration. Keep outlines, flat fills and discrete shadow shapes registered per cel.

## Colour roles
Hold character colours against the intended background values. Give the background a wider range of tones and preserve simple colour blocks on figures.

Example palette. background #F6EDD8, foreground #263746, accent 1 #718E9D, accent 2 #BE795F.

## Lettering and captions
Compose approved lettering within the layout and keep enabled captions clear of painted cel edges at their widest extent.

## Timing and movement
Lay out the background and schedule the strongest pose as a held cel. Use new cels for acting changes and move the camera without shifting registration between paint layers.

## Framing and viewpoint
Truck painted planes only when movement motivates it and maintain cel registration. Use deliberate multiplane movement for depth and locked frames for acting.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, align contacts to cel poses and leave room for the selected track. If enabled, tie scene ambience and action sounds to different layers. If effects are enabled, cue the audible change to the contact drawing or visible source. Use background atmosphere independently of held cels so it can continue across a pose hold.

## Characteristic actions
Swap character cels over an unchanged background so expression changes clearly.

Swap a cel pose while the painted environment maintains its position.

## Review checks
Check peg alignment and edges where separate cels touch. Show the foreground and background together in a pan to catch stray gaps or drift.

## Implementation tools
Track each plane and held drawing on the same authored timeline. Render separate backgrounds, foreground masks and indexed cels driven by exposure timing.

## Project choices
Choose a scene with a clear pose change against a persistent place. Use an original actor, setting and hand-drawn pose sequence.

For new subjects, choose the environment hue from the setting and mood. Keep the set slightly lower in saturation and detail than the characters, and save the warmest, most saturated accent for the object of desire or conflict.

> Visible placement and swapping of paper drawings give the motion purposeful, handmade steps.

## Visual identity
Let small, deliberate placement changes show the handmade movement. Make drawn paper assets change by visible incremental placement or replacement.

## Surfaces and construction
Give the drawings paper edges and actual contact with the work surface. Use drawn contours, uneven paper borders and a fixed tabletop surface.

## Colour roles
Keep object and ground values separated through replacement frames. Use a small stock-and-ink palette with stable colour between replacement poses.

Example palette. background #F7EEDD, foreground #344344, accent 1 #B6785D, accent 2 #819B81.

## Lettering and captions
Put approved handwritten copy inside a stable paper area. Use the same hold for words that need reading regardless of how quickly nearby details change.

## Timing and movement
Keep the main poses in discernible steps. Give paper or drawn details a small change tied to a visible hand adjustment, and keep the framing settled while the drawing changes.

## Framing and viewpoint
Fix the viewpoint so small steps and deliberate drawing changes remain visible. Use a top or shallow view that retains the paper edge.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, put a modest paper contact cue on the largest visible movement. If enabled, use brief paper handling sounds at meaningful replacements.

## Characteristic actions
Replace a drawn hand or profile at a held pose while the paper body stays registered.

Swap a drawn piece, leave a small hold and seat the next piece.

## Review checks
Check that small position changes read as material movement. The face and outline should stay traceable through nearby poses.

## Implementation tools
Render explicit positions for each exposure and stabilise backing texture. Use discrete key times for clipped piece transforms and replacement images. Keep a register point for the drawing and store deliberate position offsets per exposure. Use the same sequence of offsets for a seek as for playback so the paper movement stays intentional.

## Project choices
Choose a physical drawing or shape that changes through successive placements. Choose a paper prop, figure or drawing with reproducible step spacing.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Jointed flat pieces move against stable layers. Their edges, pivots and overlaps keep the construction visible.

## Visual identity
Show the construction of acting figures through their flat parts. Build a scene from flat photographic, drawn or paper fragments.

## Surfaces and construction
Use clear cut edges, visible layering and stable joint positions. Preserve individual cut edges, paper thickness and consistent overlap shadows. Give joints and pins individual centres and keep each paper part on an independent layer. Paint a little edge or shadow at overlaps where the viewer needs to see depth.

## Colour roles
Give paper pieces a shared ground and use differing local values where shapes overlap. Reserve an accent for an active part, and inspect the most crowded joints to keep their edges distinct.

Example palette. background #F0E5D0, foreground #3B3C34, accent 1 #987A5C.

## Lettering and captions
Put approved typography on its own paper field. Keep that field still while long limbs or pieces pass underneath.

## Timing and movement
Rotate each piece around a joint or paper pin and introduce secondary motion in a nearby layer after the main pose. Stop between moves so joins and silhouettes remain readable.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a shallow overhead view where overlaps explain front and back. Let one held shot establish the visible layers before travelling.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use separate sounds for a paper hinge, piece sliding across the ground and a heavier object landing. Let each begin at the corresponding contact.

## Characteristic actions
Peel a foreground fragment back on a hinge and expose the layer it covered.

Pivot a part, swap an expression or move a piece between layers.

## Review checks
Check pin positions and overlap order at extreme poses. A visible joint should stay registered as the pieces rotate.

## Implementation tools
Rig parts around shared rotation anchors and preserve layer order. Build independent keyed cutout layers with hinge anchors and stable z-order.

## Project choices
Choose a figure or object that gains clarity from its flat structure. Use an original assemblage of images, figures or lettering with deliberate cut boundaries.

> Light through a screen reveals flat puppets, joints and rods whose profiles make each gesture clear.

## Visual identity
Tell the action through profiles, the lit screen and visible means of articulation. Use the shadow itself as the main drawing. Distinguish puppet, prop and scenery by their outline and use focus softness to make distance from the screen readable.

## Surfaces and construction
Place thin rods, articulated puppet parts and props between a light and a translucent screen. Model their distance from the screen so an edge changes softness as the part moves towards the light.

## Colour roles
Preserve the difference between stained material, opaque ink and transmitted light. Use a warm light field and make translucency or outline colour refer to the puppet material.

Example palette. background #EFE0BC, foreground #272821.

## Lettering and captions
Leave approved words in a lit screen region the puppet does not cross during reading time. Allow a solid word shape only if it is part of the shadow action.

## Timing and movement
Start with the shadow settled on the screen and move the puppet along a readable silhouette path. Change edge softness through movement towards or away from the light. Let movement of the main rod lead a small tremor or trailing tassel. If a held pose is part of the action, let those secondary parts settle before the next push.

## Framing and viewpoint
Show the audience’s view, move through the stage frame and travel sideways along the lit screen. Track a puppet, snap closer on an impact or whip along a moving piece. Hold a wide through a transformation, give two figures space for hesitation, inspect cut detail or tilt from floor line to upper screen. Circle behind to reveal the apparatus and pull back to the room. Keep the camera within the lit screen during close views; join scenes through shifts in lighting or foreground cloth.

## Sound options
If enabled, use a cloth or joint cue for visible interactions and leave quiet room between gestures. When enabled, keep taps and cloth or rod contact in step with the movement.

## Characteristic actions
- Raise one arm about a fixed joint, cross behind a second puppet and hold an expressive silhouette.
- Move a puppet towards the lamp for a larger shadow, turn it through an entrance or reveal its controls behind the screen.

## Review checks
Check shadow edge and throw from the same light position. Test the silhouette at the closest intersection of rods, joints and props.

## Implementation tools
Compute shadow size and softness from screen separation and key the puppet from its joints. Parent puppet parts to visible hinge points and compute shadow softness by distance to the light.

## Project choices
Choose a duet, an audience view followed by a close view or a story carried by one articulated figure. Use a short encounter or silhouette procession. Keep joints and one consistent lamp direction.

> Clay shapes show deformation, fingerprints and incremental changes that feel made by hand.

## Visual identity
Make deformation and contact look like physical clay being worked. Make clay poses look physically adjusted between exposures.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep small pressure marks, thickness and surface variation local. Use matte clay, small stable fingerprints and broad light that exposes contact.

## Colour roles
Give silhouette and material response coherent colour on opposing poses. Keep clay colour and surface response consistent as the shape deforms. Use separate clay values where a squeezed hand, mouth or limb might blend into the body. Keep highlight shape broad and supported by visible material curvature.

Example palette. background #F0E4D3, foreground #444B3D, accent 1 #A2A680, accent 2 #C58D74.

## Lettering and captions

> Articulated puppets hold distinct poses in a practical-looking set. Their scale and contact ground the performance.

## Visual identity
Let distinct puppet poses tell the story within a practical-looking set. Tell the action through poses of an articulated puppet in a miniature set.

## Surfaces and construction
Use jointed bodies, solid grips and controlled miniature materials. Keep joints, costume pieces and set scale consistent across the movement.

## Colour roles
Keep the puppet values clear against its surroundings. Use stable local colours and lighting that shows the puppet separating from the set.

Example palette. background #EDE4D1, foreground #414638, accent 1 #8E8263.

Keep approved lettering clear of the strings and rods if they are visible by design. Place captions where the swinging figure leaves enough clear background.

Lead a puppet's action with the part a rod or string can drive, then let attached parts follow. Hold main poses while untouched limbs come to rest.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame a view that includes the relevant joint, support and end contact. Use wider stage context followed by an angle that shows articulation. Show a view that makes the full reach of the puppet and its stage clear. Include the mechanism when its pull explains the change, and let tighter crops focus on a reaction.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, distinguish a puppet joint, prop strike and stage contact. Sync each to the displayed pose and keep support movement quiet unless intentionally depicted.

Move a joint through its allowed arc while the opposite foot stays planted.

Hold an intention, articulate one joint and settle into the resulting pose.

Check support positions through the full swing and make sure successive poses preserve each attachment point. Inspect limbs for accidental overextension.

## Implementation tools
Share pose and prop anchor transforms and time each exposure explicitly. Use skeletal or hinged rigs with limits, pinned feet and discrete pose timing as appropriate.

## Project choices
Choose a character action with a clear goal and one important prop. Choose an original puppet and one physical task that suits its articulation.

sources.palette_lesson: The colour comes from the materials, not a graphic canvas. Pale blond wood and dark-brown serif ink define the tiles. The cobalt-blue pot and orange mug are scene dressing that gives the warm wood a complementary accent. What the style needs: readable contrast between the tile material and the surface it sits on, one clear light direction, and colour from physical props. styles.executable_prompt_template:
> People change position in a series of photographed poses, creating motion that reads as deliberately stepped.

## Visual identity
Make unusual movement from visibly stepped human poses. Build intentionally stepped live-performer movement from photographed poses.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep real material, support and body proportions within the chosen set. Keep costumes, props, surface marks and illumination consistent across captures. Use a stable physical floor and record hand, foot and prop contact points between poses. Keep clothing shape continuous where it can shift enough to distract from the intended steps.

## Colour roles
Use consistent exposure and distinguish the moving body from the ground. Use a stable exposure and keep costume or prop colours distinct from the floor.

Example palette. background #EEE7DC, foreground #343C43, accent 1 #8A9288.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved copy away from the full range of the performer's gesture. Use a stable caption area in the set instead of moving type with the performer.

## Timing and movement
Move the performer in measured pose increments. Give the strangest displacement a steady surrounding frame and hold a grounding pose before resuming ordinary movement.

## Framing and viewpoint
Lock the camera or track a measured route that keeps the performer and support surface visible. Frame the whole trajectory so the progression can be compared.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, align steps or prop impacts to their displayed poses. If enabled, cue visible foot and prop contacts rather than automated steps.

## Characteristic actions
Move an approved performer through a sequence of held positions that makes a slide visible.

Hold an impossible travel or position long enough for the stepped progression to read.

## Review checks
Compare adjacent frames for unwanted lighting shifts, contact slips and clothing jumps. Check a held pose at normal speed to distinguish deliberate jitter from a reset.

## Implementation tools
Use time-indexed pose exposures and keep the environment registered. Sequence consented captured frames at deliberate exposures. Label digital reconstructions according to the actual method.

## Project choices
Choose a short movement with a clearly visible setup and result. Use an original pose sequence with a safe, feasible movement plan.

> Traced drawings retain the timing, force and weight of filmed action and give it a consistent graphic surface.

## Visual identity
Retain the physical weight and rhythm of the source movement. Retain the weight and timing of filmed movement in traced drawings.

## Surfaces and construction
Use consistent line and fill treatment while tracing visible form. Trace significant contours and organise the fills around a consistent simplification rule.

## Colour roles
Keep silhouettes and overlapping limbs distinct through the palette. Reuse core subject colours across frames and choose where original lighting becomes drawn value.

Example palette. background #F1EBDD, foreground #314249, accent 1 #9D8A72.

## Lettering and captions
Mark the figure's full action path before placing approved captions. Use one stable caption area through a cross-frame move, or switch to another open area on the edit.

## Timing and movement
Trace the key weight shifts, changes of direction and contacts in the reference. Carry those timing cues into the drawing and simplify secondary traces that jitter between poses.

## Framing and viewpoint
Match the original framing or keep a documented crop anchored throughout. Keep the crop compatible with the source action and its support points.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use approved source sound or match new cues to the contact timings preserved in the tracing. Keep the cue on the same frame when the drawing is held longer.

## Characteristic actions
Trace the weight shift and dominant contour change through a short piece of real footage.

Carry a characteristic contact or shift of weight through the finished drawing.

## Review checks
Compare contact, elbow and head positions with the same moments of the reference during a quick turn. Keep contour drift deliberate and preserve silhouette breaks between limbs.

## Implementation tools
Align the trace to source time and register contours through occlusion. Track or draw contours over source frames and composite the artwork on the shared timeline. Register source video to the output canvas before tracing. Lock marked contacts across frames and use held drawings for small motion where separate traces would introduce accidental wobble.

## Project choices
Choose an action where performance matters more than surface detail. Use a short filmed action whose weight, silhouette and perspective support the idea.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Articulated parts and replacement poses let an illustrated character change expression, gesture and stance.

## Visual identity
Give a layered illustration expressive motion with a deliberate rig. Make expressive motion from articulated artwork and a small set of replacement poses.

## Surfaces and construction
Use separable joints, replacement poses and clear contact anchors. Separate the pieces at their real joints and add overlap where seams would appear.

## Colour roles
Give adjacent rig parts stable local fills and line weights. Separate eyes, hands and crossing limbs by value where they overlap, and keep the same edge treatment as their draw order changes.

Example palette. background #F4EDDF, foreground #2C4249, accent 1 #7A9A91, accent 2 #C7876F.

## Lettering and captions
Reserve a stable region for approved copy outside the limb and expression swap areas. Inspect at both the largest gesture and the closest crop.

## Timing and movement
Key the major pose at the torso or hips. Animate hands, head or cloth with delayed follow-through and build a brief hold at the end of an expression change.

## Framing and viewpoint
Choose a view where limbs can separate from the torso during the strongest action. Use a view that shows the movement while keeping the silhouette readable.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, time a footstep, prop tap or cloth movement from the actual contact or flex. Fix the cue when a pose correction moves the contact frame.

## Characteristic actions
Turn a rigged head with a hand gesture and use a replacement expression at the hold.

Use anticipation, a clear key pose and a held reaction to make the rig act.

## Review checks
Check joint pivots at the widest flex, control limits on a sharp turn and the draw order where limbs cross. Scrub a pose transition for detached shapes.

## Implementation tools
Key named joints and use shared anchors for held props. Drive a layered 2D rig with explicit pivots, depth and joint limits. Swap drawings when needed. Build a hierarchy with explicit rests, pivots and a controlled draw order for crossed limbs. Provide a corrected pose where a generic interpolated bend makes the silhouette ambiguous.

## Project choices
Choose an original figure with distinguishable gestures and expressions. Design an original actor whose walk, gesture or reaction fits the rig's range.

sources.style_evidence: The character keeps a stable body while its eye and expression shapes are replaced (dots, arcs, squares), and it rises, lands and turns. This suggests rigged parts with replaceable expressions rather than full redraws.
sources.palette_lesson: The fixed part of this example is a lighting-driven palette system laid over one unchanging landscape layout: the same mountains, lake, meadow, flowers and foliage are recolored for dusk (violet-to-peach), day (clear blue with an orange sun), cosmic night (indigo-violet nebula) and moonlit night (navy and slate). The character keeps a single warm terracotta local color throughout, so it is always the warmest and most saturated mass and stays the focal point against every sky. Glow effects (rings, HUD panels, fireflies, mushrooms) use pale cyan, white or yellow-green additive light and stay small. The specific sky hues, the planet and moon, and the terracotta mascot color are this author's choices for this subject, not style requirements. What carries over is one consistent local color for the hero, a sky/time-of-day gradient that sets the mood, and environment colors that shift together as a single lighting state.

sources.style_evidence: Characters keep the same drawn parts across pose changes (crouch, grip, boxing stance) and swap expressions. This looks like a puppet/rig workflow on a locked background rather than full redraws, but it cannot be confirmed from stills.
sources.palette_lesson: The sunny blue sky, warm-gray pavement, red bridge, dusty-blue skyline and gold crown are this author's choices for one daytime-city rivalry scene, not constraints of the style. What defines the style is a limited set of flat fills with no gradients except translucent light overlays, consistent dark outlines, clear figure-ground contrast (dark or saturated wardrobe against a light, low-detail backdrop), one glowing focal prop, and per-character color coding that can take over the frame in dramatic cutaways (blue vs peach strips on black). For new subjects, choose the environment hue from the setting and mood. Keep the set slightly lower in saturation and detail than the characters, and save the warmest, most saturated accent for the object of desire or conflict.

> A slight rhythm in the drawn outline keeps held poses alive while preserving their silhouette and position.

## Visual identity
Use outline variation to keep still drawings alive at a controlled intensity. Give held contours a small rhythmic variation without changing the subject's pose.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep shape topology and line hierarchy stable across variants. Draw a few registered versions of the same line, preserving its anchor points. Prepare several redraws around one registered contour and keep large shape landmarks fixed. Limit texture displacement to the marks meant to boil.

## Colour roles
Preserve the original fill contrast as contours fluctuate. Keep fill and stroke values stable while line shape changes slightly.

Example palette. background #F6EFDF, foreground #354142.

## Lettering and captions
Give approved small words a steady outline. Apply line boil to display lettering only when the letter structure remains legible.

## Timing and movement
Hold the underlying pose for several line redraws. Change contour samples in a regular cadence and update the actual pose independently when the action advances.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use stable framing long enough for viewers to see the intended texture. Use a crop that lets viewers see line variation without magnifying it excessively.

## Sound options
If audio is enabled, keep ordinary line cycles quiet and spot only meaningful actions. If audio is enabled, keep any cue on the actual action rather than the contour cycle.

## Characteristic actions
Hold a figure still while two or three hand-drawn contour variants alternate locally.

Hold the pose while a small change in line shape cycles around it.

## Review checks
Overlay two redraws and check that key anchors, centres and contacts stay fixed. Keep the movement within the intended thickness of the line.

## Implementation tools
Choose seeded alternates keyed by time at stable points along the outline. Use indexed contour frames with deterministic phase and shared geometry anchors.

## Project choices
Choose a stable pose with a few expressive areas that benefit from visible linework. Apply the treatment to a chosen character, prop or large title rather than every layer.

tech.implementation:
Background #FAF5E9, text #252D39, and one #B84F3F accent word. Load fonts locally and await document.fonts.ready before measuring. Words are spans (glyph spans only where meaning requires) positioned on a measured baseline grid. GSAP animates size, weight (variable font axis), tracking and position as deliberate layout changes, varying ease and duration per word and including reading holds. For the architectural recipe, chosen glyphs are converted to verified SVG paths: authored outlines are needed because font-to-path conversion (e.g. opentype.js) is not in the pool and is reported as missing. MorphSVGPlugin bends only the load-bearing stroke (e.g. a 'T' lintel), with unrelated transitions hidden under occlusion. 3s preview: phrase enters and holds 0–1.2s → key word re-weights and becomes a lintel 1.2–2.2s → final composition holds. The recipe's source palette (#102820/#F4E9D5/#F2B544) is used only if adopted explicitly. ScrambleText is optional for a short title.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Type changes position, weight or scale in ways that express the meaning and rhythm of the approved words.

## Visual identity
Make the pacing and placement of approved words communicate the idea. A repeated term can keep its position through a layout change, and a selected word can increase in weight when its meaning gains emphasis.

## Surfaces and construction
Use stable glyph layout and control clip edges by word or line. Shape text in clean editable blocks with appropriate tracking and alignment.

## Colour roles
Reserve contrast for the word or phrase carrying the change. Use colour to mark one semantic emphasis while keeping high contrast on key words. Give the phrase a high-contrast base treatment. Shift one approved term into an accent value only when the change in colour carries emphasis or groups repeated ideas.

Example palette. background #FAF5E9, foreground #252D39, accent 1 #B84F3F.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved copy and its natural reading order. Space the longest line first and give the key word a clear baseline through scale changes.

## Timing and movement
Reveal words at phrase boundaries and settle them into reading positions before the next phrase. Let weight or scale shift on a chosen word and preserve the full meaning around the emphasis.

## Framing and viewpoint
Frame typography with space for its movement and keep a stable reading axis. Stay wide during a sentence and crop only when a word needs to dominate.

## Sound options
If music is enabled, line up a phrase change or strong word with a measured accent while giving the complete line a separate reading hold. If effects are enabled, reserve a short cue for a meaningful text state change.

## Characteristic actions
Carry one word into a new line position to reveal its relationship to the next phrase.

Shift emphasis through a controlled movement and hold the complete phrase.

## Review checks
Check the complete phrase at normal speed with audio muted. Verify that position changes never reverse reading order or crop part of a word.

## Implementation tools
Separate text layout from animated transforms and retain valid line breaks. Measure layout before keying word groups. Keep shape transforms separate from text content.

## Project choices
Choose a phrase with a useful change in meaning, perspective or emphasis. Choose a short statement, contrast or question with enough empty space for the selected motion.

That is one brand-adjacent scene choice, not a fixed requirement. What defines the style is structural: one dark or quiet field with a single soft, low-contrast light source; one high-contrast neutral color for type; and one accent hue used only for thin functional marks (caret, divider rule, small eyebrow label). ## Visual identity
Build a readable sequence from consistent rules for abstract forms. Establish a recurring visual grammar from a few related shapes.

## Surfaces and construction

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Legible product screens lead the eye through a specific interaction. Cropping, movement and emphasis show how the interface responds.

## Visual identity
Give one interface operation the space and scale of a product reveal. Turn a series of screens into stations on a physical route.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate the display plane from layered controls, focus halos and the surrounding dark stage. Build raised cards and screens on one work surface, with small characters or props marking stops. Keep each window as a reusable layout with its own mask and depth. Anchors should survive a panel flight or crop so the selected row, pointer and status can move together.

## Colour roles
Use one approved brand accent on the active control and a different error state only if needed. Give the tabletop a calm base and reserve contrast for the next destination. Reduce inactive surface contrast and reserve the bright accent for the control or result. Keep desktop surfaces quiet and match the focal accent across screen planes.

Example palette. background #F7F9FA, foreground #263440.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved interface copy in the normal control layout. Keep labels, tooltips and status text attached to the state they describe during a move.

## Timing and movement
Establish the control and starting UI state. Trigger the state change at the point of interaction, let the focused panel settle, then show a meaningful resulting action before moving elsewhere. Let a selected interface item change while holding its layout anchors. For a spatial handoff, keep the cursor or selected element visible through the full move.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use empty space around one hero detail. Hold a tiny control in extreme close-up, pull back on a smooth scale curve to show accumulation, or close in on a frozen interface state. Use rapid pulls for cause and effect, dives and matching cuts for details and brief expanding inserts for overload. Present a turning object in a near-still frame, track along the plane, or use an overhead for system structure. Revisit a prior framing to quantify change. Let elements grow into the next view or shrink back into the layout. Reserve tilt and shake for disorder.

Treat the work surface as a continuous route. Drift past a nearby card in a shallow orbit, bank quickly between stations, rise for a nearly overhead reading view or track low behind a traveller. Ease through a brief impact hold, then pull back to situate the complete route. Hold the target at the start of a fast move and use a raised arc across distant stations to keep intervening stops in view. Compose each wide around the key stations and leave space for approved text.

## Sound options
If enabled, use one capacitive click on the input and leave the result free of repeated hits. If effects are enabled, distinguish a transfer from a surface click. With audio enabled, use a small activation sound at the state change and leave reading beats quiet. If enabled, attach taps, hinges and landing sounds to the objects that make them.

## Characteristic actions
- Magnify one interaction, carry the active UI part to its new state and hold for the result.
- Track a data item from one readable panel to a second panel across depth.
- Let an item expand from its control, snap an accumulated set to a grid or hold one live element in a freeze. Pop a card into place, animate a press, open a drawer or retract a stop after a traveller leaves.

## Review checks
Scrub across the trigger. Check that focus, selection and changed values agree in the same frame and that the interface remains complete on a direct seek.

## Implementation tools
Anchor expansion and collapse to the source control and key the camera in the same coordinates. Put card surfaces on known transforms and drive camera aim from the travelling subject and each station. Use discrete interface state and animate persistent elements between their original and new bounds. Texture individual readable UI planes or render DOM at coordinated transforms. Keep focal view resolutions legible.

## Project choices
Choose a feature reveal, a control sequence or a system whose scale is discovered by pulling back. Use a workflow, tour or branching route whose complete path can fit in one wide view. Demonstrate one workflow or feature per beat. Use the project's supplied or approved interface. Track an item between panels, files or diagrams. Keep its identity through the transition.

sources.palette_lesson: The scene choices in this example are a near-black warm brown/olive vignette, warm off-white headline type, a single gold/amber emphasis color, and a phone screen that changes from stark white (the problem) to a warm paper tone (the solution). The gold, the brown-black field and the paper tone are this author's mood choices for a 'late-night reading' feel. They are not rules of the style. styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A chart or physical comparison carries the explanation. Stable scales and well-defined marks give each change a measurable meaning.

## Visual identity
Show one measurable relationship at a time. Establish the baseline or reference observation and make movement show how a value, trend or distribution changes.

## Surfaces and construction
Build axes, ticks and markers on a stable coordinate plane. Use heavier visible marks for the measured values and thinner guides to keep reference, label and data legible at the same scale.

## Colour roles
Separate categories with colour while position, length or area carries the measured quantity. Choose series colours with redundant markers. Keep axes lower in contrast than the data.

Example palette. background #FAF7EF, foreground #263744, accent 1 #367E88, accent 2 #C17E49, accent 3 #856B9A.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved units next to the plotted values and describe the series at a clear legend or directly beside its trace. Keep labels fixed when data animates beneath them.

## Timing and movement
Set axes and units before moving a value. Update markers, labels and scales together and hold the comparison long enough to identify the changed relationship. Let the tempo of the data determine where a chart needs a pause. A slow rise and a steep jump should receive visibly different treatment even if the audio pace stays fixed.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a sliding, zooming view over one information surface. Introduce the whole pattern before isolating a case, or pull back from a mark as the axes appear. Track the newest mark with lead room, rise or roll as the increase becomes tense, and use a sharp push or recoil for a real break in scale. Hold for transformations and comparisons. Pull and pan to extend the data, or move across annotation strips to revisit evidence. Pin scale labels when the underlying axis moves beyond the frame.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, mark a real change or highlight. Leave the reading hold unaccented. If asked for sonification, map sound to a specific variable and keep it consistent across views.

## Characteristic actions
- Form two series on the same axis, accent their change in relationship and hold the comparison.
- Let axes appear around accumulated marks, pin an annotation past a scale move or show a single case inside the aggregate.

## Review checks
Check values, units and scale at two states and at a transition. Confirm that interpolation never implies a measured value or precision absent from the supplied data.

## Implementation tools
Drive shapes and labels from one scale function and keep axes separate from creative camera motion. Use one scale function for marks, ticks and annotations. Drive values from supplied data. Use the same domain transform for geometry, axes and labels. Keep a key of real observations and expose estimated or interpolated values in a separate treatment where the brief needs them.

## Project choices
Use a trend, distribution or comparison and choose the chart that fits the data. Animate an ordered bar set, time series or slope. Derive geometry directly from provided values.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A recognisable shape carries the eye into the next scale, so each successive zoom feels like part of the same space.

## Visual identity
Teach scale by transforming the view through connected levels. Retain at least one identifiable feature at a handoff so a closer crop or larger surrounding world reads as part of the same space.

## Surfaces and construction
Use opaque layered silhouettes and simple hard-edged rings for glow. Give each zoom level a defined aperture and matched landmarks on both sides of its join. Keep opaque foreground shapes separate from glow so hidden levels stay concealed until the handoff.

## Colour roles
Reserve each ring value for a clear depth or emission role and preserve the subject's colour through a scale change. Assign colour by layer or scale so the common landmark remains identifiable.

Example palette. background #F4EFE3, foreground #30404A, accent 1 #688D96, accent 2 #B78462.

## Lettering and captions
Use enabled text on a plane the viewer can read before approaching or on a stable overlay if it must persist across levels.

## Timing and movement
Start with a recognisable object and move towards an aperture with continuous perspective. Let the next level take over at matched scale and position as the previous one fills the frame. Use the aperture change to expose a new detail or a new point of view. If a figure reacts during the move, keep the eye or gaze fixed on the destination until the set changes.

## Framing and viewpoint
Move between scales through a ring, opening or lens, keeping an anchor recognisable between views. Pull out from an extreme detail to show its location, drift closer while the viewer reads, or travel alongside a subject while widening. Add a magnified inset when needed, match comparable shapes between levels and pass through layers to reveal a boundary. Give the main subject room and keep any approved text and instrument readouts out of its path.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, connect the scale jump with one short cue. Give the new diagram reading time. If effects are enabled, use a small mechanism sound to mark a scale change.

## Characteristic actions
- Align one landmark across adjacent scales and move through it to reveal the next layer.
- Use a guide's line of sight, move through a ring or stop to show actual size alongside a familiar object.

## Review checks
Inspect the handoff at the same world point on both sides of the zoom. Check for sudden jumps in scale, colour, horizon or focus.

## Implementation tools
Tie the scale readout, reference object and camera distance to shared scene parameters. Build nested scene groups from one landmark coordinate and explicit transforms per scale.

## Project choices
Choose connected scales in which a feature at one level can serve as an opening into the next. A casing, cell wall or view of terrain can carry a shared landmark between views.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> One continuous view lets the viewer follow a change through space and connect each action to its consequence.

## Visual identity
Let continuity reveal how successive actions and places connect. Tell a sequence through one readable camera path and action inside a continuous space.

## Surfaces and construction
Maintain one spatial coordinate system, coherent materials and stable depth. Keep scenery, lighting and object positions continuous through every viewpoint.

## Colour roles
Use light or colour as a handoff between focal points. Use local lighting or set colour to cue new zones without introducing unmotivated palette resets.

Example palette. background #F2EBDD, foreground #343E43, accent 1 #8D957D.

## Lettering and captions
Plan where each approved line becomes legible along the route. Give enabled captions a stable screen region even as world features move past.

## Timing and movement
Block the route around distinct viewpoints and give each reveal time to read while the camera is moving. Use foreground openings to change attention at clear moments.

## Framing and viewpoint
Plan a single camera route through plausible openings at a readable height and speed. Use obstructions, depth and pacing to prepare each change of attention.

## Sound options
If ambience is enabled, carry each sound position along the camera path. Crossfade at doors or walls where the environment changes, and preserve near and far cues through the crossing.

## Characteristic actions
Pass a foreground object and reveal the next action in the same continuous space.

Redirect a continuous route around an occluder or follow an action to its result.

## Review checks
Review framing along the entire path, including behind foreground items. Check that no intended cut is needed to recover a missed object or unreadable line.

## Implementation tools
Key the camera and action separately and compute focus from shared targets. Author a keyed spatial camera path with geometry-aware clearance and shot-time focus curves. Plan the camera path through usable viewpoints with explicit target and focus keys. Give occluding props stable positions and check the camera's clearance along the whole route.

## Project choices
Choose a route whose events can be followed without losing context. Use a tour, hand-off or unfolding event with staging that fits one uninterrupted view.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A shape keeps enough of its contour or landmarks through a transformation to make the new form feel related.

## Visual identity
Keep a recognisable feature alive during a change of form. Transform one shape into another while retaining a visible relationship between their contours.

## Surfaces and construction
Use compatible paths with intentional joins and shared landmarks. Match contours, holes and key landmarks before setting intermediate forms. Use corresponding points and compatible path direction for each form. Separate interior holes from the outside contour so one edge can shrink without flipping the whole shape.

## Colour roles
Carry key colour roles through the intermediate shapes. Keep shared regions in related colours so the viewer can follow them.

Example palette. background #F5EFE2, foreground #2F4348, accent 1 #5C9790, accent 2 #CB8661.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved labels where they can describe the completed form. Set caption timing to durable shape changes so nearby movement leaves text legible.

## Timing and movement
Pick corresponding corners, curves or landmarks first. Move those points through a small set of readable intermediate poses and hold the final silhouette before reshaping again.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep a stable framing and centre of gravity during the contour change. Use a stable frame so a change in shape cannot be mistaken for camera motion.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, place one cue at the semantic change or settled target. If audible, use a clear cue at the resolution of the change.

## Characteristic actions
Carry a recognisable curve from the first form into the defining curve of the second.

Align anchor points, reveal a transitional state and settle on a readable result.

## Review checks
Scrub the most compressed intermediate pose. Check path winding, hole order and any edge that can fold back on itself.

## Implementation tools
Match point order and winding before interpolating the paths. Normalise vector contour order and key matched nodes from explicit shapes.

## Project choices

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Flat pictorial layers travel at different rates as the view shifts, giving a drawn space visible depth.

## Visual identity
Use relative layer travel to make a flat image feel spatial. Create spatial depth by moving flat artwork on separate depth planes.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate foreground, middle and background plates with compatible edge and lighting treatment. Extend the artwork beyond the crop and separate genuine foreground overlaps. Separate the picture at real occlusion edges, extend background behind foreground cutouts and assign layers to observed depth. Give the nearest pieces enough image outside the frame to survive a pan.

## Colour roles
Keep figures distinct from both near framing and distant planes. Use distance and low-contrast background values to reinforce the layer order.

Example palette. background #EFE7D6, foreground #34473F, accent 1 #8A9C85.

## Lettering and captions
Attach approved world labels to their original layer. Put enabled subtitles high or low enough to clear the foreground crossing.

## Timing and movement
Move foreground, subject and background at rates tied to their planned depth. Give the foreground time to clear before the most important reveal and hold the final layered view.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a measured dolly or pan that makes relative motion and depth visible. Use lateral travel or a shallow push to reveal spacing without tearing the plates.

## Sound options
If sound is enabled, let spatially placed cues stay with their layers as the view changes. If effects are enabled, tie depth and contact cues to the intended layer.

## Characteristic actions
Move past a foreground silhouette to uncover a slower midground action.

Reveal a layer behind a foreground edge or change which plane carries the action.

## Review checks
Inspect the widest pan for gaps and sliding contact shadows. Check that every layer moves consistently with its depth at a direct seek.

## Implementation tools
Set plane distances and travel from one seekable camera path. Build overscanned layers with stable depth ordering and derive displacement from a shared camera path.

## Project choices
Choose an illustrated environment with clear depth and occluding shapes. Use an illustration, matte scene or original collage with identifiable depth planes.

> Radial symmetry makes a few repeated wedges feel like one continuously changing field.

## Visual identity
Let repetition build a recognisable radial transformation. Build evolving symmetry around a fixed centre and an intentional number of sectors.

## Surfaces and construction
Use consistent sector count, sharp seams and a stable centre point. Mirror joined sector edges and reserve detail for the main repeated motif.

## Colour roles
Keep the centre and repeated elements distinguishable as they change. Choose a small controlled palette that remains clear after mirroring.

Example palette. background #201D32, foreground #F4E8D4, accent 1 #9E7FB9, accent 2 #5EA7A0, accent 3 #D8A169.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved words in a separate stable field outside the repeated sectors. If lettering is the source shape, wait for the full readable word before mirroring it.

## Timing and movement
Begin with a clear repeated sector before altering its angle or source shape. Slow where the centre or mirror seam is changing and pause on the strongest symmetry.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the centre fixed in frame or move the whole composition as one deliberate change. Lock the centre before pulling back to reveal the complete arrangement.

## Sound options
If music is enabled, align a few pattern changes to phrase boundaries and leave rotation smooth. If sound is enabled, give the most visible state change a short cue.

## Characteristic actions
Turn one petal-like contour and let all sectors follow into a different symmetrical figure.

Shift one wedge and let the mirrored structure reveal how the whole changes.

## Review checks
Check the moving seams for cracks or double edges. Inspect the repeat at delivery size for flicker and keep the centre from drifting unless planned.

## Implementation tools
Generate sectors from shared angles and seed variation in the original wedge. Render one wedge geometry or shader sample and mirror it into a fixed sector count. Build one complete sector and mirror around explicit axes. Keep shared edges in the same coordinates and evaluate rotation independently from the image changing inside the wedge.

## Project choices
Choose a pattern with clear changes in scale or symmetry. Choose floral, graphic or architectural forms whose symmetry still reads when settled.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Strong type and a single moving visual hold together as a poster before, during and after the action.

## Visual identity
Keep both the opening view and finished view readable as a designed poster. Make a complete poster that remains readable when its main element moves.

## Surfaces and construction
Use stable type, simple structural shapes and one featured moving element. Build clear headline, image and supporting blocks before introducing motion.

## Colour roles
Use contrast to preserve hierarchy throughout the movement. Use a restrained poster palette with strong contrast where the headline sits.

Example palette. background #F4EDDF, foreground #273B44, accent 1 #B66A4B.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved type using the poster's hierarchy and margins. Reserve a clear block for the smallest copy when title scale or texture changes.

## Timing and movement
Bring the headline shape, supporting image and small details in a deliberate reading order. Hold the finished poster as a usable still before the next loop.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep a frontal poster-sized layout and use boundary crossings sparingly. Hold the whole poster and crop only when its information remains clear.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, spot the primary reveal and keep ordinary poster loops quiet. If enabled, use a simple accent at the most important movement.

## Characteristic actions
Let imagery cross one poster boundary and settle back into a complete display.

Let the main image enter or transform while the rest of the poster remains legible. Carry a key line or cut edge from one layout into the next. Use its uninterrupted direction to relate two finished poster arrangements.

## Review checks
Check a still from the finished layout as well as the major motion pose. The hierarchy and image crop should work at poster size and as a thumbnail.

## Implementation tools
Separate fixed layout from keyed illustration layers. Use a fixed layout grid with individually clipped motion elements and explicit readable holds.

## Project choices
Choose a poster whose primary message benefits from one animated change. Use an event poster, cover or campaign study with a complete static composition.

sources.palette_lesson: The lavender-to-pink gradient, the blue-violet and coral ribbons and the violet year numerals are this author's colors for one festival brand. They are not a style rule. What carries over is a structure. A single soft two-stop gradient field serves as the canvas. Two or three saturated gradient ribbons share the canvas's color family, plus one warm complementary ribbon. The type is one very dark, near-black hue taken from the gradient family so it stays readable on every part of the gradient. One accent hue is reused on a key word or number. A white label pill gives the small header text its own contrast. When dense text appears, ribbon opacity drops so the type stays legible, and it comes back up on the title cards. For new subjects, choose the gradient from the subject's mood and keep the dark-type contrast check for the lightest and darkest ends of the gradient.

sources.style_evidence: Seconds 7–8 settle into a complete static poster lockup: headline, subtitle strip, kicker, date label and stamp badge in balanced negative space.
sources.palette_lesson: The author's example palette is a grainy near-black ground, warm off-white type and one saturated crimson accent. Red builds up in stages: first a separator dot, then low-value radial rays, then a full-width flat band, and finally a stamp badge. What defines the style is not the black or the specific red. It is three things: a single dominant dark or neutral ground, one high-chroma signal color kept for punctuation and the hero band, and type with the strongest value contrast. The background never competes, because the sunburst rays sit close to the ground's value. Type that sits on the accent band stays the paper/off-white tone, so the band reads as a backing plate rather than as the canvas. For new subjects, change the ground and the accent while keeping these roles: for example, a deep indigo/ink-navy ground with a signal-orange band, a cold slate/graphite ground with an acid-yellow band, a deep forest or bottle-green ground with a vermilion band, or an inverted light warm-gray paper ground with black type and a cobalt band. Keep one accent hue, keep the rays within roughly 10–15% of the ground's value, and check the contrast of off-white type on the band.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A stable centre line, balanced sets and ordered blocking put the arrangement of subjects at the heart of the frame.

## Visual identity
Make blocking and spatial order carry the meaning of a shot. Use a clear centre axis and ordered blocking to give a scene a theatrical composition.

## Surfaces and construction
Use clear figure positions and matching perspective cues across the axis. Build sets and props with consistent scale and purposeful paired placements.

## Colour roles
Place an accent on the exception that changes the balance. Choose a compact scene palette and make the main actor or object distinct on the axis.

Example palette. background #EEE0C8, foreground #39494B, accent 1 #8B9A81, accent 2 #B97D66.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved lettering in a clear axial field or in balanced positions on both sides. Keep text baselines steady through a centred move.

## Timing and movement
Hold the centreline through the approach or reveal. Time paired actions together, or create a short deliberate delay on one side when that change carries meaning.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use frontal framing, steady pushes or lateral moves that establish when symmetry changes. Start frontal and keep off-axis views purposeful.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, point to selected stage contacts or reactions. Leave dialogue room. If sound is enabled, align spatial or contact cues with the visible choreography.

## Characteristic actions
Hold a centred composition and let one asymmetrical exit draw attention to the change.

Break the symmetry briefly and show what restores or changes the order.

## Review checks
Review the strongest spatial pose against its centreline. Check that any left-right difference has a visible purpose and that the horizon stays level.

## Implementation tools
Key positions in a shared scene frame with an explicit centre reference. Use explicit world or layout anchors for both sides and key camera moves around the chosen axis. Define the centreline, horizon and paired offsets in the same coordinate frame. Use mirrored transforms for matched movements and key a divergence only where it matters to the composition.

## Project choices
Choose an entrance, exchange or change of balance staged across one axis. Choose an original set and cast suited to formal, frontal blocking.

sources.style_evidence: Strictly frontal, axially symmetric theatrical framing: paired curtains, paired lamps, a centred cup and pelmet medallion, and a controlled pastel-plus-jewel palette.
sources.palette_lesson: The pinks, the lavender mountains, the pink castle, the violet curtains, the gold trim and the crimson train are this author's choices for one cozy, whimsical rail scene. They are not rules of the style. What actually defines the style: a saturated, opaque, fixed interior frame that contrasts with the lighter, lower-contrast moving exterior; jewel-tone drapes against a calmer wall; small metallic accents; and depth shown by saturation and value falling off with distance. One unified grain or paper texture covers both layers. Exterior hues should follow the subject, time of day and weather. When a passing object fills the window, recheck contrast against the frame, because the dominant colour can flip completely, as it does from violet to crimson at second 8. The supplied colour figures are downscaled composite dominants, not design tokens.

sources.style_evidence: Seconds 1–7 use strict axial symmetry and frontal one-point framing: a tunnel vanishing point, a central aisle and a centered screen. Theatrical repeated architecture and a slow push-in along the axis.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-black, cool slate and blue-gray world is this author's choice for an oppressive, broadcast-dystopia mood. It is not a fixed rule of the style. What defines the craft: (1) a narrow, low-saturation environment value range; (2) one dominant light source per shot (tunnel core, projection screen, ceiling strips) that sets the silhouettes; (3) exactly one saturated hue reserved for the protagonist or turning point, with matching local light spill. The orange-red accent is meaningful because nothing else in the frame is warm. For new subjects, change the environment's color family and keep the single complementary accent: deep teal-green sea cave with a coral accent; dusty violet desert dusk with a lime or acid-yellow accent; warm sepia factory haze with a cobalt accent; cold snow-white overcast field with dark figures and a crimson accent; murky olive jungle with a magenta accent. Recheck that the silhouettes still separate from the glow field, and that captions on bright surfaces keep their contrast.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Visible actions follow the pulse and larger phrases of the chosen soundtrack when music is enabled. Measured accents and holds give the viewer time to read each change.

## Visual identity
Let the relationship between visible action and the selected music carry the sequence. Make major visual changes answer the measured structure of the chosen soundtrack.

## Surfaces and construction
Use distinct elements whose movement can land clearly on an accent. Build parts that can enter, settle and leave independently on the timeline.

## Colour roles
Use a visual accent to distinguish important beats from supporting patterns. Use repeating colour roles and reserve a palette change for a real shift in the visual phrase.

Example palette. background #F3EBDD, foreground #293B44, accent 1 #628C98, accent 2 #BA7B61.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved lyrics or captions only as enabled by the idea. Let important words stay readable across nearby accents and keep reading time independent from individual beats.

## Timing and movement
When music is enabled, select a few measured accents and phrase turns. Time the main pose or change to those moments and leave room inside phrases for anticipation and recovery. Use visual phrasing when the idea calls for silence.

## Framing and viewpoint
Cut or reframe on selected structural accents and preserve a readable subject between them. Let camera changes serve the action instead of cutting at every beat.

## Sound options
When it selects silence, preserve visual phrasing without claiming audio sync. If music is enabled, measure its actual beats and use only the accents the idea needs.

## Characteristic actions
Anticipate a measured accent, land one visible change and hold through surrounding beats.

Align selected actions with the recorded pulse or phrase boundary.

## Review checks
Compare key visual event times with the selected audio markers. Scrub from several entry points to check that the same action and beat still line up.

## Implementation tools
Map motion to source time and keep the video clock authoritative. Use the existing music analysis sidecar when available and key events once on the project timeline. Where music is enabled, use measured beat or phrase markers from the approved track and assign an explicit event time to each visual accent. Give holds, anticipation and recovery their own time ranges.

## Project choices
Choose a few changes that benefit from measured alignment and allow other moments to rest. Choose the amount and kind of beat alignment based on the idea and track.

sources.palette_lesson: The near-black navy canvas is this author's choice for a night-time scene. It is not a requirement of the style. The rules that actually define it are luminance-based: (1) the ground is quiet and low-contrast so emissive events are the brightest thing in frame; (2) the resting hardware (bars, catchers, launchers) is drawn in dim, desaturated versions of each instrument's hue; (3) each instrument or voice gets one stable hue family, here cool cyan-teal, warm amber-gold and dusky violet, with a small red-pink tick reserved for percussion; (4) the struck element jumps to a near-white core with a tint of its hue, then fades back. > Compression on contact and extension in motion show an object’s weight, flexibility and direction of force.

## Visual identity
Show where the force acts by changing the shape along the direction of travel or contact. Give a light, elastic object a longer stretch and faster recovery than a heavy one. Retain the silhouette features that identify the subject.

## Surfaces and construction
Use forms that maintain believable apparent mass across poses. Use deformable silhouettes with registered surfaces and believable points of contact. Keep the main mass coherent through deformations by adjusting width as height changes. Put eyes, joints and texture in the same deformation coordinates as the body.

## Colour roles
Keep the moving silhouette distinct throughout deformation. Keep local colours stable during deformation so apparent volume is easier to follow.

Example palette. background #F4EDDF, foreground #32444A, accent 1 #66978E, accent 2 #C78461.

## Lettering and captions
Keep enabled copy outside the silhouette's stretched path. Reserve any stretching of approved letters for a large readable word and restore its full shape.

## Timing and movement
Anticipate in the opposite direction, stretch along travel just before impact and squash against the contact surface. Recover along the same action axis and give the rest pose time to read.

## Framing and viewpoint
Choose a view that shows the whole travel axis and the contact plane. Keep more room around the form at its longest pose and let the impact surface stay in view through recovery.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, time the impact cue to contact and keep rebound quieter. If audible, put the main cue at contact rather than during the stretch.

## Characteristic actions
Compress along the impact direction, widen across it, then return to the rest shape.

Show anticipation, contact, recovery and a stable finish.

## Review checks
Compare mass at the longest and flattest shapes and verify a firm contact point. Check that recovery returns the character to the intended proportions.

## Implementation tools
Separate deformation from overall movement on the same pose timeline. Use constrained scale pairs or deformation targets with an anchored contact axis.

## Project choices
Choose a bounce, collision or weight transfer whose direction is clear. Use an impact, leap, reach or elastic prop whose action establishes the need for deformation.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Different media each carry an identifiable part of the story, with transitions that show how they relate.

## Visual identity
Keep each medium responsible for a distinct part of the idea. Combine distinct media whose roles are clear in the same visual story.

## Surfaces and construction
Give each layer its own texture and match shared depths and light. Give photos, drawings, type and objects their own edges and textures, with compatible depth cues. Assign a real role to each layer, such as an inked outline for structure and a photo detail for evidence. Give contact shadows an explicit owner wherever one medium covers another.

## Colour roles
Use a common colour relationship where the media meet. Share a few colour roles and preserve original asset colours when required.

Example palette. background #F1E6D1, foreground #3B4948, accent 1 #688E87, accent 2 #B97A5C.

## Lettering and captions
Assign approved type to the medium with the clearest contrast. If an approved word changes material, preserve its placement and reading order.

## Timing and movement
Give each medium a distinct reveal or movement. Make the handoff visible at a shared edge, gesture or object, then settle before a new medium takes focus.

## Framing and viewpoint
Carry one placement, silhouette or line of action across each media change. Hold enough context before a close view of the handoff.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, let the material change be audible at the shared physical contact. Match the outgoing and incoming sound levels so the transition does not hide other approved tracks.

## Characteristic actions
Match a photographed outline to a drawn path and carry one recognisable feature across the change.

Join two materials through a matching silhouette, direction or action.

## Review checks
Check overlap shadows, texture scale and colour at each handoff. Verify the main subject stays identifiable as its treatment changes.

## Implementation tools
Composite separate media passes with a documented layer order. Layer independent vector, raster or 3D assets with matched coordinates and composited contact shadows.

## Project choices
Choose an idea where distinct materials can explain different parts of the same subject. For example use drawn arrows for a process and a supplied photograph for the contact or texture that matters to it.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A fixed isometric projection gives people, icons and measurements a shared visual scale and geography.

## Visual identity
Explain measured information with recognisable spatial icons on one readable board. Let paths, grouped units or a cutaway show the relation between a count and the objects it describes.

## Surfaces and construction
Use a shared isometric projection for objects and diagram lines. Give visible faces simple ink edges and contact shading, and keep cubes, connectors and cutaways aligned to the same axes.

## Colour roles
Use a stable category palette and reserve the focal colour for the active relation. Use a consistent light direction across faces. Emphasise the active route or group with one hue.

Example palette. background #F3EFE6, foreground #2C424F, accent 1 #63968D, accent 2 #C58662.

## Lettering and captions
Attach approved labels with short leaders to the appropriate axis or face. Keep longer copy horizontal and clear of rising paths.

## Timing and movement
Show the isometric grid or base first and move blocks along its axes. Let a figure or connector travel through a visible sequence and hold at each change in state. Let a line lead the motion and reveal the arrival or cutaway after it reaches the object. Accumulation can accelerate inside a stable scale when the magnitude remains readable.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep a fixed isometric projection while following the route. Use a wide with a circular detail inset, push through nested sections or withdraw rapidly to restore scale. Hold while the system fills, travel over open space, tilt the visible crop through strata or move to another board for comparison. Keep labels separate from the subject and preserve any caption area.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, give a platform arrival a clear cue and distinguish the mechanism that moves or seats the unit. If music is enabled, let a phrase change mark a newly visible step in the diagram.

## Characteristic actions
- Pass a small object across three related platforms, with the active annotation following its position.
- Fill a row with counted units, open a strata cutaway or connect a cause to its next station.

Lead a sequence with a connector. Let it reach one station before showing a cutaway, raising a stack or moving to the next station, so the path explains the order.

## Review checks
Inspect draw order as forms pass each other. Check that projected edges point along their assigned axis and that connector links meet their endpoints.

## Implementation tools

sources.palette_lesson:
The dark navy canvas is this author's choice for a nighttime, dashboard-style simulation. It is not part of what defines isometric diorama style. The style constraints are these:
- Neutral matte masses (grey concrete, brown soil cross-sections) give low-saturation structure.
- Exactly one emissive 'system' hue (here cyan/teal) is reserved for flow, transport and movement.
- A warm secondary light (yellow windows) shows that spaces are lived in.
- A small set of semantic UI colours (green on time, red late, amber priority) is used only in the 2D overlay.

For new subjects, keep these roles and resolve the canvas from the scene's lighting and mood:
- Daytime city logistics: a pale cool grey or soft sky-blue field, with darker charcoal UI panels.
- Agriculture or water systems: a muted sage or slate-green canvas with blue flow lines.
- Factory or energy: a deep graphite with an orange emissive system hue in place of cyan.
- Medical or lab: an off-white with cool blue-grey masses and a magenta flow accent.
- Ocean or harbour: a deep teal-blue with sand-coloured section faces.

Whatever the canvas, check that the flow hue stands out against both the canvas and the building masses, and that the UI panels stay readable over the scene.

The composition's real palette is inside the map: muted lawn green, soft grey roads, slate-blue water, and buildings in desaturated pastels (cream, blush pink, lilac, blue-grey) with charcoal factory roofs and brick chimneys. One warm orange/amber accent family marks the active state and tags. These colors are this author's choice for a sunny daytime suburban town, and the app even offers Morning/Dusk/Night modes. What defines the style is the medium: flat matte shading with no textures, a restrained desaturated base with one saturated accent hue for interaction or emphasis, soft ambient shadows, and readable 2D labels on top. For new subjects, take the ground plane and lighting from the scene rather than reusing green lawn and white UI.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A visible stroke draws the subject in one readable sequence, with direction and pauses revealing how the form connects.

## Visual identity
Make the progress of one drawn path explain the subject. Keep the drawing tip visible at a decision point so an intersection, isolated feature or retrace reads as an intentional change.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep paper and ink simple so local width and a small nib shadow are enough to show contact.

## Colour roles
Spend the accent on the moment when the stroke acquires new meaning. Use one contrasting ink against mostly empty paper. Any approved accent should be separate from the main line.

Example palette. background #F9F4E7, foreground #27434A, accent 1 #AA6945.

## Lettering and captions
Leave approved labels close to their line endpoints. Keep leaders out of crossed paths and reveal a label when its line reaches the named feature.

## Timing and movement
Draw the line in a useful reveal order, starting at the feature that explains the diagram. Slow at joins and stop after the contour or route resolves. Use a continuous tip motion and slow through high curvature. For a retrace, bring the previous line back along its own path before taking a different branch.

## Framing and viewpoint
Continuously adjust the degree of track between composed views and close tracking of the nib. Hold with a gradual push for emphasis, mirror a framing for a callback, withdraw to reveal the entire path, or scroll sideways and roll with the stroke. Let a line connect directly into the next image so transitions remain part of the drawing.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, tie paper contact to the moving tip. Let pauses follow the drawn action. If sound is enabled, bring the drawing texture forward only while contact is visible.

## Characteristic actions
- Draw through one contour joint and reuse the same stroke to turn into a second shape.
- Allow a final curve to become the beginning of a new subject, or retrace a short segment when the idea calls back.

## Review checks
Scrub across starts and joins to check stroke length, caps and direction. Verify the complete contour remains consistent after a direct seek.

## Implementation tools
Derive reveal and camera follow from distance along a continuous path. Use one continuous vector path with length-based reveals and real shared joins. Use path length to schedule the drawing tip. Slow it at tight corners without changing the final contour, and evaluate already drawn segments directly from timeline time.

## Project choices
Choose an explanation with related silhouettes that can share one line. Connect two objects, poses or diagrams with one path. Leave a recognisable complete form at each hold.

sources.style_evidence: Each chapter's icon is built from consistent thin white contours and connectors: a node-link network, an outlined house, a line chart that draws left-to-right and finishes with an endpoint dot. Objects appear first, then change state.

The gradient underline on the title is a multicolor brand-like signature specific to this author's subject and should not be reused as a default. For new projects, choose the chapter hues from the subject's meaning and check that white text stays readable against each glow. The background just needs to be dark enough for emissive strokes to read. It can be deep navy, charcoal, aubergine, dark teal or warm near-black.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Solid objects change in space so their construction, orientation and relationships remain clear from successive views.

## Visual identity
Use solid form and depth to make an object's change visible. Use real spatial form and timed movement to show an object changing in three dimensions.

## Surfaces and construction
Build separate credible surfaces and preserve scale during the move. Choose a coherent rendering treatment and keep edges, materials and light consistent with it.

## Colour roles
Use local colour and light to separate parts as they change. Set local material colours and use a stable lighting plan to separate depth and focal planes.

Example palette. background #EDE9E1, foreground #303C40, accent 1 #748E8A, accent 2 #B9866C.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved labels against a stable surface or in screen space, depending on their role. Leave room for depth movement without colliding with the text.

## Timing and movement
Key a clear object pose at each change in scale, rotation or assembly. Let contact or an exposed surface motivate the main motion and use a held angle to read the result.

## Framing and viewpoint
Choose perspective for depth or orthographic framing for direct comparison based on the idea. Move across viewpoints that reveal new information, with a steady view of the result.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use distinct cues for part contact, rotation under load and the final seated pose. Keep them tied to material and visible motion.

## Characteristic actions
Turn an assembly to show one hidden joint, then seat the moving part visibly.

Turn, assemble or reveal a form and hold where its depth is best understood.

## Review checks
Check silhouettes, contact shadows and material highlights through the strongest camera and object moves. Inspect the nearest crop for clipping.

## Implementation tools
Store camera, object and light states on separate tracks. Derive a part's rotation and position from explicit axes and contact poses so a direct seek restores its shadow and highlight as well as its geometry.

## Project choices
Choose a spatial relationship that cannot be explained as clearly from one flat view. Choose an assembly, object study or spatial diagram with one coherent finish. Choose a shape whose relation to a floor, light or other part can be seen changing. A rotation should reveal a genuinely new feature or spatial relationship.

sources.palette_lesson: Palette structure: one saturated, subject-owned hue (the bridge's red-orange paint) set against a desaturated atmospheric field (fog gray with a faint warm haze) and a darker, low-contrast ground plane (slate water). A separate cooler surround color (dark teal) belongs to the UI or page chrome. These colors come from the subject, location and weather. They are this author's example, not a style rule. What carries over is the luminance and saturation hierarchy: the hero object holds the only strong chroma, the atmosphere fades distant geometry toward the background value, and the chrome color contrasts with the scene without competing with it.

sources.style_evidence: Satin metal with cut-face bevels, translucent glass and a coherent key light. The camera moves from a close push-in to a three-quarter orbit to a side elevation, all in one weighted continuous camera move.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-black, slightly cool stage is this author's choice for an optics subject. It suits the subject because emissive ray lines need a dark field to read as light. It is not a requirement of the cutaway/exploded style. What defines the style is how colors are used, not the hues: an opaque, low-chroma shell material; lighter cut faces so the section reads; translucent glass; one or two small warm material accents (the gold mounts); semantic, legend-backed colors for flows (here red/green/blue rays plus a white converged core); and one saturated highlight for the selected part (the blue sensor). In a new scene, choose the stage from the subject and the lighting. Flow colors must stay readable against it, and the same color should mean the same thing across every camera move and state.
