tech.implementation:
Raw WebGL2 fullscreen triangle at a bounded internal resolution (e.g. 640×360, upscaled), fragment-shader raymarch at ≤64 primary steps and ≤6 light steps through a 3D density/emission field. The field is seeded fBm noise advected analytically upward by uTime (buoyancy and curl offsets as closed-form functions of time, no feedback buffers). The temperature field maps through an explicitly approximate ramp: flame_core #FFF0BC → flame_amber #FFAD42 → flame_orange #F05A28, then cooling into smoke #747B86 that absorbs and scatters light (Beer–Lambert). An analytic stationary hearth/ground with coal #4B403A receives flicker light spill. Background #101218, exposure clamped. GSAP's paused timeline sets uTime, uIgnite and uCool; every seek redraws one frame. 3s preview: ignition 0–0.6s → tall readable flame 0.6–2.0s → cooling translucent smoke 2.0–3.0s. The caption states it is an illustrative procedural volume, not a combustion solver. Full physically simulated shots need Blender/Cycles gas simulation with baked frames; it is unavailable here and reported as missing. The explosion recipe uses staged deterministic shock radius and debris uniforms.
Optional recipe blast_aftermath: Stage ignition/compression, expanding force, displaced material and cooling aftermath. Keep causal propagation visible across several states; never replace it with one white flash. Use deterministic or baked volume/debris trajectories and coherent environmental response.

> A changing volume of flame and smoke makes heat, airflow and dissipation readable through depth and motion.

## Visual identity
Use the behaviour of flame and smoke to make heat and airflow visible. Use emissive flames and cooling smoke to reveal a changing three-dimensional volume.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate the flame, surrounding emission, cooler smoke and affected surfaces. Include buoyant motion, density falloff, translucent soot and believable local light spill. Make hot regions emissive near their source and give cooler smoke separate density and shadow controls. Put the main light where it can show the thickness of overlapping plumes.

## Colour roles
Reserve the brightest values for hot sources and retain depth in smoke. Limit the hottest highlights and retain readable cooler smoke against the setting.

Example palette. background #101218, foreground #F6EFE3, coal #4B403A, flame amber #FFAD42, flame orange #F05A28, flame core #FFF0BC, smoke #747B86.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved captions away from flame cores and opaque smoke. Check the highest and lowest background values at each text position.

## Timing and movement
Show ignition at a source, then move hot material upward and advect smoke around obstacles. Slow the fade as the last visible stream disperses and preserve the timing on a direct seek.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a stable camera scale that shows occlusion and thickness from a useful angle. Use a view that shows both the source and how the surrounding volume changes.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, put combustion and smoke-related ambience in spatial proportion to the image. Use effects only when enabled and consistent with the visible material.

## Characteristic actions
Carry a plume upward from a visible source, cool it and let it wrap behind a solid form.

Ignite a source, carry its smoke along a visible flow or hold as the volume dissipates.

## Review checks
Inspect the edge of a backlit plume and the point where smoke wraps an obstacle. Check that volume shadows and density stay consistent across seeks.

## Implementation tools
Use a deterministic volume field or precomputed sequence with known playback time. Use a bounded volume renderer with seeded parameters or baked simulation data.

## Project choices
Choose a physical event with a readable ignition, flow or cooling progression. Choose a small emissive source, plume or fire study sized to the frame and scene.

> Bounded pigment shapes, letterforms and reflected light on gold draw the eye across a decorated manuscript page.

## Visual identity
Use a firm painted line and reflective gold to direct attention within a single designed surface.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate opaque pigment, thin hatching and raised or reflective gold leaf on matte stock. Give a slight change in reflected light to the gold so it reads as material before a page turn.

## Colour roles
Let the gold retain its warmth as the light changes and reserve pale ink marks for the small details. Separate matte pigment from small gold leaf areas. Keep parchment tone visible under ornament. Set a quiet ground, clear ink and a few flat pigment fields for the decorated page. Use gold at a border, initial or focal figure where a change of angle reveals the different material.

Example palette. background #EFE4C8, foreground #352D27, gold #B89B51, red #A5433C, blue #3C5487, green #66825D.

## Lettering and captions
Fit approved initials and text inside ruled spaces and leave open room for enabled captions. Keep complex decorative fields outside fine letters.

## Timing and movement
Trace the page framework before letting an initial, border detail or gilded area appear. Hold long enough to see the ornament around the reading area before a page move.

## Framing and viewpoint
Pull from the leaf texture into the painted scene. Push through a decorative opening, travel along the painted route or use a passing cloud or spire to join places. Hold while grazing light reveals relief, then use a moving band or expanding pool of reflected light when the image changes. Match a circle across a cut and withdraw to the full composition when the painted parts need context.

## Sound options
If enabled, give a page movement one quiet paper cue. Use music selected in the idea for atmosphere. If sound is enabled, tie the small impacts to the material shown and keep slow illumination changes easy to watch.

## Characteristic actions
- Draw ornament into the reading frame and let one small highlight travel across the metallic area.
- Reveal a surface through moving light, grow a decorative edge into a frame or let a touch send a patterned response outward.

## Review checks
Check repeated leaves and border joins. Tilt the page or move light to see whether gold, ink and paper remain distinct.

## Implementation tools
Apply the light response to the leaf mask and keep surrounding contour and pigment colours stable. Use separate flat pigment and metallic masks. Animate a narrow highlight only through the leaf mask.

## Project choices
Choose a decorated margin, a patterned gate or successive discoveries through illuminated panels. Vary capitals, border patterns or scenes. Keep the reading field and pigment treatment consistent.

> Faceted shapes keep several views of a subject legible within one deliberately reconstructed painted space.

## Visual identity
Bring two or more views into one painted field. Let a shared edge, rim or joint connect the fragments so the viewer can recognise the subject even when its planes disagree about depth.

## Surfaces and construction
Use visible intersecting planes and clear contour differences at overlaps. Build intersecting planes with physical paint or paper texture and compressed depth. Use simplified planes cut from different views with enough common edges to identify the subject. Give each plane a stable local stroke or grain direction so the piece reads as paint assembled on one surface.

## Colour roles
Use contrasting values to maintain separate viewpoints without losing the subject. Use muted related pigments with selective contrast around a recognisable anchor.

Example palette. background #DED5BB, foreground #332E29, ochre #AD9369, gray #85867D, umber #705F4B, paper #ECE4D0.

## Lettering and captions
Put approved words in a stable plane or treat large lettering as one readable cut fragment. Keep accents away from the edges of the letter forms.

## Timing and movement
Expose one painted plane before turning or sliding another perspective into the same composition. Let the viewer locate the shared contour before changing angles again.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a stable view of the whole composition before entering selected facets. Hold a whole composition before inspecting a particular facet.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use one dry paper or paint cue at a visible plane placement. If enabled, reserve tonal cues for a visible plane change.

## Characteristic actions
Pivot or place an intersecting plane that reveals a second view of the same feature.

Select a view, displace a plane or show how two interpretations meet.

## Review checks
Inspect the most fragmented arrangement at delivery size. A repeated eye, rim or joint should still let the viewer recognise the subject.

## Implementation tools
Keep faceted paths separate and key their transformations independently. Build independently masked planar layers with shared landmarks for placement and deformation.

## Project choices
Choose a form that can be read from more than one useful viewpoint. Use a still life, figure or original scene with identifiable points that support multiple views.

> Broken touches of paint and shifting mixtures of colour describe transient outdoor light and atmosphere.

## Visual identity
Build near surfaces from visible strokes and let distant forms soften into larger colour patches. Keep the changes of daylight visible in the paint deposits, reflected colours and separation between foreground and distance.

## Surfaces and construction
Use small overlapping paint deposits and keep important contours selective. Give individual brush marks stable scale and orientation. Keep distant edges less defined.

## Colour roles
Group colour by light and shadow while leaving room for local mixtures. Choose reflected hues from a consistent light condition and use adjacent pigments to mix optically. Group colour in neighbouring values and temperatures so the light holds together at a distance. Reserve dark edges for anchors that still survive the shifting strokes.

Example palette. background #F0E9D7, foreground #364747, sky #9EBCC8, foliage #829C79, sunlight #D8BF7A, rose #C59D9D.

## Lettering and captions
Place approved type in an even patch of painted sky, water or margin. Avoid a stroke direction or texture that breaks up small letters.

## Timing and movement
Show broad light and shade before animating local impasto or reflected colours. Let patches of moving light gather into a change of atmosphere that the viewer can see at once.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use a stable outdoor view or shallow approach that preserves the relationship between light and subject. Use a steady view for comparison or slow travel across the important light.

## Sound options
If sound is enabled, use location ambience or the idea's approved score without timing every brush mark. When enabled, tie subtle ambience to the place rather than to every stroke.

## Characteristic actions
Introduce reflected colour to a shadow area as the main patch of light shifts.

Let light or atmosphere change while the viewer recognises the setting.

## Review checks
Compare the near and distant views. Group related brush marks into coherent value masses and keep texture attached through a pan.

## Implementation tools
Anchor brush marks to their planes and key environmental light separately. Layer persistent brush marks and key controlled light or palette changes without changing stroke identity.

## Project choices
Choose a change of light where atmosphere modifies the same underlying scene. Use a fleeting outdoor scene with a specific time, weather or reflection.

> Fine bounded outlines and pale washes separate the near, middle and distant layers of a painted scroll.

## Visual identity
Use fine drawing and layered wash to reveal a scroll's spatial order. Use bounded fine outlines and pale wash to describe the layered space of a Chinese painted scroll.

## Surfaces and construction
Keep lines bounded and allow pale washes to distinguish depth planes. Keep ink boundaries, ornamental clouds, figures and architecture registered to the paper or silk.

## Colour roles
Use ink and paper value differences to preserve quiet distance. Use pale washes and reserved open space. Keep jade tones tied to the intended mountain layers.

Example palette. background #F0EEDD, foreground #3B544D, jade #86B6A2, mountain #B5CEC0, warm paper #D8C6A5, rose #D2A6A3.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved inscriptions in the planned reading direction, using an unpainted column where possible. Preserve the relationship between seals, labels and the painted passage they accompany.

## Timing and movement
Reveal the scroll gradually along its reading direction. Slow at meaningful contour details and allow open paper to mark a scene change before passing into denser ink.

## Framing and viewpoint
Move horizontally with near and distant layers at restrained different rates where the scroll supports depth. Move as if following the scroll rather than imposing a conventional lens move.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use soft paper movement where the scroll visibly advances. If enabled, choose cues whose sources are present in the depicted space.

## Characteristic actions
Reveal a pale mountain layer behind an outlined cloud and continue toward the next architectural group.

Travel past foreground details to expose a distant layer or a quiet subject. Let a lightly painted space separate two denser passages. Carry a mountain edge, tree line or path through that reveal so the scroll feels continuous even as the camera slows.

## Review checks
Check fine strokes in the widest view and during a pan. Ensure that blank paper and lightly painted distances remain distinct from clipped highlights.

## Implementation tools
Use separate scroll-aligned layers and draw precise outlines before wash. Register wash masks and line art independently and shift whole layers from a shared scroll coordinate.

## Project choices
Choose a landscape or scene with a legible route through distinct depths. Choose a specified scroll approach with an original scene or project-supplied imagery.

styles.visual_cues: Mineral red/ochre and dark charcoal animal outlines, hand marks or simplified figures follow an uneven rock field. Material pores and irregular pigment edges belong to the surface; avoid modern cartoon outlines, neon glow or decorative pseudo-inscriptions.

tech.implementation: Preview: a Three.js WebGLRenderer with a fixed orthographic full-frame quad and ShaderMaterial. GLSL computes a seeded fBm rock height field (base #AF845A with ochre #C49B6B and chalk #DDD0B4 variation) with pore cavities and finite-difference normals. Lighting is an explicit approximation: one broad warm light at a uniform position. Pigment comes from original animal contours (bison, horse) and a few hand stencils drawn once into a Canvas 2D texture as irregular-edged charcoal #3B2B21 and red #984B32 strokes, with seeded edge noise baked. The shader offsets pigment UVs by the height gradient so marks follow the relief, absorbs pigment more in cavities, and multiplies it over albedo. uReveal against a per-stroke order map reveals pigment in short meaningful strokes over 0–1.8s. Over 1.8–3.0s, uLightPos sweeps across while the rock stays fixed. GSAP tweens the uniforms proxy, and each update renders synchronously. No glow, cartoon lines or pseudo-inscriptions. Show a disclosure on screen or in credits: procedural rock and pigment approximation, not archaeological footage. Full video: cache the static height field and albedo in a WebGLRenderTarget, or use a displaced BufferGeometry relief with MeshStandardMaterial plus a normal map as an alternative. Precompute height and stroke-order maps offline (NumPy/Pillow). Authored pigment-application frame sequences or transparent hand-drawn marks can replace Canvas strokes. styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Mineral marks follow the texture of stone and become visible as the viewer moves or light changes across the wall.

## Visual identity
Let stone geometry and material light make the painted record legible. Treat mineral pigment as a mark made on an uneven stone field.

## Surfaces and construction
Use uneven stone, mineral marks and local variation in adhesion. Let pores and ridges affect pigment coverage and maintain small irregularities in painted edges.

## Colour roles
Use supported pigment and stone tones with enough contrast to read. Choose ochre, mineral red, charcoal and stone tones with enough separation to read a figure.

Example palette. background #AF845A, foreground #2B211A, ochre #C49B6B, red #984B32, charcoal #3B2B21, chalk #DDD0B4.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved copy in a calm region outside the textured figure. If it belongs to the scene, use a treatment that preserves the material grain without confusing letters with the motif.

## Timing and movement
Reveal the marking when grazing light reaches a believable ridge or hollow. Move light at a steady pace while painted forms stay fixed and partial contours join into a whole.

## Framing and viewpoint
Use raking light and a stable viewpoint close enough to show relief. Use glancing light and paths that reveal the uneven wall without losing the motif.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, use the atmosphere and distance of the depicted space. A nearby light source or the surface it touches can have a discrete cue when an actual movement is shown.

## Characteristic actions
Carry light across a shallow ridge and reveal how the painted shape follows the stone.

Move a light or viewpoint so a partially hidden motif becomes visible.

## Review checks
Check pigment against the rough surface across a moving highlight. Inspect whether soft occlusion follows the wall relief and whether the main outline remains visible.

## Implementation tools
Sample the surface and pigment position consistently across camera views. Map pigment and stone relief to the same surface and animate bounded lighting or paint coverage. Anchor the pigment mask to the same physical surface as the wall texture and derive grazing highlights from its relief. Set the moving light on an independent path.

## Project choices
Choose a documented or clearly illustrative painted surface with a meaningful relief feature. Use original hand marks, animal forms or simplified figures whose material and references fit the brief.

styles.visual_cues: A mostly black-and-white backstage manga in one continuous film set. Preserve white round-headed, faceless, short-bodied characters with pointed feet, bold ink outlines and halftone scenery. A persistent director speaks beside a shadowed presentation board while stage, camera, lighting, art and sound crew perform tasks supported by timed storyboard JSON. Backgrounds and boards travel right to left; crew make brief trips to work positions and return for reading holds. Use compact black name badges, readable rounded status labels and small board captions. Oval speech and thought balloons stay above the director, with extra headroom for thought circles. Use #F47B45 sparingly for playback progress, working-crew dots, brief dialogue-change underlines, equipment indicators and an optional opening-title accent. Keep the opening title optional and opening-only; never repeat title cards per scene. Default cast identity: whenever Manga Production Theatre is selected or named, use the established storyboard crew as its character reference without requiring the brief to repeat it. Figures have a large blank white circular head, a compact white cutout body with small side arm points and two pointed feet, a continuous bold black contour and no facial features, fingers or jointed skeletal limbs. Keep head/body proportions, outline weight and prop scale consistent across scenes; use short whole-figure tilts, turns and pose changes rather than substituting generic line-stick people, rounded capsule mascots or realistic humans. The director is slightly larger and remains the persistent narrator beside the board. Roles must be recognizable from their silhouettes and equipment as well as their readable badges: DIRECTOR with a clapperboard; STAGE CREW carrying a prop box; ART DEPT with an oversized pencil; LIGHTING with an adjustable lamp on a stand; SOUND wearing headphones and operating a small mixer; CAMERA with a twin-reel camera and tripod. Keep each figure attached to the same role and prop throughout the film. Show only crew with an actual task, preserving the role-specific action and idle rules; do not invent work just to fill the cast. Explicit user changes take precedence.
styles.note: Application-authored style derived from the code-driven manga storyboard viewer and user-directed revisions. Not extracted from external reference footage.

tech.implementation: Build the manga from structured timed scene/beat JSON using HTML/CSS, with SVG only where precise contours help. Use one deterministic, seekable composition clock for board/scenery travel, crew trips, equipment actions, statuses and dialogue. Plan crew roles and tasks from actual recorded props/assets, captions, camera moves, lighting and sound cues; omit unsupported specialists, never imply real production footage, and do not make a model call to animate existing JSON. Preserve the established faceless silhouette rather than adding jointed limbs. Let stagehands deliver props, artists set lettering, lighting crew adjust lights, sound crew cue effects and camera crew aim toward the board. Crew travel out, work, return and settle; pausing, replay and backward seeking reproduce the same poses and labels. Reserve separate board, dialogue and crew zones; stagger crew lanes and stack zones on narrow screens. Keep the director balloon visible, use a concise cue summary, raise thought balloons to clear their trailing circles, and briefly gesture/react only when dialogue changes. Give every board a persistent ink shadow outside its reveal mask and keep captions smaller than dialogue. Use black pill name badges, high-contrast compact rounded task labels and an orange dot only while working. Share #F47B45 with small equipment indicators and dialogue-change underlines; do not use orange for low-contrast body text, permanent reaction rays or large color washes. In an interactive viewer, center a naturally scrolling bounded stage in the content area, hide scrollbar chrome while preserving scrolling, and use orange timeline progress/thumb. Playback controls and status chrome are viewer features, not mandatory video artwork. An opening-only Glitch Type Build is optional; omit it when not requested, and never add a title card per scene. A gentle phased character wave is a visual tempo effect unless actual audio beats were analyzed. Keep export resolution, frame rate, GIF size and excerpt duration in delivery settings rather than hardcoding them into this style. Retain readable holds, exact word spacing and reduced-motion access. Rough.js adds cached sketch contours; PixiJS is optional for a complex world; Matter.js is only for baked physical props. Anime.js may replace the motion owner after seek verification. HyperFrames owns composition/export, with Remotion only for a verified limitation. Crew performance rules: Give each crew member an independent cue-based schedule with explicit idle/frozen, travel, work, react and settle intervals; one shared seekable clock does not mean synchronized movement. Stage crew make a quick delivery and stop after placing a prop; art crew work deliberately on a lettering/drawing cue and freeze once it is readable; lighting crew make a short adjustment then hold the light steady; sound crew make a brief cue-triggered control action and then wait; camera crew use a slower smooth tracking move only during the recorded camera action, aiming at the board, then lock off. Stagger starts, travel duration, task duration and return timing by role so some crew remain still while others work; never make everyone run, bounce or react on every beat. Idle characters stay fully still, especially during reading holds; omit unsupported specialists. Reactions are short and motivated by a new instruction, reveal, impact or completion. A shout-out is a brief visual callout only for an explicit action/cut, warning or meaningful payoff, never every caption and never invented audible speech; keep callouts away from the board and director dialogue. Keep the director dialogue visible while its text updates; at a new cue, allow a subtle 1–3 degree head nod or turn toward the board, optionally a small body gesture, then settle. Preserve the faceless round-head silhouette without adding facial features or jointed limbs. Orange reaction marks appear briefly only with a reaction, not for the entire dialogue interval. Store each role's timed actions, pauses, reactions and callouts in deterministic code derived from storyboard cues; do not add unvalidated fields to STORYBOARD.json. Preview the same conditional acting language in a concise sample, rather than uniformly animating every character. Verify that unsupported and idle crew stay frozen, role timings differ, gestures end, callouts do not overlap, and direct/backward seeking recreates the same character states. Default character construction: start from the same reusable storyboard crew silhouette for every role, then attach the role-specific prop. Build a blank round head and a short pointed white body with bold black contours; hide the head/body seam so the cutout reads as one coherent figure. Do not replace it with thin line arms and legs, add a face or improvise a new mascot per scene. Keep separate head, body and prop groups only for controlled posing; no articulated human rig is required. Give the director a clapperboard, stage crew a box, art crew a pencil, lighting crew a lamp and stand, sound crew headphones and a mixer, and camera crew a twin-reel camera on a tripod. Assign stable role IDs and reuse their geometry, proportions, badge style and equipment across shots. Map each role to its existing independent cue-based schedule; the prop action must match the role. Describe the chosen crew and their tasks in the normal storyboard scene descriptions without adding new schema fields. Credits names, monogram avatars and contributions are replaceable content, separate from the crew role; a personal avatar must not silently replace the theatre figure. In every implementation, inspect an overview and a work pose to confirm the same silhouette, identifiable equipment, readable role badge, clear board/dialogue zones and idle crew remaining still. MANDATORY CHARACTER IMPLEMENTATION: Use the self-contained HTML/CSS in tech.reference_implementation.files returned with this style metadata as the canonical crew construction. Copy the supplied CSS and role markup before animating; do not redraw the cast from the prose alone or substitute another stickman. Preserve the exact head/body contours, proportions, bold outlines and role-prop geometry. Uniform scaling, deterministic posing and scene placement are allowed; a non-DOM renderer must faithfully port this geometry rather than inventing replacement characters. Keep timeline-driven idle, work and reaction behavior consistent with the performance rules. This metadata contains all required drawing code; no application source files or imports are needed.

Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. > A drawn director and a backstage crew tell the story through distinct cues, props and a stable presentation space.

## Visual identity
Keep the director and crew readable as different roles in a continuous stage. Stage a continuous backstage manga with the established faceless crew and a persistent director beside the presentation board.

## Surfaces and construction
Reuse the required character layers, props and anchored backdrop. Use white cutout bodies, bold outlines, halftone scenery and role-specific props at fixed proportions. Keep panel borders, figure drawing, speed marks and screen tones as separate layers. Keep the contrast of the black ink independent from the density of the tone so a new crop preserves the drawing.

## Colour roles
Separate crew, key display activity and background illustration by value. Keep white paper and dark ink dominant. Use #F47B45 only for the existing activity and optional opening accent roles.

Example palette. background #FFFFFF, foreground #151515, reaction #F47B45.

## Lettering and captions
Fit approved dialogue into a balloon with a clear speaker tail. Give enabled subtitles a quiet area away from the drawing's strongest blacks and effects. Keep any enabled stage dialogue, crew status and narration captions in separate regions.

## Timing and movement
Lay out a readable manga panel, then change acting drawings or crop on the decisive gesture. Keep any panel effects tied to the visible action and leave a settled beat for reading. Give each backstage crew member an independent cue-based schedule for travel, work, reaction and settling. Hold idle characters in their positions and preserve the reading holds for a scene or status board.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep one film-set orientation as boards and backgrounds travel right to left. Maintain the director's place in the wide and crop only where the crew action stays clear.

## Sound options
If the idea enables speech, time the director's lines to approved script cues. If effects are enabled, cue visible crew actions. If enabled, give specific work and prop contacts distinct cues.

## Characteristic actions
Take an assigned crew member to its practical task, then return it while the board carries the next beat.

Let one crew action finish before showing its consequence on the board.

## Review checks
Inspect panel order, letter clearance and the strongest held pose in the same pass. Verify that generated drawing layers reproduce at a direct seek. Check cast proportions and props, storyboard attendance, balloon clearance and one optional opening title. Check role poses, gazes, timing and visibility against the approved storyboard.

## Implementation tools
Keep crew cues and scenery paths independent and validate direct and backward seeks. Use the existing storyboard timing and role-specific pose rules with independently keyed crew, board and scenery layers. MANDATORY CHARACTER IMPLEMENTATION. Use the HTML and CSS in tech.reference_implementation.files for the crew. Keep its proportions and props and do not redraw the cast from the prose alone. Use the defined cue fields and do not add unvalidated fields to STORYBOARD.json.

## Project choices
Choose a backstage task with a visible sequence and a clear outcome. Adapt the production tasks, diagrams and story to the idea while preserving established crew identity.

styles.visual_cues: Cassette Futurism: the 1970s–80s imagined spaceship and mission-control console, a hardware-first branch of Retrofuturism rather than cyberpunk, vaporwave or Y2K. Compose a modular dashboard of chunky charcoal and olive panels set into beige plastic cases with visible screws, seams, vents and black or white embossed labels, banded by restrained amber, orange and rust livery stripes. Recessed black CRT screens glow in ONE phosphor per screen — green #74FF9A or amber #FFB23E — with modest scanlines, soft glow, a screen-bounded vignette and seeded deterministic noise. Use monospace or pixel-like type from locally available system mono fonts: condensed uppercase panel labels such as NAV, PWR and SYS, numbers, timecodes and segmented readouts. Physical hardware carries the scene: cassette tape reels and transport, toggles, knobs, square keys and indicator lamps. Red appears only for warnings. Motion is typed text, 12fps stepped hardware actions, a brief boot flicker and short channel-static transitions that resolve into readable holds. Avoid continuous strobing, smooth generic easing, pink or purple neon, glassmorphism, gradient blobs and round flat cards.
styles.note: Authored by Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) on 2026-10-18 from a user-specified creative brief; not extracted from external reference footage. A distinct, period-specific branch of Retrofuturism (style-065) fixed to 1970s–80s spaceship console hardware, which applies CRT / Analog Video Effects (style-066) only as a screen-bounded display treatment. Not Cyberpunk, Vaporwave or Y2K Design.

tech.implementation: Build each console as real hardware modules, not a flat UI: HTML/CSS grid or absolute layout for module placement and real text; SVG for beige cases, charcoal/olive panels, screws, seams, vents, embossed label plates, livery stripes, cassette window, reels, tape path, heads, toggles, knobs, square keys, lamps and seven-segment readouts; Canvas 2D only for seeded screen noise when SVG specks are insufficient. Use code-drawn geometry only; no external images, photographs or downloaded fonts. Set type with generic monospace or locally installed system mono fonts and verify fallback metrics; give CRT text a fixed character advance (for example textLength per typed substring) so typing never reflows. Panel labels are condensed uppercase (horizontal scale or narrow mono) with letter spacing; embossing is a 1px offset highlight or shadow copy, not a glow. CRT treatment (the style-066 CRT / Analog Video Effects vocabulary, confined to screen glass): one phosphor per screen, green #74FF9A or amber #FFB23E on a near-black screen; scanlines about 3–4px apart at 720p at modest opacity; a short blur glow merged under sharp glyphs; a radial vignette clipped to the rounded screen; static noise from a seeded generator evaluated by 12fps step index, never Math.random or wall clock. Keep scanlines, glow, noise and vignette inside the bezel and keep phosphor text at or above 4.5:1 on the composited screen. Red is warning-only: master caution lamps, fault legends and alarm readouts, paired with a text label; never stripes, titles, idle lamps or decoration. Motion: derive every visual state from absolute composition time quantized to 12 steps per second (step = floor(time × 12)); hold each pose for the whole step instead of tweening with smooth generic easing. Toggles and keys snap within one step; knobs turn in detents; tape reels rotate by fixed angles per step at different rates as the supply pack shrinks and the take-up pack grows; counters, timecodes and segmented gauges step to new values. Typewriter text reveals characters in order beside a block cursor, then holds the completed line. A boot flicker lasts at most a few steps (about 0.3s) and never repeats as a strobe. A channel-static transition between screen pages lasts about three steps (≈0.25s): a bounded band of seeded static and a small horizontal line offset inside the bezel, then a stable readable page. Allow full reading holds after typing and after each page change; vary quick snaps with deliberate holds; do not animate everything at once. Build a single time-state function that returns every module's pose and readout for an arbitrary time, apply it to the scene from one paused seekable timeline, and verify identical frames for forward, backward and direct seeks, including a fresh page. styles.executable_prompt_template:
> A hardware-first console tells the story through chunky controls, physical state changes and recessed CRT readouts.

## Visual identity
Show the physical operation of a period-influenced instrument. Build a hardware-first mission console with chunky modular controls and recessed CRT instruments.

## Surfaces and construction
Use chunky controls, recessed glass and believable hardware joins. Use charcoal or olive panels, beige cases, screws, vents, seams, cassette transport and tactile controls.

## Colour roles
Reserve a clear display accent for the active state or warning. Keep amber, orange and rust in the existing accent roles. Each CRT uses one approved phosphor. Reserve #D7322B for labelled warnings.

Example palette. background #1A1C18, foreground #ECE3CC, panel charcoal #2E302B, panel olive #4B5038, case beige #CFC2A2, label black #121311, crt black #060907, phosphor green #74FF9A, phosphor amber #FFB23E, stripe orange #E2762B, stripe rust #9A4526, warning red #D7322B.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved labels using the physical scale of the buttons, tags and display. Keep fine lettering away from glare and enforce visible units for approved measurements.

## Timing and movement
Show a control's idle position before it travels, clicks into a detent and changes the display. Keep subsequent readout movement on the same device clock and hold the new state. Give display start-up a short flicker that resolves to a readable state. Key the moving physical controls in steps where it helps the cassette-era treatment.

## Framing and viewpoint
Show the physical input and display response together with a slight view into the recessed glass. Use a whole panel view and close in on the active control only when it helps.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, match a detent, relay or tape transport cue to the visible hardware action. If enabled, separate mechanism clicks from display feedback. If effects are enabled, give the selector a detent click and the spinning or scanning mechanism a quieter sustained texture. Time both from the visible hardware so the display changes after the control engages.

## Characteristic actions
Operate a physical control, show its cassette or indicator movement and let the CRT update after it.

Operate a switch and hold until the CRT or indicator confirms the result.

## Review checks
Inspect detents, labels and indicator values at the moment of change. Check glow and scan effects at the nearest framing so the readout remains crisp. Check phosphor count, warning colour usage, stepped motion and text clarity after the transition. Check that material contact, travel and readout states agree.

## Implementation tools
Key hardware position and display response as named states on the same clock. Use a bounded CRT layer with seeded scan or grain effects plus independent keyed hardware and readout states.

## Project choices
Choose a hardware operation or short mission sequence with readable status. Choose a vehicle bay, control room or instrument panel with consistent 1970s or 1980s hardware cues.

styles.visual_cues: Terminal Lyric Duotone Anime: a flat anime music-video grammar in which every composition sits on a CRT-style terminal screen and the subject is read as data. Despite the traditional 'Duotone' name it is a strict three-ink tritone: ultramarine, cream and near-black as hard-edged posterized flat shapes with no gradients, rendered shading or soft airbrush; supplied anime character and scene illustrations appear mostly as held poses staged like cutouts (slow push, rotation, scale, translucent hologram states). Red is a reserved accent for warnings and dark emotional peaks only, used briefly; a whole-frame negative inversion or a short red palette swap may mark one peak. Frame every shot with a mild CRT finish: an oval dark vignette, fine scanlines, seeded grain and thin corner brackets, a §NN section header at top centre and a small audio meter at bottom left. Captions are bilingual monospace lines at the bottom (English above, Chinese below) whose characters resolve from seeded scrambled glyphs into the exact copy with a fine underline that grows like a progress bar; keywords are tinted signal blue (or red at warning beats). One keyword per section may be promoted to a large hero title that enters with a brief RGB-offset split and settles inside a thin elliptical ring. HUD overlays — detection boxes, specimen cards, feature maps, scan percentages, counters — annotate the subject with authored, labelled-illustrative data. Cut to a new composition every few seconds with plain cuts or brief glitch cuts, then hold long enough to read. Avoid gradients, glossy cel shading, neon rainbow palettes, continuous glitching, strobing flashes and illegible microtext.
styles.note: Authored by Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) on 2026-10-18 from Claude Opus 5.5's frame analysis of a user-supplied anime-style music video (1 fps overview plus six 6 fps dense windows; no audio, no transcription). The entry records reusable visual and caption rules only: the source character, creature, song, lyrics, artwork and title are content, are not reproduced and must not be imitated. Colour values are authored defaults, not measured source hex. The traditional 'Duotone' label is kept, but the ink system is a blue/cream/black tritone with a reserved red accent. Related to Anime (style-033), CRT / Analog Video Effects (style-066), Glitch Art (style-067), Kinetic Typography (style-093) and Futuristic UI (FUI) / HUD Design (style-112), none of which fixes the three inks, red reservation, terminal frame layout and bilingual decode-caption grammar together. Review record: assets/catalog/reviews/terminal-lyric-anime.json.

tech.implementation: Separate three layers. (1) Artwork: use supplied, rights-cleared anime character and scene illustrations, or purpose-drawn original art, already in the three inks; posterize existing art to ultramarine/cream/near-black only when the user is authorised to alter it. Do not generate character animation in code: stage held poses as cutouts with slow push, rotation, scale and opacity, and pre-render any drawn in-betweens. A code-drawn bust or silhouette is acceptable only as a clearly labelled illustrative placeholder. Never claim AI-generated or reference footage. (2) Frame and HUD (HTML/CSS and SVG, Canvas 2D for grain): a CRT finish of an elliptical radial vignette, scanlines about 3px apart at modest opacity and seeded grain evaluated from a frame or step index, never Math.random or wall clock; thin cream corner brackets; a §NN section header at top centre; a small audio meter at bottom left whose bars come from authored or seeded per-step levels (do not claim beat sync without measured audio). Detection boxes, specimen cards and counters use cream hairlines on near-black with monospace labels; mark invented data illustrative. (3) Typography and motion (GSAP paused timeline, Scrambled Text Reveal or a cached seeded glyph table): bilingual captions in a monospace English line over a CJK line from locally available system fonts (verify glyph coverage; use @font-face local() names, never downloaded fonts). Each character shows a seeded scrambled glyph until reveal_i = t0 + i·dt, then the exact character; the underline length equals caption progress; keyword spans take signal blue. Hold the resolved caption long enough to read. A keyword hero title reuses Glitch Type Build (motion-036): enter with a decaying RGB offset (red and blue copies offset by a few pixels, scale settling to 1), then draw a thin cream ellipse ring around the settled title. HUD readouts build with Data Build (motion-030), scene changes use plain cuts or a brief seeded Glitch Cut (motion-020), closing code can use Terminal Typing (motion-022), and searching or erasing beats may use Rotating Sonar-Sweep Reveal (motion-047) or Pixel-Tile Materialize & Targeted Delete (motion-048). Red stays reserved for warnings and peaks; limit negative inversions and flash montages to brief, photosensitivity-safe events (no more than about three flashes per second). Derive every state from absolute composition time through one pure time-state function with one owner per property, and verify identical frames for forward, backward and direct seeks, including a fresh page. Twirl distortion or radial motion blur, if requested, needs a WebGL/GLSL shader or pre-rendered frames. Relationship: narrower than Anime (style-033) by fixing three inks and the terminal caption grammar; borrows CRT / Analog Video Effects (style-066) only as a mild finishing layer and Glitch Art (style-067) only at transitions; its HUD is narrative, unlike functional Futuristic UI (style-112). styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Held anime drawings appear as information on a CRT-style terminal, with a strict three-ink base and brief warning accents.

## Visual identity
Make held anime poses read as deliberate terminal imagery. Stage mostly held anime drawings as data on a restrained CRT-framed terminal composition.

## Surfaces and construction
Separate drawn cels, terminal glass and readable signal information. Use hard-edged posterised artwork, subtle scanlines, fine corner marks and explicitly illustrative diagnostic graphics.

## Colour roles
Preserve the limited ink roles and use warning accents only when relevant. Keep the artwork in the existing ultramarine, cream and near-black inks. Use signal blue for lit annotations and warning red for reserved peaks.

Example palette. background #06070B, near black #0D0F16, ultramarine #2747C8, cream #F1E8D2, signal blue #7A93FF, warning red #F0473A.

## Lettering and captions
Set approved lyrics or captions in a steady reading lane with a separate intensity from the image. Keep line breaks intact through type-on or character pose changes. Keep any enabled lyric highlights on the selected line and preserve its original wording.

## Timing and movement
Let the terminal state appear in discrete writes while the held anime pose changes on its own cadence. When music is enabled, choose specific lyric or image transitions from the song's phrase boundaries. Use a brief signal cut at a marked change or peak, then let the recovered image and words remain steady.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the terminal surround stable and use restrained internal pushes or cutout turns. Frame a clean screen, then move to the detail that carries the change.

## Sound options
Use only the idea's authorised music, speech and effects. Show an audio meter only with meaningful project cues or a clearly illustrative display. If a soundtrack is enabled, use only the requested lyric or audio timing.

## Characteristic actions
Resolve a seeded glyph scramble into approved copy and promote a selected keyword within a brief bounded offset.

Hold the pose, reveal a status change or let a terminal state frame the subject.

## Review checks
Inspect the densest text and brightest part of the duotone shot. Compare the intended word and pose changes at a direct seek and with the audio muted. Check ink count, reserved red, caption accuracy and readable holds. Inspect for strobing and persistent glitch. Check flat ink separation and readability before display effects are added.

## Implementation tools
Keep cel exposure, terminal state and text timing separately seekable. Use registered hard-edge art layers, deterministic glyph schedules and bounded CRT effects. Keep text editable. Schedule the type, pose changes and scan effects independently. Keep terminal glyph coordinates discrete and anchor the duotone hatch to the drawing rather than the screen crop.

## Project choices
Choose a pose or image that reads as data and preserves the requested audio behaviour. Choose original actors and section data that fit the idea and use its approved lyrics or captions where present.

candidates.usage_guidance: Keyword hero titles: the promoted lyric keyword enters with a decaying RGB-offset split and scale settle, then a thin cream ellipse ring draws around the settled title and holds. Repeated word stamps at scattered positions are a layout parameter of the same motion.

Adapt as a brief timeline-driven glitch cut between compositions: one or two seeded slice frames, optionally red-tinted at a warning beat, then a clean readable frame. Never continuous or strobing.
Closing or opening code lines on the terminal screen: cursor typing on a fixed monospace grid in cream, then a reading hold. Lyric captions use the scramble decode instead, not a cursor.

Searching or closing beats: one clockwise sector beam around a fixed pivot over a held three-ink illustration, clear inside and dark dot matrix outside, with the caption and header kept readable above the mask.

Loading or erasing a character: tiles of one supplied illustration converge into the full image, or a red selection box deletes fixed cells of a memory grid while a terminal progress bar in the caption advances; cells stay empty.

Preserve authored transforms, fixed backgrounds and reading layers. For an opening or gallery demo, prefer motion-016 when separable illustration and text layers exist; animate both focal objects and meaningful lettering.

palette.direction: A dark CRT screen around flat three-ink art: ultramarine, cream and near-black, with signal blue for on-screen keyword text and red reserved for warnings and peaks.
constraints: Choose the screen surround from the scene; #06070B is an illustrative swatch. The artwork itself stays three inks: ultramarine #2747C8, cream #F1E8D2 and near-black #0D0F16, as flat hard-edged shapes with no gradients.
Signal blue #7A93FF is the lit on-screen form of ultramarine for keyword text, HUD lines and rings on near-black; it is not an additional fill ink for artwork.

styles.visual_cues: Particle Flow Network: a stable node-link diagram in which transfer is shown as streams of fine particles travelling along curved connections between circular hubs. Hubs sit in branching clusters around one or a few primary nodes; node size and a soft halo carry importance, and a small set of semantic state accents (active, idle, waiting, fault) mark status alongside text labels. A sparse dotted field and a quiet dark or paper-light surround keep the graph legible. Particle density, direction and speed communicate volume and flow; the layout itself does not drift. Typography is compact and technical: short node names with small secondary metadata in a monospace or neat sans. Applies to knowledge maps, biological pathways, logistics routes, team collaboration and cause-and-effect systems, not only software. Avoid neon rainbow networking clichés, random floating dots with no source or destination, dashboard chrome without a graph, crowded unreadable labels and constant flashing.
styles.note: Authored by Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) on 2026-10-20 from observation of two user-supplied screenshots and four chronological frames of a 7-second, 84-frame GIF: https://github.com/tomtomsatnav/agent-orchestration-standard/blob/main/docs/screenshots/01-graph-dark.png, https://github.com/tomtomsatnav/agent-orchestration-standard/blob/main/docs/screenshots/02-graph-light.png and https://github.com/tomtomsatnav/agent-orchestration-standard/blob/main/docs/hero.gif. The entry records reusable visual and motion rules only; no source code, layout, labels, data, product name or branding is reused. Colour values are illustrative defaults, not measured source hex. Related to Particle Art (style-062), Scientific Visualization / Data Storytelling (style-097) and Futuristic UI (FUI) / HUD Design (style-112), none of which fixes a stable node-link layout with particle streams that carry meaningful source-to-destination transfer.

tech.implementation: Author the graph first: a fixed node list (id, position, radius, cluster, state) and an edge list with an explicit source, destination and curve (quadratic or cubic Bézier control points), sized for video with roughly 7-20 visible nodes and labels that never overlap streams. Render the dotted field, edges, halos, nodes and labels in SVG or HTML/CSS; draw particles in Canvas 2D (or SVG for low counts). Each particle has a seeded edge, phase, lateral offset and size; its position is p = curve(edge, frac(phase + t·speed)) plus a perpendicular offset that narrows near both endpoints so streams leave and enter nodes cleanly. Evaluate everything from absolute composition time with a seeded PRNG; never Math.random, wall clock or free-running loops. Script beats as states of one timeline: activation (source halo and state accent rise), transfer (stream density ramps along the edge), arrival (particles converge, destination pulses once, counter or label updates), settle (density returns to idle level) and overview (hold the whole graph readable). Node emphasis changes by halo, ring and fill, not by moving nodes. Mark any counts or states as authored or illustrative unless the user supplies measured data; never imply live telemetry. Use one owner per animated property and verify identical frames for forward, backward and direct seeks. Use the user's chosen renderer when specified.
alternatives: SVG dotted strokes (stroke-dasharray with round caps and animated dash offset) for low particle counts or static frames
Pre-sampled curve lookup tables cached per edge instead of evaluating Bézier math per particle
PixiJS or WebGL point rendering only when particle counts exceed what Canvas 2D can draw at the target frame rate

tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Moving particles travel along a stable network and show the direction and amount of transfer through each connection.

## Visual identity
Make each visible stream explain transfer between actual endpoints. Show transfer through visible streams along stable node-link connections.

## Surfaces and construction
Use stable node positions and particle paths anchored to the connections. Use fixed branching hubs, gently curved edges and sparse supporting field marks.

## Colour roles
Code flow and state consistently and reserve high contrast for the active route. Assign role colours to field, nodes, particles and alerts. Pair states with a label, ring or icon.

Example palette. background #0B0F17, field dot #2A3242, node idle #7D8698, node active #E2B66B, particle #E9E1CF, text primary #ECE7DC, text secondary #9AA3B5, accent alert #E8705F, foreground #ECE7DC.

## Lettering and captions
Use approved labels next to stable nodes and keep units close to the value. Place them away from the densest flow traces.

## Timing and movement
Emit particles from the reason a flow starts, let them travel along the connections, and update the destination when they reach it. Stop or thin a path after its last meaningful arrival.

## Framing and viewpoint
Keep the topology fixed in the frame and enlarge one branch only if its context remains visible. Hold the network wide before following the route to its result.

## Sound options
If effects are enabled, cue a meaningful transfer or state change once and keep normal particle traffic quiet. If enabled, cue representative arrivals rather than every particle.

## Characteristic actions
Emit a stream from one named source and show it receive and branch at the next hub.

Start a pulse, show it branch and hold the resulting change at its target.

## Review checks
Check a particle's arrival against the destination state. Inspect the densest branch to ensure a thinner or inactive path still differs from an active one.

## Implementation tools
Derive flow speeds and phase from an explicit timeline or graph model. Compute particle positions from deterministic time on existing connection paths and key node states separately. Represent routes as fixed paths with start and end events. Compute tracer position from progress along a route, and drive node intensity and totals from the same arrival event.

## Project choices
Choose a connected system with a readable source, branch and destination. Use domain-appropriate labels for a knowledge, logistics or cause-and-effect network.

styles.visual_cues: Vintage Rubber Hose Animation: early sound-era hand-inked cel cartoons. Strong, irregular ink silhouettes and organic, slightly imperfect contours vary in line weight. Build focal subjects from interlocking asymmetrical drawn masses, varied contour rhythms, angular and curved features, overlapping forms, inset details and coherent perspective. Resolve secondary structure at delivery size while keeping the silhouette readable. Colour the hand-inked forms with flat cel fills and bold painterly or cel shadow masses, preserving articulated geometry and surface planes. Where scenery is present, stage foreground silhouettes, midground subjects and receding background planes with distinct light/dark values, atmospheric separation and restrained parallax. Integrate directional light, contact shadows and selective edge highlights into the drawn forms. Distribute dense detail around the focal action and quieter shapes around reading areas. Scenery and architecture must be expressive, warped and asymmetric, with leaning shapes and layered atmosphere. Environmental acting is mandatory wherever scenery is present: architecture rocks and its structural parts flex or skew, while trees sway and their branches move independently. Adapt these behaviours to the chosen setting, with deliberate readable holds; a static environment with only moving texture does not satisfy this style. When characters appear, they may be any original human, animal, robot, object or environmental subject, built from rounded elastic masses with curved, jointless rubber-hose limbs and broad theatrical expressions; keep one consistent design per project and never resemble an existing cartoon character or mascot. Shots without characters, such as landscapes or buildings, are equally valid, and architecture need not become round. Motion is hand-drawn acting: expressive elastic poses, anticipation, squash and stretch, overshoot, curved arcs and playful, rhythmic, jazz-like timing, with readable holds and no mandatory perpetual bounce. Drawings are stepped, typically 12 unique drawings per second against a 24 fps film reference, adapted to the project's delivery settings. Use charcoal ink, muted grey and brown middle values, aged ivory light accents and deliberate dark shadow masses as the default tonal structure. Recolour only when explicitly requested for this style's assigned scenes, preserving the defined tonal contrast; palettes assigned to other scenes must not bleed into this style. The only optional effects, used only where a project needs them, are film wear and a vintage film-leader countdown. Avoid clean corporate vector icons with grain pasted on top, neon, glossy gradients, modern 3D rendering, photorealism and fixed-grid pixel art unless explicitly requested.
styles.note: Authored by Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) on 2026-10-21 from a user-supplied example brief and user-provided reference images (a cartoon drawing, a film leader and a description of rubber-hose traits); only stylistic properties were extracted, and no depicted characters, buildings, compositions, text or images are reused. Not application-authored. Self-contained visual metadata revised on 2026-10-23. The written drawing, tonal and acting requirements define the reusable style for any original subject or setting. Sample subjects and sequences are optional examples. Distinct from Rubber Hose Animation (style-034) and related to Traditional Cel Animation (style-081).

tech.implementation: Core drawing (always): Build focal subjects from interlocking asymmetrical drawn masses, varied contour rhythms, angular and curved features, overlapping forms, inset details and coherent perspective. Resolve secondary structure at delivery size while keeping the silhouette readable. Colour the hand-inked forms with flat cel fills and bold painterly or cel shadow masses, preserving articulated geometry and surface planes. Where scenery is present, stage foreground silhouettes, midground subjects and receding background planes with distinct light/dark values, atmospheric separation and restrained parallax. Integrate directional light, contact shadows and selective edge highlights into the drawn forms. Distribute dense detail around the focal action and quieter shapes around reading areas. Construct an original staged illustration from the subject, story and supplied project assets, using this written metadata as the complete visual contract. Scenery and architecture must have expressive warped, leaning or asymmetric construction suited to the subject. Build depth from layered atmospheric planes with subtle parallax. Environmental acting is mandatory wherever scenery is present: rock architecture about its base and flex or skew structural parts; sway trees and animate branches independently. Give equivalent scenery elements their own restrained elastic squash, sway or lean cues in other settings. Author explicit environmental key poses and readable holds; moving texture alone is insufficient. Author the artwork as drawn vector shapes or supplied hand-drawn cels, not generic icons with texture added afterwards. Characters (only when present): adopt or design the project's original subject (human, animal, robot, object or environmental) on one construction sheet: rounded elastic masses, a root that squashes and stretches about its contact point, curved jointless hose limbs drawn as single quadratic or cubic strokes with an ink outline and inner fill, simple hands or ends and replaceable features. Species, costume, occupation, props and shape come from the project. Keep proportions, line weight, colours and costume consistent, note the identity in the storyboard, and reject designs that resemble existing cartoon characters or mascots. Shots without characters are valid. Acting and time: author key drawings (anticipation, squash, stretch, overshoot, settle) on curved arcs rather than continuous tweens, with rhythmic timing and readable holds; idle sway is optional. Derive state from absolute composition time: drawing = floor(time × 12) by default, and a project may choose another drawing rate. Never derive state from a frame counter, so the stepped cadence survives any delivery frame rate (24 fps holds each drawing two frames, 30 fps alternates two and three, 60 fps holds five). Keep delivery resolution, frame rate and duration in the project's settings. Seed every random choice; never Math.random, wall clock or free-running loops. Use one owner per animated property and verify that forward, backward and direct seeks give identical frames. Colour and type: Use charcoal ink, muted grey and brown middle values, aged ivory light accents and deliberate dark shadow masses as the default tonal structure. Preserve the project's exact copy. Recolour only when explicitly requested for these scenes, retaining the defined tonal contrast, flat fills and opacity; keep branding and palettes assigned to other scenes confined to those scenes. A monochrome-to-colour progression is an optional storytelling choice. Cartoon titles and captions use real text in a locally available face chosen for the project; this does not apply to optional film-leader numerals. Drawing acceptance: inspect representative rendered frames at delivery size for articulated focal silhouettes, varied ink weight, overlapping structural details, distinct depth planes where scenery exists, directional shadow masses and controlled highlights. Review the drawn forms with optional surface effects disabled so their structure, lighting and depth remain legible on their own. Inspect motion over time for independent environmental acting, stepped key poses and readable holds. Refine the affected artwork before assembly when these features are missing. Optional effects (only when a project needs them): Film wear: treat it as photographic film material separate from the cartoon artwork. Apply seeded grain, flecks, dust, hairs, thin vertical scratches, subtle exposure variation, slight registration drift and whole-plate gate weave to the entire frame, stepped from a film frame index such as floor(time × 24); optional line boil cycles two or three contour variants of the cartoon artwork only. Vintage film-leader countdown: a separate photographic plate with mechanically precise, centred concentric registration circles and thin crosshair lines fixed relative to each other; large, pale, bold sans-serif numerals with clear breathing room over a darker coordinated ground; a broad, darker, translucent clock-wipe sector rotating behind the numeral and rings; grain, vertical scratches, dust and exposure variation. Gate weave moves the whole plate, never individual rings. Do not give the leader cartoon ink outlines, line boil, serif numerals, decorative paper borders or wobbly circles. Present it as a creative hybrid of historical leaders, not a strict historical reconstruction, and keep any exposure flashes partial and at most three per second. Offer a reduced-motion version with plain cuts. Composition and export use the project's renderer setting. Relationship: Rubber Hose Animation (style-034) is a broader normalized label from a modern retro reference; this entry fixes early hand-inked cel drawing, stepped cadence and the optional film wear and film-leader countdown. It borrows Traditional Cel Animation (style-081) drawing discipline.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
> Elastic limbs, bold ink shapes and decisive pose holds give vintage cartoon actions a clear sense of weight and recovery.

## Visual identity
Use broad silhouettes and curved limbs to tell a physical gag. Establish an action, show its most extreme direction and hold a clear contact or recovery pose before another movement starts.

## Surfaces and construction
Draw elastic curved limbs with a stable ink outline and simple hands, shoes and face shapes. Pin a moving prop to the hand drawing and keep its contact visible through deformation.

## Colour roles
Reserve the strongest values for acting silhouettes and keep background contrast lower. Keep strong silhouette values and avoid busy backdrops during elastic poses.

Example palette. background #F1E3C6, foreground #25221F, ink black #25221F, aged ivory #F1E3C6, sepia brown #856548, dusty grey #77736D, muted rust #B5523A, vintage gold #E8B65B, faded teal #7EA9A3, pale sky blue #B9D8D2.

## Lettering and captions
Keep approved title cards in their own readable beat, with clean lettering and a still border. Place enabled subtitles clear of the longest limb extension.

## Timing and movement
Use a broad anticipation, a limb bend that travels through the action and a clear contact pose. Hold the recovery for a beat and let a small secondary part bounce after the main body stops. Give the body a visible rise and fall in a walk. Break the loop by holding a pose on the actual contact or reaction.

## Framing and viewpoint
Set the action in an eye-level stage wide. Cut close for a reaction, track a running character, tilt with a fall or use a higher unbroken view to relate a problem to its answer. Move across a miniature tabletop or withdraw from a face to show a group reaction. Use an iris or sharp cut with the whole arc inside the frame. Establish a destination prop before the gag reaches it.

## Sound options
If sound or music is enabled, use visible contacts as optional accents and leave pose holds readable on their own. If effects are enabled, match impacts and elastic rebounds to the drawn motion.

## Characteristic actions
- Load weight into an anticipation pose, extend along one arc and land into a readable recoil.
- Roll into an anticipation, stretch through the action and hold the recovery just long enough to read.

Turn a limb bend into a repeating walk, then break the cycle on a visible obstacle or prop. Use a held bend and a clean contact pose to make the change in intent readable.

## Review checks
Check hand-to-prop contact at the most stretched pose. Scrub across squat and rebound to keep the character volume and silhouette readable. The feet or base contact remain readable and the body retains a consistent silhouette language. Check that faces read at the selected scale and feet, hands and props meet at contact.

## Implementation tools
Keep each handle and grip registered to its intended joint through the cel holds. Draw elastic limbs as curves with pinned endpoints and pose them with intentional exposures.

## Project choices
Choose a physical gag, a dance-like action or a prop that changes a character's balance. Use original figures and practical e.g. lift, run or landing. Preserve flexible limbs and grounded weight. Add the only optional effects, film wear and a vintage film-leader countdown, only where the project needs them. Treat either as a separate photographic plate.

styles.visual_cues: Pixel RPG Quest Explainer: a technical or educational explainer staged as a game run in which game-progression UI is the narrative scaffold and every progress element carries meaning. Defining grammar: (1) a persistent HUD that keeps its position across scenes, a framed chip with a short heart row and a collectible counter that only ever rises across the film (in the source it never changed on a visible event; stepping it at authored concept milestones is an optional production choice, never a meaningless count), plus a thin runtime progress bar along one frame edge that grows with elapsed time; (2) chapter breaks as a quest-map card: numbered level nodes joined by a dotted path whose cleared segments take the completion colour while uncleared ones stay muted, held under a dark STAGE N title plate; (3) a cumulative skill-inventory recap: a header and a row of framed slots that fill one at a time as each concept is named, with unfinished slots left visibly empty; (4) pixel dialogue plates: captions sit at bottom centre in a solid dark plate with a stepped pixel border and small accent end caps, sized for the finished line, with keywords in the highlight colour; (5) an original pixel guide character who introduces topics, reacts to results and closes; (6) two working surfaces chosen by content, a dark charcoal-navy surface with a faint pixel grid for code, terminals and mechanisms and a warm cream paper surface with sparse specks for metaphors, maps and the guide, framed by thin corner brackets. Mechanism diagrams are built from whole-pixel blocks (cells, tokens, slots, tables, cards, icons) on a deliberate logical grid; each item keeps one identity colour through a scene, a success colour marks completion and a warning colour with an X mark marks failure. Optional motifs, only where the story needs them: an RPG status panel with a level number and segmented gauge as a premise or recap, a warm sunset bookend, map props such as pixel trees and a castle, treasure or question blocks, a short diamond-lattice pixel wipe between scenes, typed terminal or code windows. Render on a low logical resolution (for example a 4 px grid at 1280 × 720) with integer coordinates, hard edges, no gradients and a limited palette; HUD numbers, titles and labels use bitmap or pixel-style lettering and captions stay crisp and readable. Motion is stepped and purposeful: inventory slots unlock in one step on their narration cue, map cards arrive with cleared segments already drawn, and any authored counter step lands with the concept it marks, diagrams build nodes before connectors, captions type into pre-sized plates, scene changes are hard cuts or a brief pixel wipe, and held states give reading time. Topic, layout, chapter count and colours adapt to each production. Never copy an existing game's sprites, HUD, mascot or map, or any source channel branding, and never show HUD values that do not reflect the story's structure.
styles.note: Authored by Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) on 2026-10-24 from Claude Opus 5.5's frame analysis of a user-supplied pixel-art technical explainer (contact sheets of 35 overview timestamps plus six 3 fps dense windows; no audio, no transcription). Only reusable structural, visual and motion rules are recorded: the source topic, mascot, artwork, captions, title and channel marks are content, are not reproduced and must not be imitated. Colour values are authored defaults, not measured source hex. Distinct from Pixel Art (style-057), which covers pixel rendering only, and from Cassette Futurism (style-137) and Futuristic UI (FUI) / HUD Design (style-112), whose HUDs carry no game-progression meaning; Scientific Visualization / Data Storytelling (style-097) supplies explanation discipline but no visual identity. Review record: assets/catalog/reviews/pixel-quest-explainer.json.

tech.implementation: Separate four layers. (1) Progression model: before drawing, list the concepts and chapters in story order and derive every progress value from that list: the collectible counter only rises and, as an authored choice rather than a source observation, may equal the number of concepts resolved so far, quest-map nodes are cleared for finished chapters, inventory slots unlock in concept order and stay filled, and the runtime bar is elapsed time over total duration. When an authored value changes, change it only at the moment its concept resolves on screen or in narration; a counter that simply holds through a scene is equally faithful to the source; never animate HUD numbers decoratively. (2) Pixel drawing (SVG rects/paths with shape-rendering crispEdges, or Canvas 2D with imageSmoothingEnabled false at an integer scale): choose one logical grid, snap every position and size to it, build sprites and icons from string or index maps with a limited palette, and draw original guide, map props and item icons. HUD numbers, stage titles and labels use a bitmap glyph table or a locally available monospace face declared with @font-face local() names; never download fonts. Grid lines, specks and brackets stay outside letterforms; text sits on solid plates. (3) HUD and captions (persistent top layer): heart row, collectible counter, runtime bar and corner brackets keep fixed positions; the dialogue plate is sized for the finished line before characters type in with Terminal Typing (motion-022), with keyword spans in the highlight colour and a readable settled hold. (4) Motion (GSAP paused timeline driving one pure time-state function): diagrams and counters build with Data Build (motion-030), schedulers or fixed capacity pools may use Step-Tick Slot Refill (motion-049), title letters or the guide may land with Elastic Arrival (motion-027) in whole-pixel steps, and chapter changes are hard cuts or a short seeded pixel wipe. Arrowheads stay hidden until their shafts arrive. Keep stepped motion on whole pixels, limit flashes to brief single events, mark invented numbers illustrative, and verify forward, backward and direct seeks plus rendered frames at delivery size.
alternatives: Canvas 2D at a fixed logical resolution with integer upscaling instead of SVG rectangles
Aseprite sprite sheets for a supplied or purpose-drawn guide character and item icons
Remotion for a verified export limitation
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Prefer SVG or Canvas 2D on one logical pixel grid for scenes, sprites, HUD and diagrams, HTML/CSS for layout and caption text, and GSAP for one paused timeline driving a pure time-state function. Aseprite is optional for authored sprite sheets. Do not add 3D engines, physics or shader stacks; pixel wipes are seeded geometry.

motion_guidance.application: Progress elements never move decoratively: inventory unlocks land on narration cues and any authored counter step lands with a resolved concept; diagrams build nodes before connectors; captions type into pre-sized dialogue plates; chapter changes are hard cuts or a short pixel wipe to a held quest-map card; the guide reacts with small stepped hops.
motion_guidance.cadence_guidance: Brisk, game-like rhythm: stepped whole-pixel moves and discrete counter changes, short slides only for travelling tokens, and a settled hold after every caption, stage card and result. Never pulse HUD elements continuously or flash more than briefly.
motion_guidance.implementation: Evaluate every layer from absolute composition time through one pure time-state function derived from the ordered concept list; snap positions to the logical grid; seed any specks, trees or wipe order; keep one owner per property and verify forward, backward and direct seeks.

style_renderer.selection_basis: Use visual_cues and tech.implementation for styles, or the selected style and this pattern implementation for motion recipes. Select by visual fidelity and medium, not pipeline availability.

motion_engine.selection_basis: Use the authored action, style cadence, trajectory, material behavior, and simulation requirements. Select one owner for each animated property.
